# Silo database: build rules (apply to every table)

**Engine.** PostgreSQL 16 or later, one primary per cell, synchronous standby in a second zone, one read replica for reporting. Extensions: `pgcrypto`, `ltree`, `citext`, `btree_gist`, `pg_trgm`, `vector` (metadata embeddings only). PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of every service.

**Schemas.** `iam`, `gov`, `audit`, `platform`, `connect`, `ontology`, `clone`, `workspace`, `recognition`, `simulation`, `automation`, `files`, `action`, `fde`, `siloes`, `billing`. Global tier (outside cells) uses a separate database: `directory`.

**Primary keys.** `id uuid` generated by the application as UUIDv7 (time-ordered), so inserts append to the right of the B-tree and indexes stay compact. No serial keys except on append-only ledgers, which use `bigint generated always as identity`.

**Tenancy, three layers.**
1. Every tenant table has `organisation_id uuid not null`.
2. Every tenant table has `unique (organisation_id, id)`. Every foreign key to a tenant table is composite: `(organisation_id, x_id) references schema.x (organisation_id, id)`. A row can never reference another tenant's row, even with a bug in the application.
3. Row level security: `enable` and `force` on every tenant table. One policy per table: `using (organisation_id = (select current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid)) with check (same)`. Changed (review 2026-10-28): wrapping it in a scalar subquery lets Postgres evaluate it once per statement instead of per row. Services call `set local app.org_id` and `set local app.membership_id` at the start of every transaction. `set local`, never `set`, so a pooled connection never carries a tenant into the next request.

**Database roles.**
- `silo_app`: what every service uses. No `bypassrls`, no DDL, no `truncate`.
- `silo_audit_writer`: `insert` and `select` only on audit ledgers.
- `silo_migrate`: DDL and `bypassrls`, used only by Fleet migrations and partition retention.
- `silo_report`: read-only on the replica, subject to RLS.
- `silo_credential`: the only role with `select` on the sealed credential columns (`ciphertext`, `nonce`, `dek_wrapped`). Used only by the credential service. Every other service reads `connect.connection_credentials_safe`. This enforces the single-mediator rule in the database.
- `silo_outbox_relay`: reads `platform.outbox` across organisations and updates its publication columns only.
- `silo_auth`: the only role with privileges on `iam.users`, `iam.sessions`, `iam.password_resets`, `iam.mfa_factors` and `iam.user_identities`. Used only by the auth service. Added (review 2026-10-28): the identity section relies on it and this list omitted it.

**Foreign keys.** `on delete restrict` everywhere. Nothing is hard-deleted while audit, receipts or lineage reference it. Removal is a status change plus a `*_at` timestamp. The only physical deletes are retention partition drops and Silo purges, both run as `silo_migrate` and both receipted, plus deletes on the ephemeral tables, which nothing audits or references: `clone.live_subscriptions`, `clone.layout_precomputations`, `workspace.recent_items`, `workspace.favourites`, `workspace.dashboard_tiles`.

**Enumerations.** `text` columns with a `check (col in (...))` constraint, not Postgres enum types, so values can be added without a lock-heavy migration.

**Timestamps.** `timestamptz` always. `created_at timestamptz not null default now()`. Mutable tables carry `updated_at`, set by a shared trigger.

**Polymorphic references are banned.** Where the spec has `grantee_type` + `grantee_id` (or `resource_*`, `target_*`, `subject_*`, `element_*`), use an exclusive arc instead: one nullable typed FK column per target table, plus `check (num_nonnulls(a_id, b_id, c_id) = 1)`. Every reference then has real integrity.

**Record values.** Customer record values may exist in Postgres only in the columns listed below. Each is `bytea`, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a per-organisation data key wrapped by the KMS key (UK HSM in the sovereign cell). Never indexed, never logged, purged with their owning record.
`action.prior_states.value`, `action.mutations.diff`, `action.mutations.manifest_values`, `action.mutation_verifications.intended` and `observed`, `action.revert_conflicts.post_write_value` and `current_value`, `action.receipts.document`, `simulation.staged_action_bases.base_value`, `workspace.ask_turns.question`, `siloes.transitions.previous_value` and `new_value`, `siloes.silo_baselines.last_observed_value`, `siloes.silo_extractions.value`. Added (review 2026-10-28): `simulation.staged_action_bases.staged_value`, `automation.automation_run_state.previous_value`, `action.mutations.intent`, because each holds record values in its domain.
This closes three stress-test findings: `mutations.diff`, `staged_action_bases.base_value` and `ask_turns.question` were plain text or jsonb in the spec.

**Append-only ledgers.** Trigger rejects `update` and `delete`; grants are `insert, select`. Range-partitioned by month on the time column; primary key `(id, occurred_at)`; no foreign keys into them. Retention is a partition drop by `silo_migrate`. Changed (review 2026-10-28): every range-partitioned table also has a default partition, so a write is never refused for its date. A daily job runs `platform.maintain_partitions()` as `silo_migrate`: it keeps partitions at least `create_ahead` units ahead (three months; fourteen days for the outbox) and moves any row that reached a default partition into a partition of its own. It alerts through `platform.partition_status()` when a table is behind or its default holds rows. The linter fails a range-partitioned table without a default. Tables: `audit.audit_events`, `audit.auth_events`, `clone.render_selections` (Changed (implementation 2026-10-28): the clones section defines it in `clone`), `billing.token_transactions`, `platform.model_calls`, `iam.credential_unwraps`, `connect.discovery_probes`, `siloes.transitions`, `action.action_commits`, `gov.lineage_edges`.

**Indexing rules.**
1. Every foreign key gets an index with `organisation_id` leading, `(organisation_id, x_id)`. Changed (review 2026-10-28), actor columns: a foreign key into `iam.users`, `iam.memberships`, `iam.service_principals` or `platform.operators` (who did it: `created_by`, `granted_by`, `revoked_by`, `approved_by` and the like) needs no index for the key's sake. Those rows are never deleted, and the linter checks that no service role holds `delete` on them, so the key is never checked from the referencing side. Such a column is indexed only where a query reads by it ("my proposals", "what did this person change"). Any other exception is stated on its table and carries a `lint:no-index <reason>` comment on the constraint.
2. Every list screen gets `(organisation_id, created_at desc)` or its own sort key.
3. Live-row lookups use partial indexes: `where revoked_at is null`, `where status = 'pending'`, `where archived_at is null`.
4. `ltree` paths use GiST. Name search in Explorer metadata and pickers uses `gin (name gin_trgm_ops)`.
5. Large append-only time columns use BRIN, plus a B-tree on the lookup key.
6. `jsonb` gets a GIN index only where a query filters inside it. Each one is named in its table.

**Speed comes from the architecture, not from tuning.** Postgres holds metadata, policy and receipts only. Query results live in Redis (`redis-data`) and live clone state in Redis (`redis-state`), with persistence disabled. A request touches Postgres for permission resolution (cached per session, keyed by policy version) and a handful of indexed lookups. Targets, untested: p95 under 5 ms for any single metadata lookup, and under 20 ms for full permission resolution on a cache miss.

**Deployment modes.** Added (review 2026-10-28): one codebase serves hosted and customer-run installs. Silo runs as hosted cells and as self-managed installs on customer premises or customer cloud, including air-gapped, from one codebase. A self-managed install is one cell plus its own `directory` database in the same install, with no dependency on Silo's global tier. Keys: `iam.kms_key_versions.provider` accepts `gcp_kms`, `uk_hsm`, `pkcs11_hsm` (a customer HSM over PKCS#11) and `vault_transit` (Vault-compatible transit: HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao). Changed (decision 2026-10-29): Vault is for development only. Production uses Cloud KMS in commercial cells and the UK HSM in the sovereign cell; a Vault for the sovereign cell would have to be backed by the UK HSM, which waits on the sovereign-provider decision. Keys come from Terraform only: the Vault policy grants read on keys and update on encrypt, decrypt and hmac, so it can never create, change or delete a key, and the credential service reads every configured key's metadata at start-up and refuses to start if any is missing. Object storage is any S3-compatible store in place of Google Cloud Storage. BigQuery-backed features (Import row store, Object Index BigQuery baseline, Warehouse, the BigQuery Action ledger) follow the sovereign-cell rule: unavailable unless a local equivalent is configured. Model calls use a self-hosted model route. `pgaudit` and partition maintenance jobs are deployment configuration, not migrations.

**Every table below.** States its purpose, every column with type and null rule, keys, foreign keys, indexes, and security. Domain messages follow in this order: identity and security, platform and audit, Connect, Ontology, clones and workspace, recognition, scenarios, Crons and files, Actions, AI FDE and Siloes, billing, then Redis and BigQuery.
# 01 Identity and security: schemas `iam` and `gov`, and the `directory` database

Spec chapters 55 to 61 (part-09.html). Applies `00_conventions.md` throughout. Tables: 27 in `iam`, 10 in `gov`, 3 in `directory` (separate database), 40 in all. Changed (review 2026-10-28): `iam.user_identities`, `iam.organisation_keys` and `directory.cells` added. One view, `iam.member_profiles`, is defined under `iam.users`.

## Relationships

- `iam.memberships.user_id → iam.users`; `iam.memberships.organisation_id → iam.organisations`
- `iam.sessions.(organisation_id, active_membership_id) → iam.memberships`; `iam.sessions.user_id → iam.users`
- `iam.user_identities → iam.identity_providers, iam.users` (Added (review 2026-10-28))
- `iam.scopes.(organisation_id, parent_scope_id) → iam.scopes`; `iam.scope_memberships → iam.memberships, iam.scopes`
- `iam.role_permissions → iam.roles, iam.permissions`; `iam.role_assignments → iam.memberships, iam.roles`, plus one optional target arc
- `iam.connection_grants.(organisation_id, connection_id) → connect.connections`, plus a grantee arc
- `iam.field_policies → connect.connections or ontology.properties, iam.roles, gov.markings, iam.scopes`
- `iam.service_principals → iam.scopes, iam.memberships (owner), fde.fde_engagements`; `iam.service_principal_roles → iam.roles`
- `iam.credential_unwraps → connect.connection_credentials, iam.identity_providers or iam.mfa_factors`, and `→ iam.users` for `mfa_verify` (Changed (decision 2026-10-29)); `iam.kms_key_versions` is referenced by credentials, MFA factors, identity providers and organisation keys (Changed (review 2026-10-28): organisation keys added)
- `iam.organisation_keys → iam.organisations, iam.kms_key_versions` (Added (review 2026-10-28))
- `iam.policy_versions.organisation_id → iam.organisations` (one row per organisation)
- `gov.clearances → iam.memberships or iam.service_principals, gov.markings`
- `gov.resource_markings → gov.markings`, plus a resource arc over ten target tables
- `gov.purpose_definitions → gov.markings`; `gov.purpose_eligibility → gov.purpose_definitions`, plus a grantee arc; `gov.purpose_sessions → gov.purpose_definitions, iam.sessions`
- `gov.artefact_markings → gov.lineage_nodes, gov.markings, gov.marking_declassifications`
- `gov.lineage_edges.(organisation_id, from_node_id / to_node_id) → gov.lineage_nodes`
- `directory.organisation_directory.cell_id → directory.cells (id)`; `directory.identity_routing.cell_id → directory.cells (id)`. Changed (review 2026-10-28): the directory database has its own `directory.cells`, keyed by `id` text like `platform.cells`.

## Decisions taken in this file

1. **One `iam.organisations`**, merging chapters 26 (calendar, 7 columns), 37 (sharing, 3 columns, two duplicate chapter 56 columns) and 56 (18 columns). The ontology and workspace domains must not define `organisations`; they reference `iam.organisations`.
2. **One `iam.object_type_markings`**, merging chapter 21 (`element_kind`, `element_id`) and chapter 57. Chapter 21's other element kinds map as follows: `link_type`, `action_type`, `function` to arms of `gov.resource_markings`; `interface` added as a new arm of `gov.resource_markings`; `object_set` has no direct marking and takes markings by inheritance in `gov.artefact_markings`. The ontology domain must drop `ontology.object_type_markings`.
3. **`connect.connection_credentials` is not defined here.** Connect owns it (chapters 15 and 61 merged there). This file only references it, and fixes the contract it relies on: the AAD is `(id, organisation_id, connection_id, field_name, purpose)` as the connect section defines it; Changed (review 2026-10-28): `key_version_id` is never in the AAD, because the key version is bound to the wrapped DEK through the KMS encryption context, so rotation re-wraps DEKs without decrypting ciphertext. `last_used_at` is written in the same transaction as the unwrap row in `iam.credential_unwraps`.
4. **`auth_events` is not defined here.** The inventory and chapter 63 place it in `audit`; `00_conventions.md` lists it as `iam.auth_events`. The audit domain decides the schema. This domain only emits its events.
5. **Unwrap audit.** `iam.credential_unwraps` is the system of record for the `credential_unwrapped` event. `audit.audit_events` does not duplicate it; the Governance page unions the two.
6. **`mfa_verify` and `sso_assert` are unwrap reasons.** Changed (decision 2026-10-29), replacing "not unwrap reasons": the closed set is the nine reasons plus `mfa_verify` and `sso_assert`. An MFA unwrap stays in the tenant ledger: `organisation_id` is the organisation being logged into, which login routing resolves before MFA, and `user_id` names the person. `iam.mfa_factors` remains `silo_auth` only (chapter 64.5): the auth service reads the sealed factor and passes it to the credential service, which unwraps it and writes the ledger row. A successful challenge is still recorded in `auth_events` as `mfa_satisfied`. `sso_assert` is an unwrap of an identity provider's secret during an assertion; `idp` stays for other uses of that secret.
7. **Sessions also serve service principals** (chapter 60.5 says an `api_client` exchanges its secret for an opaque session, but the spec table only has `user_id`). `iam.sessions` gets an exclusive arc `user_id` or `service_principal_id`.
8. **`gov.lineage_nodes.ref_id` stays a plain typed reference, not an exclusive arc.** Receipts, Siloes files and exports are purged under chapters 46 and 70 while lineage must remain, and `on delete restrict` on an arc would block the purge. Integrity is held by a `kind` check, the lineage writer inserting in the artefact's own transaction, and a nightly orphan sweep that reports (never deletes). This is the single exception to the exclusive arc rule and needs sign-off.
9. **Extra database role `silo_auth`**. Chapter 64.5 says "only the auth service's role has privileges" on the user-keyed tables, which needs a role other than `silo_app`. Changed (review 2026-10-28): `silo_auth` is now in the conventions role list and covers five tables: `iam.users`, `iam.sessions`, `iam.password_resets`, `iam.mfa_factors` and `iam.user_identities`.
10. **`identity_routing` primary key is `(email_hash, cell_id)`**, not `email_hash`, because chapter 55 states a person has one user record per cell.
11. **SSO identities link by subject, never by email.** Added (review 2026-10-28): `iam.user_identities` binds an identity provider's stable subject (OIDC `sub`, Entra `tid:oid`, SAML persistent NameID) to a user, SSO login resolves the user only through it, and `iam.memberships.scim_external_id` holds the SCIM `externalId`. A first link needs proof by invitation, JIT creation of a new user or the person's existing sign-in in the same flow, so an email claim set by the provider's tenant admins can never take over an existing account.

## How the user-keyed tables are protected

`iam.users`, `iam.sessions`, `iam.password_resets` and `iam.mfa_factors` have no tenant, so tenant RLS cannot apply (chapter 64.5). They are protected by six layers:

1. **Privileges.** `revoke all` from `public`, `silo_app`, `silo_report` and `silo_audit_writer`. Only `silo_auth` holds `select, insert, update` (no `delete`, no `truncate`). The `silo_auth` connection string is held by the auth service alone. `silo_report` cannot read them even on the replica. Added (review 2026-10-28): the same privileges apply to `iam.user_identities`, which is tenant-keyed (RLS standard) but auth-service-only.
2. **Access by key only.** The auth service queries them by `id`, `email`, `token_hash`, `user_id` or `credential_id`. There is no list or scan query. Other services never read them: the gateway reads the Redis hot copy of the session and falls back to an auth service call.
3. **User-keyed RLS as defence in depth.** `enable` and `force` RLS on `users`, `password_resets` and `mfa_factors` with the policy `user_id = current_setting('app.user_id', true)::uuid` (on `users`, `id`). The auth service runs `set local app.user_id` per transaction. Lookups before the user is known (login by email, reset by token hash, session by token hash) go through three `security definer` functions owned by `silo_migrate` (`iam.find_user_for_login(email)`, `iam.consume_password_reset(token_hash)`, `iam.resolve_session(token_hash)`), each returning one row. Changed (implementation 2026-11-01):
- `iam.consume_password_reset(token_hash, password_hash)` also sets the new password, so consuming the reset, setting the password and revoking every session happen in one statement.
- `iam.resolve_session` also returns `issued_at`.
- A fourth function, `iam.find_organisation_for_login(slug)`, returns what a password login needs from the organisation it names (id, status, the MFA and SSO rules, the session timeouts) before `app.org_id` can be set. Password login is per organisation, because sessions and auth events carry one. Changed (review 2026-10-28): the owner is `silo_migrate`, not `silo_auth`, because `silo_auth` is itself subject to the user-keyed RLS and could not perform a lookup before the user is known. `execute` on these functions, and on `iam.list_user_memberships` (under `iam.memberships`), is granted to `silo_auth` only. `sessions` has forced RLS with a `session_owner` policy (its user, or its organisation), because it carries `organisation_id` and spec 64.2 is binding; lookups by token go through `iam.resolve_session` (Changed (implementation 2026-10-28, D20)).
4. **No secrets in clear.** `password_hash` is Argon2id; `token_hash` columns are hashes of random tokens; `ip_hash` and `user_agent_hash` are keyed hashes; TOTP secrets are sealed under the chapter 61 envelope scheme.
5. **Tenant services see profile data only through `iam.member_profiles`**, a `security_barrier` view owned by `silo_migrate` (Changed (review 2026-10-28): not `silo_auth`, for the reason in layer 3) that exposes `membership_id, organisation_id, first_name, last_name, email, avatar_object_key, avatar_content_type, user_status` and filters on `organisation_id = current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid`. `silo_app` holds `select` on the view only. It excludes password, lockout and MFA columns. Changed (review 2026-10-28): the explicit `organisation_id` filter is essential, because the view's owner bypasses RLS.
6. **Detection.** `pgaudit` logs every statement by any role other than `silo_auth` that touches these four tables or `iam.user_identities` (Added (review 2026-10-28): auth-service-only like the four), and alerts on any occurrence. Changed (review 2026-10-28): the alert keys on the session (login) user, not the current user, so the `silo_migrate`-owned definer functions called by the auth service's login do not alert; any login role other than the auth service's that touches these tables still alerts. `silo_migrate` is the only other role that can reach them and runs only inside Fleet.

# Directory database (`directory`, global tier, outside every cell)

No RLS and no customer data: no plaintext email, password material, organisation name or logo. Reads by the login router; writes by the directory service only, called by the cell's provisioning service. Roles in this database: `directory_reader` (select), `directory_writer` (insert, update). No deletes.

### `directory.cells`
Purpose: the directory's copy of the cell registry, written by Fleet. The shape mirrors `platform.cells`. Added (review 2026-10-28): the directory tables reference it and no section defined it.
Columns:
- `id` text, not null. Primary key. The cell identifier, for example `uk-lon-1`. Check `id ~ '^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$'`.
- `kind` text, not null. Check in (`commercial`, `sovereign`, `dedicated`, `self_managed`).
- `residency` text, not null. Check in (`uk`, `eu`, `us`).
- `hostname` text, not null. Unique.
- `status` text, not null, default `provisioning`. Check in (`provisioning`, `active`, `closed_to_placement`, `draining`, `retired`), the same values as `platform.cells`.
- `created_at` timestamptz, not null, default `now()`. `updated_at` timestamptz, not null, default `now()`.
Keys: primary key `id`; unique `hostname`.
References: none.
Indexes: primary key and unique `hostname`. No others.
Security: no RLS, no tenant data. `directory_reader` and `directory_writer` hold `select`; `directory_writer` holds `insert, update`. No deletes. Writer: Fleet.

### `directory.organisation_directory`
Purpose: routes an organisation slug to the cell that holds it. Spec chapter 55.1.
Columns:
- `organisation_slug` citext, not null. Primary key. Changed: `text` to `citext` so case-insensitivity is enforced by type.
- `cell_id` text, not null. Cell that holds the organisation. Changed (review 2026-10-28): not immutable; changed only by the directory service during a tenant migration (6.4, stage `directory_updated`), and audited. `organisation_slug` is the immutable column.
- `status` text, not null, default `active`. Check in (`active`, `suspended`, `closed`). Mirrors `iam.organisations.status`.
- `created_at` timestamptz, not null, default `now()`.
- `updated_at` timestamptz, not null, default `now()`. Added.
Keys: primary key `organisation_slug`.
References: `cell_id → directory.cells (id)`. Changed (review 2026-10-28): the directory database has its own `directory.cells`, primary key `id` text, the same shape as `platform.cells`; this closes the "no cells table" finding.
Indexes: primary key serves the login lookup. No others.
Security: no RLS, no tenant data. Changed (review 2026-10-28): `cell_id` is changed only by the directory service during a tenant migration, and audited; `organisation_slug` is the immutable column. Writer: directory service. Rows are never deleted; closing sets `status`.

### `directory.identity_routing`
Purpose: routes a login email to the cell holding the user record, without storing the email. Spec chapter 55.1.
Columns:
- `email_hash` bytea, not null. HMAC-SHA-256 of the normalised (trimmed, lower-cased) email under a directory-held key. No plaintext email.
- `cell_id` text, not null.
- `hash_key_version` smallint, not null. Added: allows rotation of the HMAC key, which is held in the directory's KMS and never in the database.
- `created_at` timestamptz, not null, default `now()`. Added.
Keys: primary key `(email_hash, cell_id)`. Changed: spec has `email_hash` alone.
References: `cell_id → directory.cells (id)`. Changed (review 2026-10-28): target is `directory.cells (id)`.
Indexes: primary key serves the lookup by `email_hash`. If several rows return, the login asks for the organisation slug and resolves through `organisation_directory`.
Security: no RLS, no tenant data. Dumping the table gives hashes that cannot be reversed without the HMAC key. Writer: directory service, called by the auth service on user creation and email change.
