## Redis keyspaces

Sources: chapters 7.9, 8.1, 8.3, 8.5, 9.2 (part-02.html), 30 (part-05.html), 60.2 (part-09.html). The spec fixes contents, TTLs and persistence. It does not fix key names, eviction policy or byte sizes; those are decisions made in this section and are marked "decision" or "assumption, untested".

### Settings common to the three instances

Three separate deployments per cell, never one shared instance: `redis-session`, `redis-data`, `redis-state`. Each has a primary and a replica in different zones. Losing a Redis node is a normal event: sessions rebuild from Postgres, queries retry, subscription groups take fresh snapshots (12.2, 7.9).

- Persistence disabled on every instance (8.3): `save ""`, `appendonly no`, `repl-diskless-sync yes`, swap and core dumps disabled on the node, TLS in transit, no `dump.rdb` path writable. A starting node checks `CONFIG GET save` and `CONFIG GET appendonly`; `state-plane` refuses to start if either is on (30.7), and the other services apply the same check to their own instance. Where a managed offering cannot guarantee these settings, the instance is self-operated on Kubernetes (8.3).
- TTL on every key. All writes go through one client wrapper that issues the write and `EXPIRE` (or `SET ... EX`) in one command or one `MULTI`; the wrapper has no call that writes without a TTL. A scheduled job scans for keys with TTL -1 and pages on any (8.3, 13.2). The same job reconciles the per-organisation byte counters below.
- Eviction policy (decision): `maxmemory-policy noeviction` on all three. Documented Redis behaviour: with `noeviction`, writes that would exceed `maxmemory` return an error and reads continue; the alternative `volatile-ttl` would silently delete live state, idempotency keys and locks, which breaks the spec rules "refused with the bound named, never truncated" (9.5, 30.5) and "a stale value is never presented as current". Writers treat the out-of-memory error per class: cache writes fail open (skip caching), page writes fail the query with the bound named, capture queue writes become a counted gap, state writes refuse the subscription. Memory alarms fire at 70% of `maxmemory` and admission control starts refusing new subscriptions and new result pages at 85%.
- Key format: `<class>:{<organisation_id>}:<rest>`. The braces are a Redis Cluster hash tag, so all keys of one organisation and class land on one slot and multi-key scripts are legal. Changed (implementation 2026-10-29): keys looked up before the organisation is known (rate limits) are a closed set whose hash tag is the subject, a keyed hash of the address or email, so they spread across slots and never hold the address. Every key belongs to a keyspace declared in `app/server/src/infra/keyspaces.infra.ts` with its instance, schema, TTL cap and size bound; hash field names are camelCase there. Hot-organisation skew is accepted for `redis-data` and `redis-state` and revisited if measured. `redis-state` uses a finer tag, `{<organisation_id>:<group_id>}`, only where noted.
- Access control: one ACL user per service, limited to the key patterns that service owns (listed per keyspace). No service holds `FLUSHALL`, `FLUSHDB`, `KEYS`, `CONFIG`, `DEBUG`; the key audit job uses `SCAN`.
- What must never be stored, all three instances: secrets and credential plaintext, derived credential tokens, prompts and completions, embeddings, audit events, anything from `iam.credential_unwraps`, passwords, MFA material. Record values appear only where a keyspace below says "values".
- Values are serialised as MessagePack (maps) or Redis hashes; no Lua script stores a value outside its declared key.

### `redis-session`

Holds: hot copy of sessions and purpose sessions, and the resolved permission set per session. Never holds record values, secrets or prompts. Postgres is the record of truth; a revoked row is refused even if a copy remains (60.2). Missing key means read Postgres and repopulate. Writers: `auth` (session and purpose keys), `policy` (permission keys). Instance quota (assumption, untested): 100,000 concurrent sessions per cell, 4 GB `maxmemory`.

| Key pattern | Value | TTL | Size bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sess:{<organisation_id>}:<session_id>` | Hash: `membership_id`, `user_id` (or `service_principal_id` for a service principal's session, Changed (implementation 2026-10-29)), `auth_strength`, `policy_version_at_issue`, `issued_at`, `idle_expires_at`, `absolute_expires_at`, `revoked` (0 or 1). No token, no secret. Changed (implementation 2026-11-01): also `token_hash` (SHA-256 of the token, as Postgres stores it, so a request is checked against the copy alone), `idle_minutes` (the idle window: the cell's or the organisation's shorter one) and `mfa_satisfied_at`. `auth_strength` also says where the session stands on MFA. The session token carries the organisation and session ids, so the key is known without a lookup. | Changed (implementation 2026-11-01): until `absolute_expires_at`, with the idle deadline in the hash. A key that vanished at the idle deadline would be rebuilt from Postgres, which keeps no idle clock, and the idle session would come back; a session found idle is revoked in Postgres instead. | 2 KB |
| `sessmem:{<organisation_id>}:<membership_id>` | Set of `session_id` for the membership, so deprovisioning deletes every copy in one operation | Longest TTL among its sessions: extended on add, and each time a session slides; never shortened (Changed (implementation 2026-10-29): refreshing only on add let it expire before a sliding session) | 100 members |
| `perm:{<organisation_id>}:<session_id>:<policy_version>` | Resolved allow set: permission names, scope identifiers, field policy obligations as names. No record values. | Session TTL, capped at 15 minutes (decision) | 64 KB; above it, not cached and resolved each request |
| `purp:{<organisation_id>}:<purpose_session_id>` | Hash: `purpose_definition_id`, `membership_id`, `started_at`, `ends_at` | Until `ends_at` (purpose sessions never renew, 60.2) | 1 KB |

Keying `perm` by `policy_version` means a policy change applies on the next request without invalidation, as chapter 7.7 requires; stale versions expire by TTL. The current `policy_version` itself is not stored in Redis: it arrives on `control.policy` (durable bus) and is held in process memory.

Deprovisioning: one Lua script sets `revoked = 1`, deletes `sess:` keys named in `sessmem:`, deletes `perm:` keys by pattern for those sessions and deletes `sessmem:`. The Postgres revocation commits first.

### `redis-data`

Holds: result pages and result cache, tunnel registry, refresh locks, the capture queue, idempotency keys. Never holds secrets or prompts. Holds record values in result pages, the cache and the capture queue only, with the maximum lifetimes of 8.5 (15, 5 and 10 minutes). Writers: `executor` (pages, cache), `connect-runtime` (tunnel registry), `oauth` (locks), `executor` and `state-plane` (capture queue producers), `siloes-capture` (capture queue consumer), any service (idempotency keys). Per-organisation memory quota (spec 8.1, decision on the figure): 256 MB for pages plus cache, 64 MB for the capture queue, both raised by contract. Instance assumption, untested: 32 GB `maxmemory` per cell.

| Key pattern | Value | TTL | Size bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| `res:{<organisation_id>}:<query_id>:meta` | Hash: `plan_hash`, `permission_fingerprint`, `membership_id`, `status` (running, complete, failed), `page_count`, `row_count`, `bound_hit` (name of the bound or empty), `created_at` | 15 minutes after last read; every page read re-arms meta and the pages read | 2 KB |
| `res:{<organisation_id>}:<query_id>:p:<n>` | One page of rows (values) | Same as meta | 1 MB per page (assumption; set in executor config) |
| `cache:{<organisation_id>}:<plan_hash>:<ontology_version>:<period_resolution>:<permission_fingerprint>` | Changed (implementation 2026-10-29): ontology version and period resolution added, as spec 24.6 requires of every cache key. `query_id` of a complete result plus `computed_at`. A hit requires the `res:` keys to exist; otherwise it is a miss. | 5 minutes default; 0 disables the cache for an organisation and then no key is written. The TTL never exceeds the page TTL. | 200 bytes |
| `tun:{<organisation_id>}:<agent_id>` | Hash: `connect_runtime_pod`, `tunnel_id`, `agent_version`, `connected_at`, `last_heartbeat_at`, `pool_id`, `relay_url` (where other replicas relay its work), `healthy`, `active_calls` (D127) | 30 seconds, refreshed by each agent heartbeat (heartbeat every 10 seconds, three misses unhealthy, chapter 10) | 1 KB |
| `lock:{<organisation_id>}:oauth:<connection_id>` | Random owner token (`SET NX PX`), released by compare-and-delete script | 30 seconds, renewed by the holder while refreshing | 64 bytes |
| `lock:{<organisation_id>}:<purpose>:<resource_id>` | Same, for other refresh locks (conformance re-run, schema refresh) | 30 seconds | 64 bytes |
| `cq:{<organisation_id>}:<silo_id>:<yyyymmddhhmm>` | Redis stream, one per minute bucket. Entry fields: `object_type_id`, `object_ref`, `property`, `value` (values), `observed_at`, `connection_id`, `origin` (query or change stream). Consumer group `siloes-capture`. | 10 minutes from the creation of the bucket key, not refreshed, so no entry outlives the 8.5 limit of 10 minutes | 50,000 entries per bucket and 200,000 entries or 64 MB per organisation, whichever first |
| `cqgap:{<organisation_id>}:<silo_id>` | Hash: `dropped_count`, `first_dropped_at`, `last_dropped_at`. Counts only. | 24 hours, refreshed on each drop | 200 bytes |
| `idem:{<organisation_id>}:<scope>:<idempotency_key>` | Hash: `state` (in_progress, done), `result_ref` (an identifier, not a result) | 24 hours | 200 bytes; 5 million keys per cell (assumption) |
| `rl:{<subject>}:<limit>` | Integer: attempts in a fixed window (login attempts per address or email before the organisation is known). Changed (implementation 2026-10-29): added. | Set by the first attempt, at most 1 hour, never moved | 8 bytes |
| `quota:{<organisation_id>}:<class>` | Integer: bytes in use for class `pages`, `cache` or `capture`, incremented by the writer and decremented on delete; corrected nightly by the key audit job | 48 hours, refreshed on write | 8 bytes |

Notes on the capture queue:
- The queue carries observations, not transitions: the comparison against `siloes.silo_baselines` runs in the consumer. This reorders two boxes of the flow in 67.2 so that the request path does no Postgres access for Capture, which is how "a query never waits on storage" is met. The outcome (a transition only when the value differs, none on first sighting) is unchanged. `siloes.capture` on the durable bus carries only batch references and counts (9.2).
- Bucketed streams make "every wipe drains the queue first" (67.2, 70.3) a bounded operation: the wipe reads the Silo's buckets, writes or discards them, then `UNLINK`s them. Entries are stored once per observed nominated property.
- Over the bound the producer drops the newest observation and increments `cqgap`. The gap count is written to the audit trail at the next drain. A Redis failover loses queued entries without a count; `siloes-capture` records a `capture_queue_lost` marker with the time window when it detects a primary change (decision; the spec says "counted gap" only).
- The capture queue is the one place in `redis-data` that holds values for a Silo that the customer enabled; it carries the Silo's `silo_id` so a purge can find it.

### `redis-state`

Holds: live object state, the subscription registry, sequence numbers, source change de-duplication keys (7.9, 30.2, 18.6). Never holds secrets, prompts or history: only the latest value per input, object and source, never a previous value. Values appear in `st:` only. A value is never written anywhere to keep it longer (30.6). Writers: `state-plane` only; `change-stream` writes de-duplication keys. Bounds (spec): 1,000,000 distinct live objects per organisation by default (contractual on Enterprise), 100,000 objects per subscription, 250,000 per user, 20 concurrent subscriptions per user, 500 Cron watches per organisation, 64 watched properties per type, 50 subscriptions per session. Sizing (assumption, untested): 2.5 KB per live object including per-source entries, so one organisation at the bound holds about 2.5 GB; the cell admits subscriptions while the sum of live objects times 2.5 KB stays under 70% of `maxmemory`. Instance: size per cell from that sum.

| Key pattern | Value | TTL | Size bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| `st:{<organisation_id>}:o:<object_id>` | Hash. Field `_seq` (object sequence number, integer), `_abs_expires_at` (first interest plus 24 hours), `_state` and `_rule_version` (visual state). One field per input and source, named `<input>@<connection_id>`, value `{value, received_at, source_seq}` (values). | Idle 15 minutes after last interest, re-armed by interest, and never beyond `_abs_expires_at`. At the absolute limit the key goes and the next subscriber triggers a fresh read from sources even while watched (7.9). | 2.5 KB average, 16 KB hard cap per object; larger objects are refused with the bound named |
| `st:{<organisation_id>}:m:<connection_id>:<source_key_hash>` | The `object_id` that an exact match key resolves to. Hashed source key, so no source value is stored. | Same as the object it points to | 100 bytes |
| `live:{<organisation_id>}` | Sorted set of `object_id` scored by absolute expiry (epoch seconds). Admission control counts members with score above now (`ZCOUNT`) for the 1,000,000 bound, after `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` of expired members. | 24 hours, refreshed on add | 1,000,000 members |
| `sub:{<organisation_id>}:g:<group_id>` | Hash: `object_set_hash`, `permission_fingerprint`, `projection_hash`, `object_count`, `subscriber_count`, `created_at`. Group id is a hash of organisation, set hash and fingerprint (7.9), so values are never shared across different permissions. Contains no values. | 15 minutes idle after the last subscriber leaves | 1 KB |
| `sub:{<organisation_id>}:g:<group_id>:objs` | Set of `object_id` in the resolved set | Same as the group | 100,000 members |
| `sub:{<organisation_id>}:s:<subscription_id>` | Hash: `group_id`, `holder_kind` (session or cron), `holder_id`, `session_id`, `last_acked_seq`, `connected_at`, `buffer_mode` (live or snapshot). No values. | Viewer: 60 seconds after the page's last heartbeat, re-armed by each 15-second heartbeat (30.1). Cron watch: 120 seconds, renewed by the scheduler lease while the watch is active. | 500 bytes |
| `dedup:{<organisation_id>}:<connection_id>` | Sorted set of truncated SHA-256 of the manifest `dedup_key`, scored by receipt time; entries older than 10 minutes are trimmed on each add | 10 minutes, refreshed on add | 100,000 members (assumption) |

Notes:
- The replay window (60 seconds or 10,000 deltas per subscription) is a ring in `state-plane` process memory, not in Redis (30.6, "in-memory ring"). A `state-plane` node loss therefore loses the ring and the next reconnect gets `resync_required` and a snapshot, which the spec already allows. Subscriptions are re-established from `clone.live_subscriptions` (metadata only) and values re-resolved from sources.
- Losing a Redis primary triggers fresh snapshots (7.9). Nothing is restored from disk because nothing was written.
- Time scrubbing never reads this instance. It reads `siloes.transitions` (30.8).
- Scenario overlay content never enters `st:` keys (30.9).

---

## BigQuery and object storage

Sources: chapters 66.7, 66.8, 68.6, 69.6, 69.12 to 69.23, 70, 48.2 (Action ledger), 8.1, 56.2. The sovereign cell has no BigQuery or GCS (66.8, 69.18): everything below is compiled out there unless a UK-resident equivalent is configured, which is an open decision in the spec. The names `bq-siloes`, `gcs-siloes`, `object-index`, `object-files` and `object-backup` are the store names of 8.1.

### Physical layout

| Store | Where | Granularity | Created by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bq-siloes` (Import rows, Object Index documents) | One shared Google Cloud project per cell, `silo-<cellcode>-siloes` | One dataset per organisation and Silo | `siloes-import` provisioning job at Silo creation |
| Warehouse | One Google Cloud project per organisation, `silo-<cellcode>-wh-<org12>`, in a folder per cell inside Silo's Google Cloud organisation | One dataset, `warehouse` | `siloes-import` at "Create warehouse" |
| `gcs-siloes` | Cell siloes project | One bucket per organisation, `silo-<cellcode>-imp-<org12>` | `siloes-import` at the organisation's first Import or Object Index Silo |
| `object-files` | Cell files project | One bucket per cell, `silo-<cellcode>-files`, path scoped by organisation id | Files domain |
| `object-backup` | Separate backup project | One bucket per cell, `silo-<cellcode>-backup` | Fleet |
| `object-index` | Same as the Object Index datasets above (BigQuery baseline) | Per Silo | `siloes-import` |

Naming rules. `cellcode` is the cell identifier with hyphens removed (`uk-lon-1` becomes `uklon1`). `org12` and `silo12` are the last 12 hex characters of the organisation or Silo UUID without hyphens (the leading characters of a UUIDv7 are a timestamp and collide in time; the trailing ones are random). Creation checks for an existing resource with the same name and a different owner, and retries with 16 characters on conflict. The final resource name is stored in `siloes.siloes.store_ref` and `siloes.warehouse_projects` so purge receipts and audit name exactly what was removed. Project ids are at most 30 characters; `silo-uklon1-wh-` plus 12 is 27. Dataset names use letters, digits and underscores only.

### Residency (all BigQuery datasets and GCS buckets)

- The location is set from the cell's residency configuration and enforced at creation, not checked afterwards (66.8). Defaults: `uk-lon-1` is `europe-west2`, `eu-fra-1` is `europe-west3`, `us-va-1` is `us-east4` (the spec names the first two for the Warehouse and lists the third as a cell; the same rule applies). All are single-region locations; multi-region locations such as `EU` or `US` are never used.
- Enforcement: an organisation policy `constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` on each cell folder allows only that cell's region. A creation call with another location fails in Google Cloud itself, in addition to the refusal in `siloes-import`. A mismatch is refused and audited.
- The location is immutable. `siloes.siloes.location` and `siloes.warehouse_projects.location` equal the dataset or bucket location.

### Encryption (CMEK)

- Warehouse dataset: a customer-managed Cloud KMS key per organisation, in the same region, created by `siloes-import` in the cell's KMS project: key ring `<cellcode>-warehouse`, key `org-<org12>`, set as the dataset default key, automatic rotation every 365 days (chapter 61). Only the BigQuery service agent of the organisation's project and the `siloes-import` and `siloes-capture` service accounts hold `cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter`. Purge deletes the dataset and the project, then schedules destruction of the key versions, so the data is unrecoverable by key as well as by deletion.
- Other BigQuery datasets and all GCS buckets: the per-cell customer-managed key of 8.1, key ring `<cellcode>-storage`, key `siloes`. Decision: the spec asks for a per-organisation key only for the Warehouse; extending it to the Import and Index datasets is possible later and would let a purge destroy a key. Not done now because it multiplies keys per cell by the number of organisations.
- Receipts are additionally encrypted with the organisation application key (8.1); that applies to Postgres, not to the stores here. Values in `bq-siloes` are protected by CMEK and by IAM, not by the application envelope.

### Access (all stores)

- No person at Silo or at the customer has access to any Silo project by default (69.13). Staff access is only through `admin-portal` break-glass operator sessions (chapter 13), time-bound and audited.
- Service accounts, by Workload Identity, one per service: `siloes-capture` (Warehouse history writes only; Postgres Capture needs no Google access) and `siloes-import` (Import, Object Index, Warehouse, GCS). Roles are granted at dataset or bucket level, never at project level: `roles/bigquery.dataEditor` on the dataset, `roles/bigquery.jobUser` on the project, `roles/storage.objectUser` on the bucket with an IAM condition on the bucket name prefix `silo-<cellcode>-imp-`. Neither day-to-day account can create or delete datasets, buckets or projects. Creation and deletion run under a separate provisioning service account used only by the provisioning and purge jobs of `siloes-import`, which is the only account with project creation rights in the cell folder.
- Customer direct SQL (`warehouse.sql_access`, super admin only): a named Google identity gets `roles/bigquery.dataViewer` on the Warehouse dataset and `roles/bigquery.jobUser` on the Warehouse project, applied and removed together with `siloes.warehouse_sql_grants`. Queries are billed to the Warehouse project and flow through at cost plus 10% as bytes scanned. Refused for any dataset containing a marked property, because BigQuery does not enforce Silo markings (69.16).
- Reads for users go through the federated engine, which passes both authorisation gates. The engine's queries are parameterised with BigQuery query parameters, so Cloud Audit Logs, which record query text, never contain a record value. Data Access audit logs are enabled for BigQuery and Cloud Storage in every Silo project and exported to the `object-backup` audit archive. A value found in any log is a SEV1 incident (8.5).
- Purge fail-safe: BigQuery keeps deleted table data for the time travel window and then a further seven days of fail-safe that the customer and Silo cannot read. Silo sets `max_time_travel_hours = 48` (the minimum) on every dataset so purged data leaves time travel after two days. The seven-day fail-safe cannot be shortened by configuration; the disclosure of 70.6 must say that a purge completes at once for Silo and is final at the provider after at most nine days. This needs legal review with the rest of the disclosure copy.
- GCS: uniform bucket-level access on, public access prevention enforced, soft delete retention set to 0 days on `gcs-siloes` buckets so a deletion is final, object versioning on as 8.1 requires with noncurrent versions deleted after 7 days by lifecycle. A file purge deletes every generation of the object explicitly (live and noncurrent), not only the live one (70.2).

### Import rows (`bq-siloes`)

Dataset `imp_<org12>_<silo12>`, in the cell siloes project. One table per object declared in the active definition, named `obj__<object_name>` (object name lower-cased, non-alphanumerics to underscore, at most 64 characters; collisions get a numeric suffix recorded in `siloes.silo_definitions.document`).

Columns of every table:
- `_row_ref STRING NOT NULL`: key of the row; equals `siloes.silo_extractions.row_ref` for provenance.
- `_file_id STRING NOT NULL`: `siloes.silo_files.id`, the lineage to the source document.
- `_silo_id STRING NOT NULL`.
- `_definition_version INT64 NOT NULL`: `siloes.silo_definitions.version`.
- `_received_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL`: copy of `silo_files.received_at`; the partition column.
- `_loaded_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL`.
- `_marking_ids ARRAY<STRING>`: markings propagated from the file and object type (66.10); the federated engine applies them at read time.
- One typed column per declared field, named by the field.
- For each field extracted by a `near` or `inferred` method: `<field>__method STRING` and `<field>__extraction_id STRING` (`siloes.silo_extractions.id`), so the flag, the source location and the model score travel with the value into every representation (68.4). Confirmation sets `<field>__method` to `certain` by batch DML in step with the Postgres update.

Partitioning and clustering: partition by `DATE(_received_at)` (time-unit column, day), `require_partition_filter = true` so a query without a date bound is refused, which is the pruning the planner applies before submission (68.8). Cluster by `_file_id`, `_row_ref`. Purge file is `DELETE WHERE _file_id = @id` over all partitions; retention is a partition drop by received date, run as the sweep (`retention_swept` with counts). Rows are loaded only by batch load jobs from GCS staging (`siloes/<silo_id>/staging/load/...`), never by streaming insert, because rows in the streaming buffer cannot be deleted by DML for a period after insertion and a purge must be able to run at once.

Lineage: file and definition version columns above, plus the Postgres receipts. There is no connection or ontology version column because Import rows do not come through a connector; when an imported object is mapped to an object type, the mapping lives in `ontology.property_mappings`, which carries the ontology version.

### Object Index documents (`object-index`, BigQuery baseline)

The engine is an open decision (69.6). This is the BigQuery baseline design; if Postgres full-text search is chosen the same columns become tables in the `siloes` schema under RLS and this subsection is replaced.

Dataset `idx_<org12>_<silo12>`. One table per live `siloes.index_definitions` row, named `ix__<object_type_api_name>`.

Columns:
- `_object_ref STRING NOT NULL`, `_object_type_id STRING NOT NULL`, `_index_definition_id STRING NOT NULL`.
- One typed column per nominated property (text properties as `STRING`).
- `_marking_ids ARRAY<STRING>`: markings of the object; `_property_marking_ids JSON`: map from property to its markings. Both propagated along lineage (69.5). Search results pass both authorisation gates before return; a property the user may not see is never matched.
- `_row_hash STRING`: hash of nominated values, so a refresh can skip rewriting unchanged documents.
- `_refreshed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL`: partition column and the freshness stated on every result (69.3).
- Lineage: `_connection_id STRING`, `_connector_version INT64`, `_ontology_version STRING`, `_observed_at TIMESTAMP`, with the same meaning as in the Warehouse.

Partitioning and clustering: partition by `DATE(_refreshed_at)` (day); cluster by `_object_ref`. An entry not refreshed within the retention window sits in an old partition, so retention is a partition drop (70.1). Refresh is a `MERGE` from a staged table on `_object_ref`, which writes today's `_refreshed_at` for every entry the refresh observed, and for a scheduled full refresh deletes entries not observed (`WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE`, 69.4). A search index on the text columns is created once the engine decision is made; until then Explorer lists and filters use clustering only. Removing a property from the nomination drops its column at the next refresh and the values go with it. The table is dropped at index purge and at disable (8.1: "dropped at disable"). Not backed up; rebuilt from sources.

Staged batches: `gs://silo-<cellcode>-imp-<org12>/silo/<silo_id>/staging/index/<index_definition_id>/<refresh_id>/part-*.parquet`, deleted after a successful load and by a lifecycle rule at 2 days as a backstop.

### Warehouse (`warehouse` dataset in the organisation's own project)

Project `silo-<cellcode>-wh-<org12>`, dataset `warehouse`, location fixed at creation, CMEK as above, `max_time_travel_hours = 48`. Access only for the two service accounts, plus the optional customer SQL grant.

Tables per nominated object type (names are lower-case snake case of the object type API name; `siloes.warehouse_tables.table_name` records the final name):
- `<type>` (kind `current`): one row per object, current state only. Columns: `_object_id STRING NOT NULL` (the Silo object id), one typed column per nominated property, `_deleted_at TIMESTAMP` (decision: set when the object disappears from its sources, row kept until retention ends; the spec does not say how deletions appear), and the lineage columns below. Unpartitioned, clustered by `_object_id`, because the table holds current state only and is updated by `MERGE` on `_object_id`.
- `<type>__history` (kind `history`): one row per observed change, the same narrow record as Capture. Columns: `_object_id`, `property STRING`, `previous_value JSON`, `new_value JSON`, `_observed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL`, lineage columns. Partition by `DATE(_observed_at)`, `require_partition_filter = true`, cluster by `_object_id`, `property`. Retention: a sweep (audited, with counts) drops partitions older than the window; `partition_expiration_days` is set to the window plus one day as a backstop only.
- `link__<link_type>` (kind `link`), for link types whose both ends are nominated: `_from_object_id`, `_to_object_id`, `_observed_at`, lineage columns. Unpartitioned, clustered by `_from_object_id`, `_to_object_id`.
- `action_ledger` (kind `ledger`), where the customer enabled the ledger: see the next subsection.

Disputed properties (69.14, chapter 23): a disputed property is stored as `NULL` with two sibling columns in `current`: `<property>__disputed BOOL` and `<property>__sources_disagreeing INT64`. The Warehouse never stores a value the ontology would refuse to return.

Lineage columns on `current`, `history` and `link` rows (every row, as the binding rule states): `_connection_id STRING`, `_connector_version INT64`, `_ontology_version STRING`, `_observed_at TIMESTAMP`. On `current` they describe the most recent contributing observation; the per-change lineage of each property is in `history`.

Schema evolution (69.14): an added property adds a column; a removed property is kept until the retention window ends and then dropped; a changed property type adds a new column named `<property>__v<n>` rather than rewriting history. Each change is recorded in `siloes.warehouse_tables.ontology_version_id` and audited as `warehouse_schema_changed`.

Sync (69.15): backfill by bounded pages through the federated engine; incremental from change streams, or a scheduled watermark query where a source has no stream; reconciliation compares row counts and a key sample. All writes are batch load jobs plus `MERGE`, so purges and corrections can delete at once. Freshness is `siloes.warehouse_tables.last_synced_at`; a source that is unreachable marks its rows stale in the engine, never current.

Exit (69.17): either the project is moved to the customer's Google Cloud organisation, or every table is exported as Parquet to `object-files` at `org/<organisation_id>/exports/<export_id>/warehouse/<table>/part-*.parquet`, with `schema.json` and `lineage.json` beside them.

### Action ledger option

The ledger is a queryable copy; the control plane receipt stays the record of authority (48.2, 66.4). It is off by default and is a Silo enablement with its own disclosure.

- Host (decision): the `action_ledger` table of the organisation's Warehouse if one exists (kind `ledger` in `warehouse_tables`); otherwise a table `action_ledger` in the dataset of an Import Silo the enabling person chooses. The hosting Silo carries `action_ledger_enabled_at` and `action_ledger_include_values` in `siloes.siloes`. In the sovereign cell it requires a configured UK-resident store.
- Columns, from 48.2: `ledger_id STRING`, `organisation_id STRING`, `mutation_id STRING`, `receipt_id STRING`, `commit_id STRING`, `action_type STRING`, `generic_edit BOOL`, `risk_class STRING`, `object_type STRING`, `object_id STRING`, `connection_id STRING`, `operation STRING`, `fields ARRAY<STRING>`, `prior_values JSON` and `new_values JSON` (null unless the values option was chosen), `proposer STRING`, `approvers ARRAY<STRING>`, `self_approved BOOL`, `origin STRING`, `outcome STRING` (verified, diverged, failed), `reverts_mutation_id STRING`, `proposed_at TIMESTAMP`, `executed_at TIMESTAMP`. Added: `_marking_ids ARRAY<STRING>` and `_value_marking_ids ARRAY<STRING>` so markings propagate to rows and value columns (48.2); `_written_at TIMESTAMP`.
- Partition by `DATE(executed_at)`; cluster by `object_type`, `action_type`, `object_id`, `outcome`. Require partition filter. Lineage is the set of identifiers in the row (`mutation_id`, `receipt_id`, `commit_id`, `connection_id`).
- Write path: `actions` writes one row per object per Action after the receipt exists, as a batch load every 60 seconds. A receipt purge propagates by `DELETE WHERE receipt_id = @id`; because rows are batch loaded the delete can run at once. Purging a Silo that holds the ledger removes the copy only; control plane receipts are untouched (70.3).
- When the values option is chosen, `prior_values` and `new_values` hold customer values in BigQuery, which 8.5 lists as "Customer warehouses and Action ledger tables"; the dataset's CMEK and IAM apply.

### Cloud Storage bucket layouts

`gcs-siloes`: bucket `silo-<cellcode>-imp-<org12>`, one per organisation (68.6). The spec text in 8.1 says "prefix by organisation and Silo"; 68.6 says "a bucket scoped by organisation". This file uses a bucket per organisation with a prefix per Silo, so IAM, CMEK, residency and removal apply at the bucket boundary and a Silo purge is a prefix delete. Layout:
- `silo/<silo_id>/drop/<source_id>/`: where customers' files land, for both one-off uploads (signed resumable URL, short expiry, issued after the permission and marking check) and watched locations. Names are untrusted and are never reused in a key. `siloes.silo_sources.location` holds this prefix.
- `silo/<silo_id>/files/<file_id>`: the stored file, key equal to `siloes.silo_files.object_store_key`. No filename in the key. Object metadata `x-silo-file-id`, `x-silo-content-class`. `siloes-import` copies from `drop/` to `files/` after type sniffing and deletes the drop object. Asset models and site plans are stored here too (class `asset_model` or `site_plan`) and are never sent to a model.
- `silo/<silo_id>/staging/load/<run_id>/part-*.parquet`: batch loads into Import tables, deleted after load and at 2 days by lifecycle.
- `silo/<silo_id>/staging/index/<index_definition_id>/<refresh_id>/part-*.parquet`: refresh batches.
- Retention: the sweep deletes `files/` objects by `received_at` against the Silo window, with `retention_swept` counts. No bucket retention policy or lock is set, because it would block purge.
- Lineage columns: not applicable to objects; the lineage is `silo_files` plus the metadata above.

`object-files`: bucket `silo-<cellcode>-files`, owned by the files domain, listed here for the Warehouse exit path and the 8.1 settings: no public access of any kind, versioning on, copied to `object-backup`. Prefix `org/<organisation_id>/` then `exports/<export_id>/`, `uploads/<file_id>`, `brand/<key>` (logos and avatars, 56.2). Exports retained indefinitely by default; uploads by the Silo window.

`object-backup`: bucket `silo-<cellcode>-backup`, written only by Fleet jobs, write-once object lock for the stated retention (35 days point-in-time, 12 months monthly, 8.1), prefixes `pg/<cluster>/wal/`, `pg/<cluster>/snapshots/`, `audit-archive/<yyyy>/<mm>/`. The 8.1 rule asks for a second location in the same residency. Google Cloud has one UK region (`europe-west2`), so for `uk-lon-1` the second copy is a separate project and bucket in the same region with its own key, until a second UK location exists; this is an open point for the cell design, not decided here. A restore replays the purge ledger (`siloes.purge_receipts` and the other purge receipts) before opening to traffic (8.2).

### Metering hooks

`siloes-capture` and `siloes-import` report bytes held and bytes scanned per Silo and store from the first day a Silo exists. Sources: Postgres relation sizes for Capture partitions; Cloud Storage object listing sums for GCS; BigQuery `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLE_STORAGE` and job `total_bytes_billed` for BigQuery; the sum of index tables for the index store. Results are written daily to `billing.storage_measurements` with the regional provider cost split into storage, compute and egress. Backfill, sync, reconciliation and refresh queries are billed at cost plus 10% and are never metered as tokens (69.19, 73.2).
# Cross-domain decisions and the one table no domain owned

## `ontology.compiled_manifests`
Purpose: the validated plan structure produced by the compile stage, referenced by saved views, Ask turns and analysis steps (Changed (review 2026-10-28): mutations removed). Every domain referred to a `manifest_id` and none defined it. Spec chapters 26 and 43.
Columns:
- `id` uuid, not null. UUIDv7.
- `organisation_id` uuid, not null.
- `kind` text, not null. `query`, `analysis`. Changed (review 2026-10-28): `mutation` removed; a mutation freezes its own manifest.
- `manifest` jsonb, not null. The Zod-validated plan over object types, properties, filters, joins, periods and bounds. Structure only: literals are placeholders. Changed (review 2026-10-28): the sentence on mutation values removed, since mutations do not use this table.
- `manifest_hash` bytea, not null. SHA-256 of the canonical manifest, 32 bytes.
- `schema_version` text, not null. Manifest schema version.
- `ontology_version_id` uuid, not null. The ontology version it was compiled against.
- `policy_version` bigint, not null. The `iam.policy_versions.version` in force at compile, so a stale plan is detectable.
- `period_expressions` jsonb, null. Relative periods as written, stored apart from their resolution so a saved view re-resolves on each run.
- `compile_class` text, not null. `standard` or `advanced` (the single definition in chapter 73).
- `created_by_membership_id` uuid, null, and `created_by_service_principal_id` uuid, null. Exclusive arc, exactly one.
- `created_at` timestamptz, not null.
Keys: primary key `id`; `unique (organisation_id, id)`; `unique (organisation_id, manifest_hash, policy_version)`. The last one deduplicates identical compiles, which the rephrase window and cache hits use.
References: `(organisation_id, ontology_version_id) → ontology.ontology_versions`; membership and service principal arc, composite. Inbound: `workspace.saved_views.manifest_id`, `workspace.ask_turns.manifest_id`, `workspace.analysis_steps.manifest_id`, all composite. Changed (review 2026-10-28): `action.mutations.manifest_id` removed. A mutation freezes its own manifest at preview (structure in `action.mutations.manifest`, values in encrypted `manifest_values`) and does not reference this table.
Indexes: the unique key on `(organisation_id, manifest_hash, policy_version)` serves cache and rephrase lookup. `(organisation_id, created_at desc)` serves history. `(organisation_id, ontology_version_id)` finds manifests affected by an ontology change, for impact analysis.
Security: RLS standard. Insert-only (manifests are immutable once compiled). Written by the compile service only. Retention: kept while any saved view, Ask turn or analysis step references it (Changed (review 2026-10-28): mutations removed); otherwise swept after 90 days by `silo_migrate` (proposed).

## Rules settled across domains
1. `auth_events` lives in `audit`, beside `audit_events`. The conventions list is updated.
2. Three roles are added to the conventions: `silo_credential` (single credential mediator, enforced by column grants), `silo_outbox_relay` and `silo_auth` (the only role with privileges on the user-keyed tables and `iam.user_identities`). Changed (review 2026-10-28): `silo_auth` was missing.
3. The catalogue tables `connect.connectors` and `connect.connector_manifests` are mixed global and tenant tables. References into them are plain FKs on `id`, guarded by the trigger `connect.assert_catalogue_visible()`. This is the one documented exception to composite tenant FKs.
4. Ephemeral tables may be physically deleted: `clone.live_subscriptions`, `clone.layout_precomputations`, `workspace.recent_items`, `workspace.favourites`, `workspace.dashboard_tiles`.
5. `clone.render_selections` is an append-only ledger, partitioned monthly (Changed (implementation 2026-10-28): defined in `clone`).
6. The encrypted record-value list adds `action.mutations.manifest_values` and `action.mutation_verifications.intended` and `observed`. Added (review 2026-10-28): it also adds `simulation.staged_action_bases.staged_value`, `automation.automation_run_state.previous_value` and `action.mutations.intent`.
7. Pre-organisation lookups (OAuth callback, inbound webhook, agent mTLS, agent enrolment, login routing) use `security definer` functions that return only the identifiers needed to set `app.org_id`. Everything after the lookup runs under RLS.
8. High-frequency state (agent heartbeats, CDC lease renewals, stream last-delta times, live clone state) is held in `redis-state`. Postgres copies are flushed at most every 60 seconds and on status change.

## Still open (product decisions, not design gaps)
- Retention periods marked "proposed" in each domain file.
- The six federated detector names missing from chapter 38, needed to seed `recognition.detectors`.
- Event `org_export_failed`, proposed for the chapter 77 catalogue.

# Review changes, 28 October 2026

Decisions by the lead engineer after the cross-domain review. Each change is marked inline "Changed (review 2026-10-28)" or "Added (review 2026-10-28)".

- D1. Added `iam.user_identities` (SSO subject to user, never matched by email; first link needs invitation, JIT creation or existing-session proof) and `iam.memberships.scim_external_id`; identity decision 11. Why: email claims can be set by an identity provider's tenant admins.
- D2. Ciphertext AAD never includes `key_version_id`; `iam.mfa_factors` AAD is `(id, user_id, kind)`, `iam.identity_providers` AAD is `(id, organisation_id, kind)`, decision 3 points to the connect AAD. Why: the KEK version is bound to the wrapped DEK, so rotation re-wraps without decrypting.
- D3. `silo_auth` added to the build rules role list and cross-domain rule 2; the user-keyed `security definer` functions and `iam.member_profiles` are owned by `silo_migrate`, with `execute` granted to `silo_auth` only. Why: `silo_auth` is itself under the user-keyed RLS.
- D4. `platform.cells` keyed by text `id` (the cell identifier, `code` folded in), a documented exception to UUIDv7; every cell reference is text to `platform.cells (id)`; `iam.organisation_directory` renamed `directory.organisation_directory`. Why: cell identity crosses databases and appears in hostnames and OAuth callbacks.
- D5. `iam.service_principals` gains `unique (organisation_id, id, kind)`. Why: `fde.fde_principals` pins `kind = 'fde'` through it.
- D6. Build rules gain "Deployment modes"; `iam.kms_key_versions.provider` adds `pkcs11_hsm` and `vault_transit`; `platform.cells.kind` adds `self_managed`. Why: one codebase for hosted and self-managed installs, including air-gapped.
- D7. `ontology.compiled_manifests` no longer lists `action.mutations.manifest_id` as inbound; the three workspace `manifest_id` columns are composite foreign keys to it. Why: a mutation freezes its own manifest, and the manifest table now exists.
- D8. Added `siloes.purge_requests`; `siloes.purge_receipts` gains `purge_request_id`; `action.approval_chains.purge_receipt_id` became `purge_request_id`. Why: a chain must point at something before the wipe, and the receipt exists only after it.
- D9. `clone.spatial_plans` and `clone.asset_models` reference `siloes.silo_files` through `silo_file_id`; `files.files` gains `silo_file_id` for uploads. Why: the stored object is `siloes.silo_files`, so an upload has one storage record.
- D10. `connect.connectors` gains `unique (author_organisation_id, id)`; FDE requirement 3 corrected; `iam.organisations.is_system` marks one system organisation per cell, which holds Silo-owned OAuth clients and secrets. Why: catalogue rows carry no secrets; Silo-owned secrets need a tenant.
- D11. `simulation.staged_action_bases.staged_value`, `automation.automation_run_state.previous_value` and `action.mutations.intent` join the encrypted record-value list; `intent` becomes encrypted `bytea`. Why: each can hold record values.
- D12. Added `iam.organisation_keys` (per-organisation data and HMAC keys); the KEK retire check covers it; `ontology.match_keys.hmac_key_version_id` references it. Why: the build rules relied on these keys and nothing defined them.
- D13. `gov.purpose_sessions` hot copy is in `redis-session` (`purp:` keys). Why: matches the Redis keyspaces section.
- D14. `workspace.view_shares` gains a `scenario_id` arm with its partial uniques and indexes. Why: scenarios share through the view share model.
- D15. `workspace.notifications` references `automation.automation_run_actions` through `automation_run_action_id`. Why: Cron notify and escalate are recorded per run action.
- D16. `connect.oauth_pending_flows.session_id` and `clone.live_subscriptions.session_id` are composite foreign keys to `iam.sessions (organisation_id, id)`. Why: `iam.sessions` has `organisation_id` and `unique (organisation_id, id)`.
- D17. `clone.state_rules.proposed_by_fde_principal_id` became `proposed_by_service_principal_id → iam.service_principals`. Why: every other AI FDE proposer column does the same.
- D18. The RLS policy expression is `(select current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid)`. Why: Postgres evaluates the scalar subquery once per statement instead of per row.
- R1. `directory.organisation_directory` and `directory.identity_routing` reference `directory.cells (id)`; `organisation_directory.cell_id` is changed only by the directory service during a tenant migration, and audited. Why: the directory has its own cells registry, and a migration moves an organisation.
- R2. The connect catalogue policies, the ontology domain rules and the actions intro use the subquery RLS form. Why: consistency with D18.
- R3. Identity decision 9 says `silo_auth` is in the conventions list and covers five tables. Why: D1 and D3.
- R4. Identity Relationships cover `iam.user_identities` and `iam.organisation_keys`. Why: new tables.
- R5. `ontology.compiled_manifests` drops mutations from Purpose, `kind` and retention. Why: D7.
- R6. FK indexes added on `manifest_id` in `workspace.saved_views` and `workspace.ask_turns`, on `session_id` in `connect.oauth_pending_flows` and `clone.live_subscriptions`, and on `iam.user_identities`. Why: indexing rule 1.
- R7. `iam.organisation_keys` gains `unique (organisation_id, id, purpose)`; `ontology.match_keys` pins `purpose = 'hmac'` through `hmac_key_purpose`. Why: the foreign key alone could point at a data key.
- R8. `files.files.object_store_key` is for exports only; `files.files.silo_id` removed in favour of `silo_file_id`. Why: an upload has one storage record, in `siloes.silo_files`.
- R9. Stale open items closed: Points for the lead, the `staged_value` and `previous_value` notes, and `intent` in actions decision 2. Why: done in this review.
- R10. `workspace.view_shares` Purpose names scenarios. Why: D14.
- R11. The pgaudit alert keys on the session (login) user. Why: the `silo_migrate`-owned definer functions run inside auth-service logins.
- R12. `siloes.purge_receipts` drops `requested_by`, `approval_chain_id` and `requested_at`. Why: they are reached through `purge_request_id`.
- R13. Added `directory.cells`. Why: the directory tables reference it and no section defined it.
- R14. `siloes.silo_sources.definition_id` is nullable (required for watched sources); every Silo that accepts uploads has one `upload` source; `siloes.silo_files` gains `unique (organisation_id, silo_id, id)`; clone plans and models use one composite reference to it. Why: plan and model uploads need no Import definition, and the Silo and file cannot disagree.
- R15. `files.files.content_type` and `size` are for exports only; deleting an upload is a Silo purge; `files` writes the catalogue row and `siloes-import` the stored object. Why: an upload's object lives in `siloes.silo_files`.
- R16. Dropped `siloes.purge_receipt_approvers`. Why: approvers are the decided steps of the request's chain, or the requester holding `silo.purge` where no chain is configured.
- R17. Removed the mutation-values sentence from `ontology.compiled_manifests.manifest`. Why: D7.
- D19 (implementation): `audit.audit_events` unique keys include `retention_class`, because Postgres requires every partition key of every level in a unique key on a partitioned table.
- D20 (implementation): `iam.sessions` has forced RLS with a `session_owner` policy (its user, or its organisation), because it carries `organisation_id` and spec 64.2 is binding.
- D21 (implementation): the outbox relay uses three definer functions (claim, mark published, mark failed) instead of a cross-tenant `relay_sweep` policy; it claims only the head of each ordering key.
- D22 (implementation): the definer functions in the identity section and `iam.member_profiles` are owned by `silo_migrate` (review D3) and pin `search_path`; the TOTP AAD is `(id, user_id, kind)` and the identity provider AAD `(id, organisation_id, kind)` (review D2).
- D23. Every range-partitioned table has a default partition; `platform.maintain_partitions()` moves rows out of it and keeps partitions ahead; `platform.partition_status()` is the alert; Capture partitions are registered in the plan. Why: a ledger write must never fail because a scheduled job missed a month.
- D24. Indexing rule 1 states the actor-column exemption, and the linter enforces it with the never-deleted check. Indexes added: every element column of `ontology.ontology_dependencies`, every arc column of `fde.fde_proposal_targets`, `object_type_id` and `receipt_id` on `action.action_commits`, `object_type_id` on `siloes.transitions`, `detector_id` on `recognition.detector_runs` and `recognition.findings`. Why: about 110 keys had no index, so a reader could not tell the deliberate exceptions from omissions, and these keys serve real queries.

# Decisions, 29 October 2026

Decisions by the CEO on the spec issues raised during implementation. Each change is marked inline "Changed (decision 2026-10-29)" or "Added (decision 2026-10-29)".

- D25. D2 stands: the key version is bound through the KMS encryption context on the wrapped DEK, never the ciphertext AAD. The AAD stays `(id, organisation_id, connection_id, field_name, purpose)`. Spec chapter 61, which puts the key version in the AAD, is wrong and is to be corrected; this design is followed. Why: rotation re-wraps DEKs without decrypting ciphertext.
- D26. `mfa_verify` and `sso_assert` join the unwrap reasons; `iam.credential_unwraps` gains `mfa_factor_id` (third arc arm) and `user_id` (required for `mfa_verify`); `organisation_id` stays not null and is the organisation being logged into. Identity decision 6 is replaced. Why: every unwrap is in the ledger, and the organisation's audit shows who verified MFA into it.
- D27. `iam.mfa_factors.last_used_step`: TOTP accepts one step of drift either side and refuses a code at or before the last accepted step, by compare-and-set. Why: a code used once cannot be replayed inside its window.
- D28. `iam.organisations.session_idle_minutes` and `session_absolute_minutes`: an organisation may shorten the cell's session timeouts (30 minutes idle, 12 hours absolute) but never lengthen them. Live WebSocket deltas and heartbeats are not session activity. Why: enterprise customers set stricter policies; an open live view must not keep a session alive.
- D29. `vault_transit` is for development only; production uses Cloud KMS (commercial) or the UK HSM (sovereign). The Vault policy cannot create or delete keys, keys come from Terraform, and the credential service refuses to start if any configured key is missing. Why: Vault is not in the spec, and a mistyped key name must fail at deploy time rather than mint a new key.
- D30 (implementation): the result cache key adds ontology version and period resolution (spec 24.6 is binding); `rl:` rate-limit keys added for lookups before the organisation is known; `sess:` may name a service principal; `sessmem:` is extended each time a session slides; every key belongs to a declared keyspace (`app/server/src/infra/keyspaces.infra.ts`). Why: the keyspace tables are now enforced by code, which found these gaps.
- D31 (implementation 2026-11-01): auth and credential services built. Password login is per organisation (`iam.find_organisation_for_login`); `iam.consume_password_reset` sets the new password in the same statement; the session hot copy carries the token hash, idle window and MFA time and lives until the absolute expiry; `iam.kms_key_versions.provider` accepts `local` for development. Why: each was needed to make the spec's session, reset and MFA rules hold end to end.
- D32 (implementation 2026-11-01):
  - The migration seeds `iam.permissions` with spec 76's 135 verbs. `category` is `authorising` (spec 60.6 by name), `silo_staff` (never in a customer role) or `standard`. `scopeable` is false for super-admin-only and never-delegable verbs, which live only in the seeded Super admin role (`iam.role_permissions_guard`).
  - Every organisation is seeded with Super admin, Admin, Member, Security reviewer and Billing, plus their grantable roles (`iam.seed_system_roles`, run before the policy version row exists, so an organisation starts at version 1).
  - The delegation trigger described under `iam.role_assignments` is built: `iam.check_grant`, which auth also calls before issuing an invitation, and `iam.acting_scope` for `granted_at_scope_id`. The revocation trigger is built too.
  - The `perm:` hot copy holds the resolved grants (permission names, the scope path each applies under, resource references) instead of a flat permission list, because a permission granted on one scope must not apply on another.
  - Why: spec 57.2 says the catalogue is seeded by migration, and spec 56.7 makes delegation a database constraint.

- D33 (implementation 2026-11-02, wave 1 services):
  - `audit.auth_events.source_event_id`, unique per organisation and instant where set: the audit service stores each outbox event once. `audit.organisations_for_chain_close()` (definer, identifiers only) lets the daily close cover organisations that wrote nothing since a restart.
  - Partition seals are written by the maintenance service, not the audit service: row-level security stops the audit writer reading a partition across organisations. Maintenance runs as `silo_migrate` per transaction on its own login. `recorded_at` on `audit.audit_events` is the clock read after the chain lock, so it rises with `chain_seq`. Expired invitations are closed by setting `revoked_at = expires_at`, so the address can be invited again.
  - Every audit event travels as the one `audit_event` message; connect and billing list their event names in the audit catalogue rather than having messages of their own, because the outbox relay publishes only listed messages.
  - `silo_billing` is a new role, held only by billing's login, with update on `iam.organisations.billing_status`. `billing.token_balances.auto_topup` holds the opt-in; `billing.contracts.daily_token_limit` holds Enterprise's configurable daily limit.
  - `simulation.simulation_runs.metering_transaction_id` is dropped: the ledger row names the run (`billing.token_transactions.simulation_run_id`) and is written for it, so the run cannot hold the ledger's bigint id first.
  - `platform.model_calls.caller_service` adds `ask` and `connector-builder`.
  - `connect.connections.parameters` holds a connection's declared parameters as plain data (public, never secret). Revoking a connection revokes its credentials in the same transaction (`connect.connections_revoke_credentials`, definer, since silo_app may not write the credential table). A connection secret's plaintext never leaves the credential service: it places the secret and sends the request itself.
  - Directory: `directory.cells` gains `placement_open`, `organisation_count`, `connection_count` and `counts_at` (spec 6.2); `directory_writer` may delete an identity route, for leaving a cell, a changed address, erasure and key rotation.
  - New Redis keyspaces: `mslot` and `mcell` (model-gateway concurrency leases), `mchg` (metering's rephrase window) and `mnot` (one refusal notice per member per day).
  - Why: each closes a gap a wave 1 service hit; none changes a decision above.
- D34 (implementation 2026-11-02, wave 2 services):
  - Connection grants are enforced by the database like role assignments: `iam.connection_grants_delegation` (invoker, before insert) refuses through `iam.check_connection_grant`, and `iam.connection_grants_revocation` allows the issuer, a super admin, or an admin holding `connection.grant` over the scope it was issued under. `iam.holds_connection` is the shared test (owner, `connection.grant` at the owning scope, or a live grant of at least that access). Grants and role assignments are silenced at a membership's own `suspended_at`/`removed_at`, so reinstatement restores exactly what that step silenced.
  - `iam.revoke_membership_sessions` (definer, guarded by `app.org_id`) lets policy revoke a suspended or removed member's sessions in the same transaction, though `iam.sessions` belongs to auth. `iam.system_organisation_id()` returns the system organisation's id, for Silo-registered OAuth clients.
  - The seeded Admin role carries `marking.manage` (spec 58.10). A field policy aimed at a marking applies to readers who do not satisfy it. Policy's administration and governance events are stored in `audit.audit_events`, which carries scope and resource, so a scope admin reads their subtree's administration (spec 63.5).
  - Ontology: main and its first version (kind `migration`) are created the first time anyone touches the ontology; a new branch's head is its base until its first commit; reading a version walks its parent chain and takes the newest entry per element; a merge copies the branch's entries onto main as one `merge` version and brings the current-state rows level. Status is derived (`active` on main, `proposed` on a branch). Derived mappings carry confidence 0.9. The read model is `OntologyManifest`, not `ontology.compiled_manifests`, which holds compile's plans.
  - Connect: connection parameters are plain data in `connect.connections.parameters`. A conformance summary is derived from runs, never written into the immutable manifest; an abandoned run is recorded as a failed `suite.completed` test. Catalogue releases are signed under their own prefix (`silo.catalogue.v1`).
  - Auth: an identity provider's configuration and client secret are sealed together as one credential document; the OIDC PKCE verifier is derived from a binding only the browser holds; SAML completes through a one-time ticket; ID-token signatures are always checked; just-in-time and SCIM grants are made as the member who configured the provider or issued the token.
  - Directory database: `status.cell_reports`, `status.component_states`, `status.notices`, `status.notice_updates` and `fleet.releases`, `channel_heads`, `bundles`, `promotions`, `rollouts`, `rollout_waves`, `verdicts`, written by `status_writer` and `fleet_writer`. Signed documents are kept exactly as signed; channel heads are numbered by a trigger (each the previous plus one); at most one rollout runs per channel.
  - Metering consumes outbox messages in the relay's envelope; model usage is recorded for cost, never charged.
  - Why: each closes a gap a wave 2 service hit; none changes a decision above.
- D35 (implementation 2026-11-02, wave 3 services):
  - `gov.marking_propagations`: a marking applied upstream, requested by trigger (`gov.request_marking_propagation`, definer) in the transaction that applies it, walked downstream by the lineage service in bounded batches with a second pass after 60 seconds, and counted by policy at read time until complete. `gov.pending_marking_propagations` lists the queue across organisations, identifiers only. Lineage is written in-process in the producer's transaction; inherited markings are stored with their nearest upstream node.
  - `iam.field_policies.property_id` references `ontology.property_identities`: a property by its identity, stable across type versions, as plans, the manifest and `resolveAccess` name it.
  - Stored plans are structure with `{param}` placeholders, one row per manifest hash and policy version; values travel separately. New redis-data keyspaces: the result head (`res:{org}:<queryId>:head`), the compile outcome (`res:{org}:<compileId>:outcome`), executor leases (`xslot:{org}`), the view's last run (`wsrun:{org}:<viewId>`), resolution runs (`rrun`), and change epochs (`cep:{org}:<connection>:<object>`) for result-cache invalidation; redis-state gains the change-stream keyspaces (`cs:*`) and subscription indexes.
  - Entity graph: the hash input is `entity_graph.<purpose>\0value` under the organisation's HMAC key; a match key is the JSON array of normalised components; `silo_object_id` is UUIDv5 under a fixed namespace from the organisation, the type and the sorted key hashes. Confirmed rules live in `resolution_proposals`, applied after the type's declared normalisation. Field authorities are written by resolution.
  - Organisation keys (`data`, `hmac`) share one store in the credential service: created on first use at the next version, wrapped with a context binding row, organisation, purpose, version and KEK version. Record values are sealed with a one-byte format, the four-byte data key version, the nonce, and the AES-256-GCM ciphertext and tag, with the row's binding as associated data. Neither organisation-key unwraps nor record-value opens are written to `iam.credential_unwraps`, whose rows name a credential.
  - Write-back: approvers need read access (connection grants) to every field a diff writes; conformance's read gate counts read-suite runs only, and enabling writes needs a passed `write_verify_undo` run on the current manifest.
  - Live state: masked or redacted fields are withheld from live state, never transformed; groups are keyed by the set (with its ontology version) and the permission fingerprint; a silent webhook stays delayed while polling stands in.
  - Why: each closes a gap a wave 3 service hit; none changes a decision above.
- D36 (implementation 2026-11-02, wave 4 services):
  - Every key from another domain to a property names its identity (`ontology.property_identities`), stable across type versions, as D35 did for field policies: `gov.resource_markings`, the five property keys of `clone.clone_layouts`, and `workspace.app_references`. The versioned `ontology.properties` row would break each at the type's next version. Keys inside the ontology's own versioned rows are unchanged.
  - `ontology.plan_bindings` keeps a stored plan's bound values sealed under the organisation data key, under the id of what holds the plan (an ask turn, a saved view; copied when a view is saved from a turn), so a stored plan replays exactly and plans themselves hold only placeholders.
  - `recognition.detector_configurations` names a detector's properties and time field by identity. `recognition.detectors` is seeded with eight detectors (`disagreement`, `missing_value`, `outlier`, `duplicate_value`, `unmatched_record`, and the history detectors `timing_deviation`, `drift`, `recurrence`); the spec's two further federated detectors are unnamed, so the "at least ten active" rule waits for them. Lineage node kinds gain `finding`.
  - `connect.heal_proposals.disposition` gains `applied` (a repair a person accepted, tested and applied, naming the version and the reviewer); a private connector version may name no creator when it is a self-heal repair, which its heal proposal names; `connect.connections_due_for_recheck` lists due connections across organisations, identifiers only.
  - `files.claim_expired_files` claims expired exports across organisations for the retention sweep, identifiers only and locked.
  - An approval chain's `policy_snapshot` conditions are stored with snake_case keys, the form `action.approval_steps_guard` reads (`self_approval_permitted`); the services convert at the boundary. Approving a discovery scan needs `discovery.authorise`.
  - A Cron's automation principal reads the connections recorded on its Cron and holds `file.export`, bounded by its owner's authority at run time; its change condition is an HMAC (purpose `cron_result`) and its figures are sealed.
  - Why: each closes a gap a wave 4 service hit; none changes a decision above.
- D37 (implementation 2026-11-03, the Warehouse core):
  - `siloes.siloes.status` gains `provisioning`: a Warehouse's Silo stays there while it cannot yet be queried through the federated engine (spec 69.16 needs its query connection); `siloes.warehouse_projects.status` says whether it is built and synchronised.
  - `siloes.warehouse_projects.service_principal_id`: the Warehouse's automation principal, owned by its creator and granted read on the connections its types are read through; it is the actor of every internal Warehouse call and is bounded by its owner at run time. `siloes.active_warehouses` lists active Warehouses across organisations, identifiers only, for scheduled sync and reconciliation.
  - Warehouse tables carry lineage as lists (`_connection_ids`, `_connector_versions`) because a merged object comes from several systems, and a `_hashes` column of each property's value hash, so a history row is written only for a change of Silo's canonical value. A disputed value is null with `<col>__disputed` and `<col>__sources` (the systems mapping it; the executor does not say how many disagreed). A changed type gets `<col>__v<n>`. Link tables are `link__<link_type>`.
  - Freshness is derived: a table whose last sync run failed is stale, never current.
  - Policy: a service principal's connection bound counts the connections its owner owns (owning one reaches it with write), not only those granted to the owner.
- D38 (implementation 2026-11-03, Import rows, the Object Index, BigQuery metering and Warehouse access):
  - `siloes.siloes.service_principal_id`: the automation principal of a Silo that runs scheduled source queries (the Object Index, spec 69.4), owned by its creator, bounded by them at run time, granted read on each nominated type's connections by the person nominating it. An Object Index's Silo stays `provisioning` for the same reason as the Warehouse's (no Silo source connection yet, 66.5).
  - `siloes.warehouse_sql_grants.revoked_reason` (`revoked`, `marked_data`, `handed_over`, `purged`): a person's revocation names them; the system's (a marking reaching the dataset, a hand-over, a purge) names none, so `revoked_by` is null exactly when the reason is not `revoked`.
  - Cross-organisation listings, identifiers only: `siloes.due_index_definitions` (scheduled refresh, claimed by moving `next_refresh_at` on with a compare-and-set), `siloes.bigquery_siloes` (metering), `siloes.warehouses_with_sql_grants` (the marking check).
  - Import rows are loaded by a batch load job from the request itself (a media upload of newline-delimited JSON), not staged in `gcs-siloes` first: the rows arrive in the request, and a load job is deletable at once, which is what the staging rule protects. The job id derives from the request's idempotency key. A file loaded again replaces its rows: all of them under a new definition version, the same row refs under the same version.
  - Object Index tables are named `ix__<definition id>` rather than by the type's API name, so a renamed type keeps its table and a removed nomination drops exactly its own. Property markings are a column per property (`<property>__marking_ids ARRAY<STRING>`) rather than one JSON map, so a search filters on them without a JSON path; entries hold a disputed, masked or redacted value as null.
  - Search routes a type to the Object Index only when a live, refreshed nomination holds its title and the reader sees the type, sees the title in full and reaches every connection the entries were read from (entries keep no per-object source). Within a type, an entry matches only when every marking it carries is one the reader satisfies.
  - BigQuery metering measures fixed windows aligned to the metering interval; a measurement's `measured_at` is its window's end, so the point key makes each window count once whatever the relay's lag. Jobs are attributed by a `silo_silo` job label in the shared siloes project and by project for a Warehouse. A query job runs and bills in its dataset's project.
  - The marking check for direct SQL reads `iam.object_type_markings` and `gov.resource_markings` for the nominated types, the nominated properties (by API name across the type's versions), their contributing connections and the Silo, whatever the requester may see: a marking cannot hide itself from the check.
  - Why: each closes a gap these four services hit; none changes a decision above.
- D39 (implementation 2026-11-03, Siloes Capture and Import):
  - `siloes.create_capture_partitions` is a security definer function that `silo_app` may run: siloes-capture creates an organisation's Capture partitions when its first Capture Silo is created (Fleet may still run it).
  - The Capture tables are append-only and the extraction tables have no delete grant, so wipes and sweeps delete through owner functions that act only on the transaction's organisation and return their counts for the receipt: `siloes.purge_capture` (entity, concept or whole Silo), `siloes.sweep_capture` (retention), `siloes.purge_extractions` (a file's, an object's or a Silo's extracted values with their confirmations). `siloes.capture_bytes` measures a Capture Silo for metering.
  - Cross-organisation listings for the workers, identifiers only: `siloes.live_siloes`, `siloes.open_purge_requests`, `siloes.files_to_process`, `siloes.watched_sources_due`.
  - A purge's approval chain (`action.approval_chains`, subject `purge`) is created by siloes-capture with the request, as discovery creates its chains: required when the organisation has a default approval policy, its approvers holding `silo.purge`, its `diff_hash` the hash of the purge document an approver quotes. With no default policy the requester is the approver. A purge request is inserted first, then its chain, then the request names its chain.
  - A concept purge reaches every live Silo of the organisation holding the type and leaves one receipt, on the Silo it was asked from. Imported objects are not mapped to object types yet, so it removes nothing from Import Siloes.
  - Import files are stored in the cell's siloes bucket under `org/<organisation>/silo/<silo>/files/<file>` (watched drop points under `.../drop/<source>/`), not a bucket per organisation as the design proposes: the object store holds one bucket per class. A purge deletes every version of the object.
  - A document's extraction is charged when the file arrives (after its row exists, which the ledger references); a refused charge removes the stored object and fails the file. A watched location's files are charged to the source's creator.
  - Import and Object Index Siloes stay `provisioning` (no Silo source connection yet, 66.5); the model gateway's carve-out check accepts any Import Silo that is not purging or disabled.
  - Every Silo store is metered in the same windows (D38): Capture in Postgres and Import files in object storage, from their own services, at prices that each service requires before it starts.
  - Why: each closes a gap these two services hit; none changes a decision above.
- D40 (implementation 2026-11-03, the gaps the spec coverage check found):
  - Seats (spec 72) are written by billing and auth. Billing creates the subscription's purchased seats unassigned as it learns the seat count, and releases spare (unassigned or reclaimed) ones when the count falls, never an occupied seat. Auth assigns, unassigns, releases, and moves seats between pools: a scope's pool takes free seats from its parent's (the organisation's own seats have no `allocated_scope_id`), and `seat_allocations.seats_allocated` records what the scope was given. A joining member takes a free seat from their scope's pool or the organisation's in the joining transaction. Policy's suspension reclaims the seat in the suspending transaction; removal does not touch it (72.4).
  - Every assignment is followed, after its transaction commits, by metering's `grantAllowance`, which creates the period's allowance and on first activation the onboarding grant (73.4).
  - The provisioning script registers the organisation's slug in `directory.organisation_directory` (and a local cell in `directory.cells`) when `DIRECTORY_MIGRATE_URL` is given, with the directory service's own checks: the cell exists, is not sovereign, takes placements, and the slug is not placed elsewhere.
  - Why: phase 1 needs a new member to hold an allowance and an organisation to route; none changes a decision above.
- D41 (implementation 2026-11-04, tenant migrations and the organisation export):
  - `platform.tenant_migrations`:
    - A rebalancing is requested by a Silo operator (`requested_by_operator_id`), and every other reason by a customer's super admin. Exactly one of the two is set.
    - A rebalancing needs no membership approval: it goes ahead on its notice unless the customer objects, and its window is at least 30 days after the notice.
    - `contract_operator_id` records the operator who confirmed the contract a promotion needs.
    - The destination's import key is stored as its public PEM (`destination_import_key`) beside its SHA-256 identifier.
    - `move_siloes` says whether the destination's residency permits Siloes.
    - `bundle_bytes` and `purge_receipt_sha256` are recorded.
    - A migration has a row in each cell. The source's row is deleted by its own purge, so the receipt object is the source's record. The destination's row completes once the receipt is handed over.
  - A table's checksum (`tenant_migration_tables`) is SHA-256 over its rows for the organisation, each the text of `to_jsonb(row)` without identity columns, sorted. Identity columns are the cell's own sequences: the destination assigns its own, and no foreign key references one. The audit chain hash excludes `id`, so moved audit rows keep their chain.
  - The load and the source purge run as `silo_migrate` with `session_replication_role = replica` for the transaction (bootstrap grants `SET` on it). Triggers that guard live writes do not re-judge history, and the strict append-only ledgers can be purged with the receipted source purge, which spec 6.4 requires. The load recomputes every checksum inside its transaction and is refused whole on any difference.
  - A seal covers the rows a partition held when sealed, in id order. Retention checks that many rows again, so rows a migration later loads into a sealed partition (with later ids) leave it matching. A removed sealed row still changes the hash.
  - `platform.org_exports.cleared_marking_ids`: the organisation's markings the requester satisfied when they asked, resolved in their session. A policy decision for a member needs a live session, and the run happens in the background without one.
  - `platform.org_exports_due` lists requested exports, and runs left by a stopped process, across organisations (identifiers only). A stale run is failed as `interrupted`, to be asked for again.
  - `automation.automation_runs.skipped_reason` gains `tenant_migration`: a Cron firing in the window is skipped, not queued.
  - Why: each closes a gap these two services hit; none changes a decision above.

The stage 7 proposal kind is `detector_configuration` (which fields a detector examines), so its applied target is the configuration, not a persisted threshold.

Constraint triggers on `iam.service_principal_roles` and `iam.role_permissions` (`iam.reject_forbidden_for_fde_principals`) refuse, at commit, any role holding a forbidden permission for a principal of kind `fde`, whichever side changes. They lock the role row first, as `iam.reject_authorising_for_principals` does.

A refusal at that ceiling is recorded as `fde_ceiling_refusal`.

A chain's `policy_snapshot` gains `markings` (the touched markings, read when the chain is requested), and a `marking_holder` condition carries `marking_ids`.

- D60 (implementation 2026-11-10, probabilistic simulation; no schema change):
  - `simulation.dependency_edges.evidence_ref.history.samples` keeps an observed lead time's observations in seconds (at most 2,000, evenly chosen) beside D58's summary, so a run can sample them.
  - `simulation.scenarios.bounds` may carry `iterations` (100 to 10,000, default 1,000); `simulation_runs.iterations` records the number used.

Any stated edge on the path makes the object `deterministic`, computed from stated lead times with no probability or spread. An object affected in no iteration is not a result.

  - Why: probabilistic propagation over observed edges only (39.5).

- D62 (implementation 2026-11-10, declassification):

  - `gov.marking_declassifications.resource_type` and `resource_id` (frozen): the resource the direct marking was on, which execution removes it from and a revert puts it back on.
