- D178 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage B17m: proposing a Cron from Ask; spec 36.4, 40.3, 40.4, 40.7): where changes may be asked for, the model may return a schedule in a closed vocabulary (every hour, day, weekday, week or month; the time; the weekdays or day of the month; when to act: always, rows returned, none, differs from the previous run, the count above or below a number; notify or report; the asker's words), with no defaults in its schema (the model gateway refuses sample values). Compile writes the five-field expression itself (compile/schedule.service.ts), never the model, and maps the condition to a result condition; charged as a compile, saved nowhere. Ask's propose_cron (refused before compiling where the thread has nothing to re-run) records a proposal turn whose draft is createCron's body but its name: the subject is the thread's saved view, or its latest answer to save as a view first (36.11), the plan as the turn's manifest; kept whole in ask_turns.proposal (kind cron; no record value) and shown as the turn's cron; ask_cron_proposed records the schedule, the condition's operator, the action and the subject's kind.
- D179 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage B17n: starting a scenario from Ask; spec 36.4, 39.4): askQuestion's start_scenario names the object that fails (subject); compile's compileFailure (keyed, Ask only) has the model state the failure in simulation's forms (unavailable, delayed, unavailable for a period, reduced capacity, each with its own measure; no schema defaults), for a type the asker may see, checks it as simulation's statedFailure does and charges it as a compile; Ask saves it through simulation's saveScenario (simulation.run; Ask is now a caller of the scenario contracts) as the asker's private failure scenario, named in the asker's words, ready to run (running is a simulation, charged then). ask_turns gains scenario_id (present only on a start_scenario answer); ask_scenario_started records the scenario, the form and the count of objects. Staging an Action in a branch from Ask is not built: a staged Action is made from the branch (39.8).
- D180 (decision 2026-11-18, settling spec 47.8's open decision; backend stage P9a, phase 9 begins): Silo ships a default physical-operations role. iam.seed_system_roles provisions "Physical operations" in every organisation, the only role holding actuation.approve; Super admin now holds every customer permission but that one (20.8: never granted by default), and may assign the role. A physical connection is enabled only once someone holds it (connect-registry's demandPhysicalOperations): registering an outbound webhook target declared physical, and enabling writes on a connection that is physical (physical_webhook, or a manifest object whose writes are of class physical), are refused as connection.physical_operations_unstaffed until then, so two-person physical approval (47.2) can always be met. Phase 9's other library decisions the same day: the agent may add gopcua/opcua and paho.mqtt.golang (chapter 20); ssh2 for SFTP on the cell.
- D181 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9b: SFTP connections; spec 14.4 "SFTP and file share", ssh2 approved the same day): a manifest may speak sftp: transport.baseUrl sftp://host[:port][/base] (a {params.<name>} part one DNS label), the required connection parameter host_key_sha256 pinning the server, a login of username_password or the new ssh_key strategy (auth field roles private_key and passphrase), and objects whose source names a directory under the base, a file name pattern (* and ?), CSV (by its header, any of four delimiters) or JSON Lines, and maxFiles and maxFileBytes; SFTP objects declare no writes and no pushdown, and SFTP through the agent is refused until built. The credential service runs the session (credential/sftp.service.ts, sendSftpRequest: list a directory's regular files, or read one file within its bound), opening the login as for any egress (every use an unwrap on the ledger), over TCP under the cell's egress rules (egress.infra createTcpEgress: public addresses, or private ones inside the organisation's link), verifying the host key before authentication so an impostor never sees the login. connect-runtime's sftp engine lists, matches, reads in name order and parses (the delimited parser moved to utils/delimited.util.ts, shared with Import Silos); more files, bytes or rows than allowed are refused, never truncated. No schema change.
- D182 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9c: industrial endpoints and MQTT reads through the agent; spec 20.1, 20.2, 20.7; paho.mqtt.golang approved the same day): connect-registry creates and lists a connection's industrial endpoint (connect.industrial_endpoints, already in the schema): industrial.connect at the owning scope, always the connection's agent pool, opc.tcp:// for OPC UA and tcp:// or ssl:// for MQTT with its policy (plain or tls); OPC UA's None only with the owner's recorded exception (industrial.declare_writable), industrial_endpoint_created and opcua_insecure_exception_recorded newly catalogued and raised. A manifest may speak mqtt (3.1.1 or 5.0; via the agent, no base URL, login none or username_password, reads only): an object's source names a topic filter (+ and #), JSON or text payloads, QoS, a snapshot window, and decode, the new source.decode JSONata block over { topic levels, payload, receivedAt } giving the record. A read sends the agent mqtt.snapshot (a new work kind): the agent (internal/work/mqtt.go, paho) checks the broker's host against its owner's targets, opens a sealed login only for the work, subscribes clean, gathers the retained messages for the window (the backfill of 18.5; live publishes are not a snapshot's) and reports truncation; the cell decodes each message and refuses more than a step may read. The agent's sealed-login parser no longer insists on a database: an industrial login names none, and the SQL path checks its own. Tests: the agent's against the test environment's NATS with its MQTT listener (docker compose mqtt), and end to end through the built agent. Live telemetry (the change stream), Sparkplug B, OPC UA and physical writes follow.
- D183 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9d: MQTT telemetry through the change stream; spec 20.2, 20.6, 18): a manifest's change stream may name an mqtt source for an MQTT object. The subscription is a capture (connect.cdc_slots gains method mqtt; setChangeCapture sets it up, the slot name being the client identifier the broker sees, confirmed by the owner, no publication) leased to one agent of the pool and failed over as change data capture is. Its cdc.start names the connection's broker, the streamed objects' topic filters and, where the manifest declares a login, the login sealed to the agent for the lease (bound to the slot as its work). The agent (tunnel.startTelemetry, work.MQTT.Subscribe) subscribes clean and sends messages frames up its capture stream as they arrive, never through the spool, so telemetry never reaches the agent's disk; a cell not keeping up, a lost broker or a dropped stream ends the subscription and the cell leases it again, resuming from the retained messages. change-stream decodes each message with the matching objects' source.decode (draftsFromMessages; values in memory only) and publishes them as the existing rules say: bus-live only where the state plane holds the object, to Capture where a Capture Silo holds the type. The stream's status shows mqtt in use; capture failures gain target_refused and login_refused. Dropping an mqtt capture removes nothing on the broker.
- D184 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9e: writable points; spec 20.3, 20.5, 20.7): connect-registry declares, lists, raises, sets test safety on and retires a connection's writable points (connect.writable_points, already in the schema with its raise-only guard), under industrial.declare_writable at the owning scope, against the manifest version the connection runs. The address is the transport's: an MQTT topic with no wildcard, an OPC UA node by namespace URI and identifier (never a namespace index), or a webhook action's name; the value check is required and must compile as CEL over values and prior (write.valueCheck); the risk class is at least the transport's default (every MQTT and OPC UA write physical) and only raised. writable_point_declared and writable_point_risk_raised are catalogued and raised. Physical writes (P9g) will write only declared, live points, checked against their value check.
- D185 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9f: OPC UA reads; spec 20.3, 20.7): a manifest may speak opc_ua, read by the Silo Agent's plugin (gopcua, approved 2026-11-18); the server is the connection's industrial endpoint, never the manifest's. An object's source names a root node by namespace URI and identifier (nsu=<uri>;i=|s=|g=|b=<id>, never a namespace index, which can change on restart), an optional type definition, and maxInstances (default 1,000, at most 10,000); its records are the root's child objects (of that type where one is named), and each field's path is a browse path under the instance, browse names split by / ("Motor/Speed"), or $browseName or $nodeId for the instance itself. A field reads a path, never a computed value (computation belongs in a derived property); pushdown and writes are refused (writes are physical Actions, P9g); the login is none or a username and password, sealed to the agent for one piece of work. The agent resolves the namespace URIs through the server's NamespaceArray (an unknown one is refused, never guessed), browses hierarchical references to find the instances and each path, reads the values in chunks of 500, and returns one row an instance with done marked truncated past maxInstances; the cell refuses more instances than the source declares or one step may read (opcua.too_many_instances, connect.rows_per_source_step), never truncating. Work kind opcua.read; the agent checks the server against its host's allowed targets. This release reads under security policy None, which the endpoint registry allows only with the owner's recorded exception; an endpoint with a signed policy is accepted and its reads refused with industrial.policy_unsupported until the agent's application certificate is issued and trusted (next stage). The endpoint registry now checks the plugin against the protocol the connection's manifest speaks (industrial.plugin_mismatch), and names OPC UA security strictly: None, or Basic256Sha256, Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep or Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss with Sign or SignAndEncrypt (Basic128Rsa15 and Basic256, deprecated by the OPC Foundation, are refused); the MQTT and OPC UA engines and MQTT captures use an endpoint only of their own plugin. Tested end to end against a gopcua test plant (agent/internal/opcuatest, command plant) through the built agent.
- D186 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9f: OPC UA signed and encrypted policies; spec 20.3, 20.7, 61): a signed OPC UA endpoint (Basic256Sha256, Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep or Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss, with Sign or SignAndEncrypt) is reached as one application, whatever agent of the pool does the work, so the customer trusts one certificate per server. At creation connect-registry asks the credential service (issueOpcUaApplicationCertificate) for the endpoint's application instance certificate: an RSA-2048 key and a self-signed certificate as OPC UA Part 6 describes one (application URI urn:silohq.io:agent:opcua:<endpoint> in the subject alternative name; digital signature, non-repudiation, key and data encipherment and certificate signing; client and server authentication; SHA-256 with RSA; two years), made with @peculiar/x509 (already a dependency). The key is sealed as a connection credential of new purpose opcua_application_key (one field per endpoint) and never leaves in clear; for one piece of work on one agent it is sealed to that agent's X25519 key with HPKE (sealOpcUaApplicationKey, info silo.agent_opcua_key.v1, bound to organisation, agent, connection and work, two minutes), the document assembled from the opened bytes (a string-free base64 encoder, utils/crypto base64Bytes), and each opening is in the unwrap ledger (probe for a verification, query for reads). The certificate is public: industrial_endpoints gains app_certificate_pem beside app_certificate_thumbprint (SHA-1, as servers list trusted certificates), shown in the endpoint view for the builder's customer step. The owner pins the server's certificate by its thumbprint as the server shows it (SHA-1 or SHA-256, colons and case ignored; new column server_certificate_thumbprint); a check ties both to signed OPC UA endpoints only. A signed endpoint is created untrusted. verifyIndustrialEndpoint (POST .../industrial-endpoints/:endpointId/verifications, industrial.connect) asks connect-runtime (probeIndustrialEndpoint) to give an opcua.probe to an agent: the agent asks the server for its endpoints, takes the one with the policy and mode, refuses a leaf certificate other than the pinned one before opening any channel, checks the sealed key is the certificate's, connects as the application with the login, and reports the namespace array and the certificate presented. Outcomes: trusted (status active, namespace_uris and the new verified_at recorded, industrial_endpoint_verified, an event added beside the spec's industrial_endpoint_untrusted), untrusted or server_certificate_mismatch (status untrusted, industrial_endpoint_untrusted with the reason), unreachable (status unreachable only for an endpoint never verified), login_refused and policy_not_offered (status unchanged). Reads go only through an active endpoint; a read that finds the server no longer trusts the application marks the endpoint untrusted once (industrial_endpoint_untrusted, found_by read) and is refused (industrial.endpoint_untrusted). gopcua's client reads a server's ERR message during OpenSecureChannel as the connection's end (it checks for an empty read before the protocol error), so the agent reads a signed channel that ends as it opens, on a server that has just answered GetEndpoints, as the server refusing the certificate; status codes the server does return are mapped (certificate and security codes to untrusted, identity codes to login). Fixed with it: the agent's MQTT and OPC UA plugins sent source_refused with reason login, which the cell's strict error frame refused; the frame now takes the industrial reasons (login, untrusted, server_certificate, policy). The work relay carries the key request (sealKey) as it does a login. The test plant gains a secured mode (StartSecure; plant -trust-dir -cert-out): its own certificate, Basic256Sha256 Sign and SignAndEncrypt beside None, and a trust directory read at each connection by a relay in front of gopcua's server (which keeps no trust list), answering an untrusted OpenSecureChannel with Bad_SecurityChecksFailed as servers do. An agent-custody connection's application key is still made and held by the cell: a key made on the customer's host would mean one certificate per agent, and follows if wanted.
- D187 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9f: OPC UA subscriptions; spec 20.3, 18.1, 18.5, 20.6): a change source of kind opcua, for an OPC UA object only, with samplingMs (default 1,000; 0 as fast as the server samples), queueSize (default 10) and an optional deadband (absolute, or percent of the variable's range, at most 100). A subscribed object is identified by its instance ($browseName or $nodeId), so each value names its record without a read. It is leased as a capture of new method opcua (connect.cdc_slots.method), set up and shown as MQTT telemetry is (setChangeCapture; inUse opcua). The start frame names the connection's active server and its security (the application certificate and the pinned server certificate, the key and login sealed to the agent for the lease, the slot being their work) and per streamed object its root, type definition, the fields' browse paths and the sampling. The agent connects as a read does, finds the instances and the variable at each path, and makes one subscription (publishing at the smallest sampling interval) with a monitored item per instance and path, each with its sampling, queue and a data change filter (status and value, with the deadband), created in chunks of 1,000 and at most 10,000; the server's first notification of each item is the backfill. Values go up the capture stream as samples (object, browse name, node, path, value, status good, uncertain or bad, source and server timestamps), batched as MQTT messages are and never spooled; when the session ends (the client's state, or a failed publish) or the cell falls behind, the capture ends and is leased again. change-stream makes one partial update a sample (the field at its path, the identifier from the instance), with the server's timestamp as source_at (else the source's, else now); a bad value is not a change and counts as unmatched. A capture's health is told by its own source (mqtt, opcua or cdc) on start and failure. Fixed with it: a Cron's stream source was written to connect.change_stream_subscriptions unmapped, so an email-streamed object failed its check; it maps email to provider_events and opcua to opcua_subscription (the spec's values). The test plant stamps its values with source and server timestamps, as servers do, and changes a speed on request (Plant.SetSpeed; SIGUSR1 to the plant command), told to its monitored items.
- D188 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9f: industrial discovery; spec 19.2 to 19.4, 20.1 to 20.3): the agent carries out discovery's opcua_browse and mqtt_observe, which it reported unavailable before. "Where credentials already exist" is read as the organisation's active industrial endpoints of the agent's pool whose host is one of the authorisation's targets, one per address, at most 50 a scan: connect-runtime sends them with the scan, each login and (a signed OPC UA policy) application key sealed to the agent with the scan's id as their work (reason probe), and the agent checks each host against the authorisation's targets and its own allowed targets again. The agent runs the industrial methods first, while what was sealed is fresh, then host configuration, catalogues and the port scan; each endpoint is one probe and, where it answers, one finding. OPC UA browse descends from the Objects folder (not the server's own namespace 0 objects) through folders (FolderType, and untyped objects holding no variables), takes as instances the objects of a server type and untyped objects with variables, and groups them by type, or by folder when untyped; for up to three instances of each it walks the variables (browse path, data type and access level: attributes, never a value; a typed child's variables too) and the child objects of other types (references). At most 5,000 nodes and 8 levels; truncated says so. MQTT observation subscribes to # for ten seconds (no $ topics) and keeps of each message its topic and its payload's shape (a JSON object's field names and JSON types; else text or binary), the payload discarded at once; topics are gathered into families, a level that is an identifier (a number, a UUID, long hex) or varies among three or more topics otherwise alike becoming +. At most 10,000 messages and 2,000 topics. foundStructure gains opcua (namespaces, types with root, instances, variables and references) and mqtt (families with topics, encoding and fields; the key is encoding, not payload, so the redaction rules leave it); every name is checked against value patterns as the others are. Proposals: an object type per OPC UA family (identified by browse name, matched to existing object types by name and fields) and links from references between proposed types (one to one, declared, 0.8); an object type per MQTT JSON or text family (a field per + level, named by the level before it, the identifier; else the topic). Promotion builds a private opc_ua connector (an object per family with variables: root, type definition, id at $browseName, node at $nodeId, a field per variable at its browse path, typed from the data type) or mqtt connector (an object per family, its JSONata decode reading the + levels and payload fields), read through the agent with no login, which the reviewer sets where the server needs one; the new connection takes its industrial endpoint as any does. Fixed with it: discovery's singular took status to statu; us and is endings are kept.
- D189 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g1: the actuation allow-list; spec 47.4, 47.7, 47.8): actions keeps action.actuation_allowlists, which was in the schema unused. An entry is asked for by the connection's owner (industrial.declare_writable at its owning scope; whether they hold actuation.approve is recorded) for a live physical writable point of the manifest the connection runs (D184), on an OPC UA or MQTT connection or one whose webhooks are physical: its kind (setpoint, command, or an OPC UA method), data type, range and largest step (a setpoint's only), least interval between writes, inverse command (a command's), simulator node and the digital clone object. The request waits in the new action.actuation_allowlist_requests (decided once, by its guard), since an entry is inserted only signed and approved. Another person decides: the owner or a holder of actuation.approve, one of the two people holding actuation.approve; self-approval is never permitted. Approved, the entry is signed by the control plane with the execution grant key under its own prefix (silo.actuation_allowlist.v1, NUL, the text) over its canonical JSON (decimals as normalised text, the approval time to the millisecond), so the agent can check exactly the bytes signed; signature and key reference are stored with it. Never an interlock, safety function, alarm limit or protection setting (47.4): a node, inverse command or simulator node whose own name (an OPC UA identifier, not its namespace; a topic's levels), split into words, includes one of interlock, safety, SIS, SIF, ESD, trip, alarm, protection, e-stop, emergency, shutdown, bypass, override or limit is refused, a guard on the safe side that the customer's control system backs. An entry is never edited: removal ends it (removed_at, once) and a change is a new request. Events: allowlist_entry_requested and allowlist_entry_rejected (added, read with the spec's), allowlist_entry_added, allowlist_signed, allowlist_entry_removed; gateway routes under /actions/connections/:connectionId/actuation-allowlist and /actions/actuation-allowlist. Delivery of the signed list to the agent is the next stage.
- D190 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g2: the signed allow-list on the agent; spec 47.4, 47.8): the agent holds each connection's signed actuation allow-list (agent/internal/actuation), checking every entry's Ed25519 signature with the key the cell gave it at enrolment or renewal (the execution grant key), against the entry's canonical text exactly as it arrived; an entry from another key, altered, of another organisation or connection, or that does not read as an entry refuses the whole list, and the one held stays (agent.allowlist_refused, which must never happen in normal operation). An empty list ends a connection's. The heartbeat names the lists held by connection and digest (SHA-256 of the entries' signatures sorted and joined by newlines, computed alike on both sides). At each heartbeat connect-runtime compares them with the current lists of the agent's pool's connections that are not revoked (action.actuation_allowlists joined to connect.connections) and sends a connection's whole list where they differ: a changed list, a new connection's, or an empty one for a connection whose entries were all removed, which was revoked or which left the pool. A list sent is sent again after ten seconds if the agent has still not taken it (agent.allowlist_not_taken), and is forgotten when the tunnel closes, so the next tunnel starts from what the agent reports. When the agent's digest first matches what was sent, allowlist_delivered_to_agent is recorded (connect events: the agent, the connection, the entries, the digest). Writes look entries up in this store from the next stage on.
- D191 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g3: OPC UA setpoint writes through the agent; spec 47.1, 47.4 to 47.6): an OPC UA object may declare setpoint updates, the declaration alone (writes.update {}), risk physical (refused otherwise: every OPC UA write is physical), on an object identified by its instances' browse names; other operations wait for methods. connect-runtime prepares the write as statements, one a record (the instance by browse name, the values at its fields' browse paths, the connection's physical writes a minute), whose JSON as sent is what actions' execution grant covers, as SQL's statements are (prepareWrites, then writeRecords on the grant, checked in the cell before it leaves). The agent (opcua.write) checks the grant over exactly those bytes, finds each instance and node, and before anything is written requires every node to be a setpoint in its current signed allow-list (D190), the value of the variable's own data type, within the entry's range, its step from the value read now no larger than the entry's, its last write here at least the entry's interval ago, and the plan within the connection's writes a minute; one refusal and nothing at all is written, each record saying why (instance, node, not_listed, kind, data_type, range, step, interval, rate). Then each record's nodes are written in one request: a status that is not good is the control system's rejection, the outcome, never retried (actuation.rejected_by_control_system); no answer leaves the read back to decide (unknown), never a retry. The write result carries each node's address, entry and status for the receipt. The test plant answers writes as a control system: a motor's speed only, clamped above 2000 (GoodClamped, so read back diverges), refused above 3000 (BadOutOfRange); its speeds are writable, which browsing now reports. Still to come in P9g: the intent checks and preview (current values, the binding statement), the physical write log and chapter 47's events at execution, the Cron refusal, methods and MQTT commands, revert and dry run.
- D191b (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g4: the physical Action path; spec 47.2 to 47.6, 47.8): Action types may write through OPC UA (WRITING_PROTOCOLS gains opc_ua; generic edits still skip physical objects). At intent, for each OPC UA connection a physical Action writes, connect-runtime resolves through the agent each record's node for each field written and its value now (resolvePhysicalTargets; the agent's read takes <path>/$nodeId for the address of the node at path). Each node must be in the connection's signed allow-list as a setpoint (policy_gate), its declared writable point's value check (CEL over values and prior, D184) must pass and the value keep to the entry's range and step from the value now (intent), the entry's last write must be at least its interval ago (plan), and the plan within the connection's physical writes a minute (plan; physical_rate_limit_refused recorded; the canary does not apply). The preview carries a physical block: each node, its value now and proposed, its range, step, interval, the connection's writes a minute, the last write, and the statement no configuration can remove or reword (47.3). physical_action_proposed is recorded with the mutation. Approval is the existing physical floor (two people, one holding actuation.approve, the proposer neither). At execution every node a physical write named is logged in the new action.physical_writes (append-only; node, allow-list entry, outcome applied, rejected, refused, unknown or not written, the agent's reason; never a value): it gives the last write and the rate at intent. A node the agent refused although the cell passed it is physical_write_refused_by_agent and an error-level alert (actuation.refused_by_agent); one the control system rejected is physical_write_rejected_by_control_system. With the receipt, physical_action_executed names both approvers, the nodes' allow-list entries, the first node's address and the receipt. A Cron asked to execute a physical Action type is refused at creation, as before, and now recorded (physical_cron_execute_refused, the scheduler's catalogue); at run time a physical Action falls back to propose, as before. Fixed with it: connect-runtime's record reads around a write (prior state, read back) now reach an industrial connection's endpoint as reads do.
- D192 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g5: reverting a physical setpoint; spec 47.6): a revert of a physical mutation writes the stored prior values as a mutation of the physical risk class (as before), and is now checked at intent and previewed as any physical Action is: the revert service resolves each node through the agent (resolvePhysicalTargets now also takes the revert service as caller), requires it in the signed allow-list, passes the value check, range, step, interval and rate, and refuses the revert otherwise (revert.physical_refused, with the stage); its preview carries the physical block (the value now, the prior value it writes back) and the statement, which says revert restores the state value only; physical_action_proposed is recorded with it. Approval is the same two-person floor; execution writes through the agent, which checks again, and physical_action_executed names the revert. A command's revert (its inverse, or refused as not_revertible) waits for commands.
- D193 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g6: the dry run; spec 47.5): a physical Action may be proposed as a dry run (proposeMutation dryRun), the full path to verification against the simulator nodes its allow-list entries name, nothing written to production. It takes the same checks at intent but production's interval and rate (a node whose entry names no simulator node is refused at the policy gate), the same two-person approval (a dry-run flag that skipped approval would be a path to an unapproved write if a simulator mapping were ever wrong), and runs on a grant whose statements carry dryRun, so the agent, not the cell, swaps each node for the simulator node its signed entry names (no_simulator otherwise), keeps range and step against the simulator's value now, counts nothing against production's interval and rate, writes, and reads the simulator back. Verification compares what the simulator read back (production is not read); the receipt is marked dry run (receipts.dry_run, which the schema ties to the mutation's), its physical writes are logged dry run against the simulator node (not counted at intent), and physical_action_dry_run is recorded instead of physical_action_executed. A policy may require a dry run first: iam.organisations.physical_dry_run_required (setPhysicalDryRun, mutation.policy organisation-wide, physical_dry_run_policy_set); a physical proposal then names a completed dry run's receipt of the same Action type (dryRunReceiptId, kept on the mutation), and is refused at intent otherwise. The test plant has simulator speed nodes (Sim.PumpN.Motor.Speed), addressable by node and outside the browsed tree.
- D194 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g7: commands; spec 47.1, 47.3, 47.4, 47.6, 20.2, 20.3, 20.5): a physical command is a custom action on an OPC UA or MQTT connection. The manifest's custom action now takes one of three forms: a REST request (as before, declaring the fields it changes), an OPC UA method (`opcua.method`, its browse path under the instance, called on its parent; no input arguments in this release, refused in the manifest, at Action type publication and at write), or an MQTT command (`mqtt`: a topic with no wildcard and no system prefix, `{identifier}` as one whole level standing for the record's identifier; QoS; a retained flag declared per topic, default false; the payload JSON or text, with a declared schema of keys, types and whether each is required; the payload is the body's JSONata over the inputs, or the inputs). A command has no state, so it declares no changed fields and is verified by acknowledgement. An Action type over a command reverts compensating (its inverse, the manifest's compensatedBy) or not_revertible, refused otherwise (action_type.command_revert); not_revertible is now permitted only for a type that invokes a command. MQTT joins the writing transports. The allow-list entry is a method (OPC UA) or a command (MQTT); the agent now accepts only those kinds for opcua.call and mqtt.publish. At intent, connect-runtime resolves each command (resolvePhysicalTargets takes commands): the method's node through the agent (a read of `<path>/$nodeId` now finds a method as it finds a variable), or the topic and the payload, checked against its schema, so a payload off its schema, an identifier that is not one topic level, or inputs to a method are refused at intent. actions then requires the entry, its kind, a declared writable point whose value check passes over the inputs, the interval and the connection's rate, and for a dry run the simulator counterpart (the agent publishes to the simulator topic, or calls the simulator method, its signed entry names). The preview's physical block names the command and, for MQTT, the payload as published; a not_revertible command's preview carries 'This Action sends a command to physical equipment. It cannot be reverted.' instead of the setpoint statement. connect-runtime builds opcua.call and mqtt.publish statements (never mixed with setpoints in one plan, write.commands_mixed) and the grant covers them exactly; a plan carries its moment (`at`), at which an MQTT payload is computed, so the statements prepared for the grant are those sent. Execution: a good status from the server (OPC UA) or the broker's acknowledgement (MQTT, at QoS 1 or 2) is verified with reason acknowledged; no answer is failed, not_acknowledged; a status that is not good is the control system's rejection, failed and never retried. The receipt carries 'A command is verified by acknowledgement. Acknowledgement does not confirm the physical outcome.' A command is reverted by its inverse: the revert reads nothing of the record, invokes the compensating custom action with no inputs under the same two-person approval, and refuses unless the inverse is the one the original's allow-list entry names (revert.no_inverse where it names none; refused at the policy gate where it names another). A dry run's receipt is never reverted (revert.dry_run): it wrote nothing to production, and its revert would have written the stored prior values there. Tests: the manifest forms, the cell's path with a fake agent (physicalCommands.test), and through the real Go agent an OPC UA method resolved and called on a grant (agentOpcua.test) and an MQTT command published to the test broker, read back retained (agentMqtt.test); the agent's own checks in TestOPCUACall and TestMQTTPublish against the test plant's Start, Stop and Jog methods and the broker.
- D195 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9g8: physical webhooks; spec 47.1, 47.4 to 47.7, 20.3 to 20.5): a webhook declared physical is checked against the actuation allow-list as an industrial command is. An outbound target may name its webhook action (connect.webhook_endpoints.action_name, unique among a connection's live targets); a physical one must (a check), since its writable point and its allow-list entry address it by that name (writable_points.address is a webhook action name, 20.3), and registering one sets connect.connections.physical_webhook (47.7). A webhook entry is a command (no state value), its inverse another live target of the connection, and it has no simulator: its Action's record writes are not physical, so it is never dry run, and a dry run now sends no webhook at all (it would have reached production). At intent, each physical webhook side effect joins the physical plan: its target active, its action listed as a command, a declared physical writable point whose value check passes over the Action's parameters, its interval and the connection's rate; the preview's physical node names the action and the target (endpointId). At execution it is checked again when queued (entry live, interval, rate), queued under its entry (action.webhook_deliveries.allowlist_entry_id, frozen) and logged as a physical write, outcome unknown (its effect is the target's), so physical_action_executed names its entry; refused, the receipt's side effect is failed (actuation_not_listed, _interval, _rate) and nothing is queued. notify checks the entry before each attempt: removed, the delivery fails, never sent and never retried (actuation.not_listed). Through the agent, the request names the action and the connection's writes a minute; connect-runtime refuses a physical target's POST that does not name its own action (webhook.physical_unmarked), and the Go agent sends it only if its own signed list holds the action as a webhook command, outside the entry's interval (counted from sends the target accepted, so a retry after a refusal goes) and within the rate, else actuation_refused (not_listed, kind, interval, rate): final, never retried, physical_write_refused_by_agent raised and logged as an error. A revert never sends the original's physical webhooks again (before this, a revert re-fired every webhook of its Action type, physical ones included); it sends the inverse targets the original's entries name, with the references alone, under the same two-person approval, each checked as above; an entry naming no inverse refuses the revert (revert.no_inverse), an inverse with no active target too (revert.inverse_target_missing). An Action type with a physical webhook may be not_revertible. Tests: outboundWebhooks.test (the allow-list at intent, the preview, two approvers, queueing and the physical write, the interval, the revert by inverse, removal before sending, a private target marked for the agent and the agent's refusal) and the agent's TestAPhysicalWebhookIsSentOnlyAsItsSignedAllowListLets.
- D196 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9h1: the cell's Fleet agent applies cell releases; spec 11.1 to 11.3, 6.3): given the cell's Kubernetes API (`FLEET_KUBERNETES`: `in_cluster`, the service account's token read afresh each call, the cluster's CA and the pod's namespace; or an API server URL with an optional token and CA file, http only on the loopback), the Fleet agent applies the cell's own releases. No Kubernetes library: plain HTTPS (infra/kubernetes.infra.ts). Every `FLEET_RELEASE_POLL_MINUTES` (5) it asks `desiredRelease` for its channel (`FLEET_CHANNEL`; stable, or sovereign in a sovereign cell); a release it does not run is checked (the release key's signature over the manifest, sovereign builds also the sovereign key's; the digest; the release named; the cell's build target; only capabilities the cell's build approves) and applied. Going forward, migrations run first (expand before any image moves) as a Job from the release's own image (fleet-control's, else the first), `node src/db/scripts/migrate.script.ts cell`, `CELL_MIGRATE_URL` from the Secret `FLEET_MIGRATION_SECRET` (`silo-migrate`, key `url`) that only the Job mounts (the agent never reads it, and the Job mounts no service account token); the migrate script, given `SILO_EXPECTED_MIGRATIONS`, applies nothing unless the image's files are exactly the release's migrations byte for byte (`checkExpected`); each cell migration is then reported (`reportMigrationApplied`, `migration_applied`). Going back (rolled_back, wave_pending) runs none: expand and contract keeps every release compatible with the one before. The release's configuration, flags and model routing are now artefacts of fleet-control's store by digest (`release-documents/<hex>`, `npm run fleet:release-document`, read by `readReleaseDocument`; a cell channel refuses a release without all three, `fleet.release_document_missing`); the agent fetches each, checks its digest and keeps it in a ConfigMap the services mount (`silo-release-configuration`, `silo-release-flags`, `silo-release-model-routing`, key `document`, annotated with the digest), so a rollback restores configuration and flags too. Images (`FLEET_IMAGE_REPOSITORY/<service>@sha256:<hex>`) roll over the Deployments labelled `silo.io/service`, one service at a time and one zone first (`topology.kubernetes.io/zone`), each patched (container named for the service) and watched until every replica is updated and available within `FLEET_ROLL_TIMEOUT_MINUTES` (15), a stalled progress deadline failing it at once; fleet-control's own Deployment goes last, its state written before it rolls itself. What the cell runs is kept in the ConfigMap `silo-fleet-state` (release, manifest digest, the release before, rollout, applied or failed and why), so every step is idempotent across a restart. A failed Job, a stalled or slow roll, or a document that does not match fails the release: recorded, reported at once as a failing verdict (a verdict missing gates fails, 11.2), so the rollout halts and fleet-control names the release before, which the agent then applies; a failed release is never retried. The service account needs get, list and patch on Deployments, create and get on Jobs, and get, create and patch on ConfigMaps in its namespace. Tests: fleetCellRelease.test (a real global fleet-control and a fake Kubernetes API: the documents gate; the Job, its Secret and its expected migrations; the order of expand, documents and zone-first rolls with fleet-control last; the state; migrations reported; a release under another key refused whole; a failed migration halting the rollout and going back with no migration; a stalled roll going back, the images already moved rolled back) and runnerDirectory.test (`checkExpected`). Health gates and passing verdicts are the next stage.
- D197 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9h2: health gates and verdicts; spec 11.2): every process now counts what its service listener answers on contract routes (status class and latency; never a path, a caller or anything carried), into a histogram whose buckets are fixed (50 ms to 10 s, and beyond), latency only for routes with no extended bound; a service may keep gauges beside it (`ServiceDependencies.signals`). In a cell whose Fleet agent it can reach (`SERVICE_URL_FLEET_CONTROL`, and no global-tier service in the process), it reports them every half minute (`reportProcessSignals`, PUT /v1/process-signals/:processId, callers every cell service) under `SILO_RELEASE`, which the Fleet agent now sets with each image so a process reports the Fleet release it runs. The outbox relay keeps two gauges, the backlog's oldest age and how much waits, read through the new definer function `platform.outbox_backlog()` (counted up to 100,000; dead letters excluded, they alert on their own), which `silo_outbox_relay` may execute beside its three. The Fleet agent keeps the latest report of each process in memory for a day (it runs as one replica) and, once a release applied in a started wave has run `FLEET_GATE_WINDOW_MINUTES` (15), judges it at each pull over the processes running it that reported in the last two minutes (cellSignals.service.ts, pure): error_rate at most 1% (no process reporting the release fails: a missing signal is a failure); latency, the 95th percentile within 2.5 s once 20 requests were timed; refusal_rate no more than twice the release before's share nor two points above it (once 50 and 100 requests answered), or a quarter with none to compare; crash_loops, the release's pods (by the silo.io/release annotation) neither crash looping, failing to pull or start, nor restarted three times, and some pod there; audit_outbox_backlog, the oldest unpublished event at most five minutes old as the relay reports it (none reporting fails). One failing gate is reported at once as a failing verdict (the rollout halts and the cell goes back); a passing verdict carries every gate, so until the synthetic question, subscription, Action and revert tests report (the next stage), the agent reports failures only. The service account also lists Pods. Tests: fleetCellRelease.test (a real process reporting its signals to the agent; SILO_RELEASE set with the image; not judged before the window; nothing passing until the synthetic tests have run; a pass completing the dev rollout; errors, refusals against the release before and a slow 95th percentile failing it and taking the cell back; crash loops, an old backlog and a synthetic test failing it), fleetGates.test (missing signals, little traffic, refusals with and without a release before, restarts, the percentile, the store), outboxRelay.test (the backlog).
- D198 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9h3: the synthetic tests; spec 11.2; decision 2026-11-18, Tommy: a synthetic organisation in every cell, dedicated and sovereign included): `iam.organisations.is_synthetic` (one a cell, never also the system organisation, frozen, insertable by `silo_auth` alone; the login and staff lookups exclude it) marks Silo's synthetic organisation. auth makes it at the Fleet agent's asking (`provisionSyntheticTenant`, PUT /v1/synthetic-tenant, callers fleet-control): enterprise plan, UTC, two members, proposer and approver, whose users have no password and are SSO-only with no provider (no one can sign in as them; addresses at `<cell>.silo.invalid`), each made in a transaction acting as that user (row-level security on users) so a cut-short provisioning resumes, found through the definer functions `iam.synthetic_organisation_id()` and `iam.synthetic_members()`, and granted Super admin by `iam.grant_synthetic_members` (there alone, once). `issueSyntheticSession` mints a member a complete session through the sessions service (method `synthetic`, a new `iam.sessions.auth_method`; 30 minutes) for the agent alone, so no password or client secret exists to keep. The agent serves a fixture source (syntheticFixture.service.ts) on `FLEET_SYNTHETIC_PORT`, exposed by the cell's ingress at `FLEET_SYNTHETIC_URL`: three probes behind a bearer token the agent sets on the connection each round (new each start), read with `?id=` or `?since=` an `updated_at` watermark, created, changed and deleted, each change posted to the connection's stream webhook signed as its manifest verifies, its `updated_at` the sequence both the webhook and the poll order by. It drives the cell through the gateway's public listener (`FLEET_GATEWAY_URL`, origin `FLEET_GATEWAY_ORIGIN`) as the two members, as a browser does (publicApi.service.ts: the session cookie, Origin, x-silo-csrf, an idempotency key, each answer checked against its route), and over the live WebSocket. Setup (syntheticTests.service.ts), each step recorded in the ConfigMap `silo-fleet-synthetic` so a restart resumes it: a scope type and scope; the connector and its manifest (REST, bearer, writes, a change stream of webhook and poll); the connection, probed, through a conformance run, confirmed and activated; its write class and writes enabled; its stream enabled and its change-stream class passed (subscribable); the approver granted read; the probe object type on a branch, proposed by the proposer, approved by the approver, merged; a saved set of probes; an Action type setting a probe's score (data risk, one approver by default). Each round, every `FLEET_SYNTHETIC_MINUTES` (10), under the release the cell runs: synthetic_question, a structured plan over the probes answering at least three; synthetic_subscription, a live subscription to the saved set opening with its snapshot and then carrying the Action's change as a delta; synthetic_action, the Action proposed by one and approved by the other, completed; synthetic_revert, its revert approved likewise, completed with the score back. The latest round's results per release feed the gates (D197), so a cell can now report a passing verdict. Found and fixed: no public route forwarded `policy.grantConnection`, so no administrator could give a member access to a connection through the API; `grantConnection` (POST /governance/connection-grants, policy's delegation rules decide) is added beside its revoke, and the web client's route list regenerated. Tests: syntheticTenant.test (made once, for the agent alone, two Super admins, no login; a member's session minted complete and resolved), fleetSynthetic.test (a cell behind its public gateway and its agent: the whole setup through the public API as two people and a round of the four tests passing, the score back after the revert; a second round reusing the setup).
- D199 (implementation 2026-11-18, backend stage P9h4: the cell's reports; spec 6.3, 11.5, 11.6, 13.4): the cell's Fleet agent now reports to the global tier every `FLEET_REPORT_SECONDS` (60), each part on its own, whether or not it applies releases (cellReports.service.ts). - D206 (implementation 2026-11-19, backend stage P9n: the sovereign cell's Thales Luna; spec 6.5, 61; decision 2026-11-14): no table change. The PKCS#11 adapter (D90) gains profiles. `PKCS11_PROFILE=luna`, required in production for a sovereign cell's `pkcs11_hsm`, names the partition by its token label (`PKCS11_TOKEN_LABEL`, required; an HA group's virtual slot has one too, where slot numbers move), logs in as the partition's Crypto User (Luna's CKU_CRYPTO_USER, CKU_VENDOR_DEFINED + 1), which uses keys and can never create or change them, and lets the HSM generate each AES-GCM IV: in FIPS mode Luna refuses an IV from the caller and returns the one it made after the ciphertext and tag, 16 bytes before firmware 7.9.3 and the asked-for 12 from 7.9.3; both are read back, and an IV that is missing or the zeros given is refused (`kms.pkcs11_hsm.iv_not_generated`). `generic` (any other module, the default) keeps the host's fresh 12-byte IV and takes the slot by number or label (one of the two). A wrapped DEK under either profile is stored as one byte giving the IV's length, the IV, the ciphertext and the tag (nothing was yet wrapped in an HSM, so no earlier format is read). A session the HSM lost (CKR_SESSION_HANDLE_INVALID, CKR_SESSION_CLOSED, CKR_DEVICE_ERROR, CKR_DEVICE_REMOVED, CKR_TOKEN_NOT_PRESENT, CKR_USER_NOT_LOGGED_IN: a network HSM's failover) is opened and logged in again once before an operation fails. Verifying a wrap key now wraps and unwraps under the profile, so the credential service's start-up check proves a real Luna's behaviour at commissioning, and a profile that does not match the HSM refuses the start. Tests: pkcs11.test against a fake module behaving as Thales documents a Luna in FIPS mode at both firmware lines, and as a generic module (the Crypto User's login, the HSM's IV at its length, binding refused, a mismatched profile either way, a missing partition, a wrong PIN, failover); the real-module test when TEST_PKCS11_MODULE is set; config.test (the sovereign rules). The Crypto User's numeric user type and the FIPS IV return follow Thales's documentation and have not been run against a Luna here.

An MQTT source may declare `payload: 'sparkplug_b'` (its topic filter in the spBv1.0 namespace, checked with the manifest). - D212 (implementation 2026-11-22, Silo contents held in BigQuery across a tenant migration; spec 6.4, 66, 68, 69): no table change. A move carries the organisation's rows and Silo files; what a cell holds in BigQuery stays behind, so siloes-capture now moves it at each end, asked by tenant-migrations only where the organisation holds a Silo and Siloes move with it. Moved in (`adoptMovedSiloes`, at the destination, before the directory names it): each Import Silo's rows rebuilt in this cell's dataset (siloes-import `rebuildImportSilo`): a tabular file read again from its moved bytes, a document's rows from its stored extractions opened under the organisation's moved keys, so no model is called and nothing is charged again, a confirmed value loaded certain (the loader now takes `certain`); each Object Index nomination rebuilt (index-builder `rebuildIndexType`, which siloes-capture may call for no member; its refresh fills once the sources are re-authorised); the Warehouse, the organisation's own project, adopted (warehouse-provisioner `adoptWarehouse`: this cell's writers granted on the dataset and as job users, then a sync, retried on schedule). Moved out (`releaseMovedSiloes`, at the source, before it purges): each Import dataset and Object Index dataset of the organisation dropped from this cell, and this cell's Warehouse access revoked (`releaseWarehouse`); until now the source left them behind. Capture lives in Postgres and moved with the rows. Each step is safe to run again: a stage that fails is tried on the next tick. Tests: siloes (released, then rebuilt with the confirmed value certain, no model call, no charge), warehouse (released and adopted), tenantMigrations.
- D213 (implementation 2026-11-23, reads the web client's Governance and Connect pages need; W6, W7): no table change. (1) A member listed by name: policy `listMembers` now gives each member's `displayName` and `email`, read through `iam.member_profiles` (the organisation's people only), so a page that says who did something never shows an id. (2) A connector version's setup form: connect-registry `getConnectorSetup` (gateway `GET /connect/connectors/:connectorId/setup`, connection.create) gives the parameters it declares and its auth strategy's fields by name, kind, label and role, its objects by name, and whether it runs through the Silo Agent; never a value and never the manifest, whose endpoints, mappings and expressions stay with the services. (3) Where a member may act: policy `listPermittedScopes` (gateway `GET /session/permitted-scopes?permission=`, own records) lists the live scopes where the caller holds a scoped permission, by the same rule as `decide` (a principal also within its owner's authority); a form offers them before the person tries, and every action is still decided when taken. Not audited: it changes and refuses nothing. (4) The OAuth callback is the web client's `/connect/oauth/` page, which OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI names. Tests: policyAdmin (names; permitted scopes agree with authorise), connect (setup form), web governance and connect browser tests. Also: the Warehouse as-of tests waited on the wrong sync once D212's adopt started one in the background; they now wait for it to finish (the service was right).
- D214 (implementation 2026-11-23, the Studio runtime's data and expressions; spec 35.2, 35.5, 35.6; W9): no table change. An app's object set variable is a definition (a type, a CEL filter over `object` and the app's parameters, optional hops) and its members are never stored, so the web runtime asks Studio to run it: studio `runAppVariable` (gateway `POST /studio/apps/:appId/variables/:variable/runs`) loads the version the viewer may open (as `openApp` does: the published one, or a draft for its author and co-editors), turns the variable into a set definition and has the executor run it under the viewer's own access. The executor's `runObjectSet` now takes a definition given whole as well as a saved set's id (exactly one), with `bindings`: the app's parameter variables bound by name as CEL variables, never written into the predicate; an unset one is null; only the app's declared parameters are accepted. Bindings join the result cache key, so one value never answers for another. A new run trigger `app_widget` records why. Answers are complete or refused (never truncated), so the runtime's metrics, charts and filter controls compute over the whole answer, pages read in full. Visibility rules and event conditions are CEL too; rather than ship a CEL engine to the browser (a new library), studio `evaluateAppExpressions` evaluates them against the viewer's current values with the validator's own compile and bounds; a rule that fails does not hold. Tests: studioRuntime (bound parameters, unset is null, own parameters and object set variables only, not found for someone it is not shared with; expressions), query and askEngine (saved sets unchanged), web studio browser test.
- D215 (implementation 2026-11-23, large uploads from the browser; spec 41.4; W11): no table change. A file larger than one request goes from the browser straight to the object store on a signed, short-lived URL (`beginFileUpload`); the pages' policy allowed connections to the public origin only, so the browser refused it. The gateway now takes `GATEWAY_UPLOAD_ORIGINS` (comma-separated origins, each checked as an origin, https in production) and adds exactly those to `connect-src`; nothing else in the policy changes. The web client follows Cloud Storage's resumable protocol (the signed POST opens a session, the bytes are PUT to the session it names) and S3's single signed request otherwise. Test: gatewayWebClient (the origin in connect-src, a non-origin refused).
- D216 (implementation 2026-11-23, the Clone Canvas in the web client; spec 29, 30; W13): no table change. The canvas opens a saved canvas view under the opener's permissions, subscribes its set over the live socket (snapshot pages, deltas acknowledged, a sequence gap answered with a resync, heartbeats returned, reconnection with backoff except when the session ended or the set is forbidden) and keeps values in page memory only. Layouts are offered from the type's clone layout configuration (schematic by stage, timeline by time and lane, map by a Located property, hierarchy by the containment link, graph by a link between members of the type), the list always beside them; edges come from one plan hop along the link under the opener's access. Positions are computed in a Web Worker; members a layout cannot place are counted and listed with the reason. Drawing is WebGL through deck.gl (`@deck.gl/core` and `@deck.gl/layers` 9.4.1, installed on Tommy's approval 2026-11-23); without WebGL the list stands in, with the reason. Normal clones are neutral, the accent marks the selection and a change for two seconds, and the change rail is a rate-limited polite live region. The 3D asset view (three.js) is not offered, the spec leaving its first-release scope open. A gateway fix came with it: every file the gateway served carried the API's `default-src 'none'` policy, and a dedicated worker takes the policy of its own script, so the worker could load none of its chunks; scripts from the web root now carry a worker policy (`script-src 'self'`, `connect-src` as the pages'), which a page's own scripts ignore. Tests: gatewayWebClient (the script policy), web canvas browser test (live, schematic, not placed, list, object panel, a webhook on the change rail).
- D217 (implementation 2026-11-23, site plans on the canvas; spec 29.4, 32.8): no table change (`clone.canvas_views.plan_id` already existed, checked to the map layout). (1) A plan's image: canvas-layout `readSpatialPlanImage` (gateway `GET /canvas/spatial-plans/:planId/image`, clone.view) serves the PNG or JPEG the plan was registered from, base64, to a reader holding every marking on the plan; a purged plan has none. (2) Where objects stand: `placeOnSpatialPlan` (gateway `POST /canvas/spatial-plans/:planId/placements`, clone.view) takes the caller's own reading of up to 20,000 objects (values used for the answer, never kept) and places each by its own anchor, else by the first predicate anchor it matches (CEL over the type's properties by API name, bounded; a property the caller may not see arrives absent, so a predicate over it places nothing), else, on a georeferenced plan, by the least-squares affine fit through its control points (`fitGeoreference`, none from fewer than three or points on a line) applied to its WGS 84 position (`readPosition`); the rest are named with why. (3) A canvas view keeps its plan: `planId` on the configuration (only with spatial_map, only a live plan whose markings the saver holds); on open a purged plan falls back to the map with the reason, and one whose markings the opener lacks is withheld as part of a reduced open. Also: new public routes must be listed in their module's route list (CLONE_ROUTES, QUERY_ROUTES, SIMULATION_ROUTES) to be served; the three added here and in D219 and D220 are. Tests: spatialAssets (image, placements in order, georeference, a view's plan and its fallback).
- D218 (implementation 2026-11-23, one set of canvas layouts, and the canvas's level of detail and moves; spec 28.4, 29.2, 29.3, 29.6, 29.8, 29.9): no table change. The client's layouts moved into the server as `canvas-layout/canvasLayouts.service.ts`, which the web client's worker imports (app/web's Turbopack root is now app/), so a canvas laid out in the browser and one exported are one drawing. The layout engine now names the edges it reversed to break cycles (`backEdges`, drawn distinctly) and each member's container (`parents`). Added: the layered graph (offered for a directed link), nested hierarchy regions to three levels with each container's count per state, the present on a timeline with what is still to come labelled expected, British National Grid read through OSGB36 and the national Helmert transformation (about five metres; a coordinate system other than WGS 84 and EPSG:27700 is named as not converted), and the site plan layout, first in precedence. In the client: clusters at low zoom (a screen grid on a map or plan, the layout's own clusters elsewhere) with their count per state, labels only where they do not collide, the selection, pins and expansions never folded in; each state drawn as its 28.4 glyph from an icon atlas (shape and colour, readable in greyscale), unknown never in the accent colour; arrows move the selection to the nearest clone that way (linked ones first), Enter opens it, L expands its links one hop from the object view's links (each hop's bound named where it stopped), focus one to three links deep, several selected by Shift-click, box, lasso, state or Shift and an arrow, a selection naming those hidden by the filter or not placed. A map without a tile service draws a coordinate grid and says the base map is unavailable. Tests: web layouts (layouts, grid reference against the Ordnance Survey's worked example, level of detail, navigation), cloneUnits (back edges, parents), web canvas browser tests.
- D219 (implementation 2026-11-23, an Action on a canvas selection; spec 29.6, 34.5): no table change. executor `resolveActionTargets` (gateway `POST /objects/action-targets`, mutation.propose): for up to 10,000 objects of a type and a confirmed Action type the caller may see, the records the type writes, by the object view's rule (the object's record in the first system the type may write through), read now under the caller's access with each object's source records; an object not read and one with no such record are excluded with why; a type that creates objects is refused. The canvas lists the targets by name, and the excluded with why, before proposing through the ordinary mutation path. Tests: objectViewActions.
- D220 (implementation 2026-11-23, time and scenarios on the canvas; spec 30.8, 30.9): no table change. Time: the canvas's time bar scrubs and compares over Capture (`getCloneStatesAt`, in batches of 500), drawing each clone's state then and what changed; Siloes switched off for an organisation is now answered as no Capture (available false, with the reason) rather than refused. Scenarios: simulation `getLatestSimulationRun` (gateway `GET /simulation/scenarios/:scenarioId/runs/latest`, own records) returns a scenario's latest completed run as stored, the graph's version now and whether it changed since, so the overlay draws without re-running; a re-run is offered, metered as a simulation. Affected clones carry a boxed badge with the scenario's label (fails, late by, out for, short by, probability with the smallest sample size, via a soft edge), stops are named, the header names the scenario while it is on, and a branch's staged values show as "Scenario: staged, not executed" once opened (metered as a re-run), promotion recorded from the canvas. Tests: simulation (latest run, graph changed), web canvas (time without Capture says why; no overlay unless chosen).
- D221 (implementation 2026-11-23, exports drawn as the canvas draws, and the Studio canvas widgets; spec 28.4, 29.10, 35.5): no table change. A PDF export now lays out with `canvasLayouts.service.ts` from the type's clone layout, follows the layout's links (one hop, as the exporter), places a site plan's objects with its rules and prints the plan under them (`render/pdfImage.service.ts`, no library: a JPEG as it is, a PNG decoded, its filters undone and its transparency a soft mask; CMYK, interlaced or over 25 million pixels are not printed, and the export says so), prints a map with the note that no base map is drawn, draws each state's glyph with its word, regions, guides, the present and cycle edges dashed, and leaves labels out above 500 objects, saying so. A 3D canvas is refused. canvas-layout `evaluateCloneStates` (gateway `POST /clones/states`, clone.view) gives states for values a caller read, from the type's active rule now (an input not sent or not visible is unknown with why; no rule, normal and said), for Studio's Clone Canvas embed and map, which draw an app's run (not a live subscription, and say so) with the canvas's layouts; the scenario control selects, creates and switches a branch held in the app's scenario variable and shows its staged Actions; the Ask panel is the viewer's own thread scoped to the app (found again on the next visit, begun when they first ask). Settings now sets web search per scope as well (D89's policy: on or off, domains allowed or blocked, on despite marked data only for an admin holding every marking there). The editor's Clone Canvas widget had an invalid default layout and no way to choose one; it now has both, and a selection to pick into. The web client's stylesheets used --accent-text and --danger-text (text on a filled accent or danger, white in the light theme) on light surfaces for links, the pressed chip, unavailable messages and the failed state; they now use --accent and --danger, and a test reads every stylesheet for it. Tests: canvasExport (a map exported with its count not placed; 3D refused), pdfImage, canvas (states for values read), web studio (a Clone Canvas widget), web contrast.
- D222 (implementation 2026-11-23, file shares through the Silo Agent; spec 14.4 "SFTP and file share", 10.4): no table change. A manifest may speak `file_share`: read by the agent only (transport.viaAgent), its root on the agent's host as `file:///…` (a share mounted there; a drive letter kept), no login (auth none: the host's own permissions and its owner's roots decide), objects shaped as SFTP's (a directory under the root, a file name pattern, CSV or JSON Lines, maxFiles and maxFileBytes), never written and never pushed down. The agent takes new work kinds `files.list` (the directory's regular files: name, size, modification time; never what lies below) and `files.read` (one regular file in chunks of 2 MiB, each naming its offset, within the cell's 4 MiB frames; a file over its bound, or grown past it since it was listed, refused, never cut), only where the root, directory and name joined, every link resolved, lie within one of the roots the host's owner configures (`fileRoots`, absolute, never the file system's root); none configured, nothing is read (target_refused); a path not there or not readable is refused as `not_found` or `permission`. The cell's engine is SFTP's: the read context's file access (`files`, renamed from `sftp`) goes through the credential service for SFTP and through the connection's agent for a file share (`filesFor`), and the parsing is one. SFTP through the agent is still refused: the Go agent has no SSH client, and adding one is a library to approve. Tests: agentFiles (through the built agent: rows in name order, a file over its bound, a missing directory, a link out of the share listed by no one, the manifest's rules), Go TestFiles (roots, links, chunks, bounds) and the configuration's refusals.
- D223 (implementation 2026-11-23, Action ledger copies owed; spec 48.2): `action.ledger_copies` (one per receipt, its id the receipt's: the store it goes to, its rows sealed to the row as the receipt's values are, since with the values option they hold record values; the row count, attempts, when it is next due and the last failure's code, never its text; tenant RLS; `action.ledger_copies_due`, security definer, identifiers only, for the cell-wide pass). The actions service writes one ledger row per object after the receipt; a copy that still fails after its brief retries was only logged, so the ledger could miss rows for good. It is now kept, and an always-running worker (as receipt purges are) sends due copies again: written, the copy goes; failing, it waits a minute doubling to six hours; with no Silo holding the ledger any more, or the ledger moved to the other store, it is dropped, as a ledger switched off writes nothing more. Rows are idempotent (their ids are the receipt's and the target's), so a copy sent twice adds nothing. A receipt purged while its copy is owed leaves the copy its references and outcomes and clears its values, as it does to rows already written. Tests: captureLedger (a copy kept while the store is away, sealed, then purged and written without values, then gone).
- D224 (decision 2026-11-23, the marketplace dropped; spec 16.5, 17 step 6, 76, 77): Tommy decided the marketplace does not fit the product. Removed: `connect.connector_promotions` (and its status and visibility triggers), `billing.marketplace_payouts` (and its key to the connector's author), the trust tier guard (`connect.connectors_trust_tier_guard`; the tier is now frozen with the row), the `community` connector kind and the `community` and `verified` tiers (connectors are `prebuilt`, certified, or `private`), the `promotion` derivation (a fork stays), the permissions connector.promote and connector.tier_promote (134 seeded), catalogue's promotion, review and tier paths, the admin portal's review queue, tier promotion and payout transfer routes with the catalogue.review and payouts.transfer staff capabilities, billing's payout transfer and the payment provider's transfers, the events connector_promotion_requested, connector_promotion_reviewed, connector_promotion_withdrawn, trust_tier_promoted and payout_calculated, payout_approved, payout_paid, payout_failed. Kept: `connect.connectors.author_organisation_id`, the organisation that wrote a private connector (now indexed on its own). The catalogue no longer needs redis. Tests: catalogue (browsing; the database refuses a community kind or tier, and a tier never changes), delegation (134 permissions), billing, adminPortalUnits.
- D225 (implementation 2026-11-23, PNG export from the person's own browser; spec 29.10; decision 2026-11-23, replacing the headless renderer of 2026-11-14): `clone.render_jobs` loses `rendering`, `claimed_at`, its queue index and `clone.claim_render_job`, and gains `printed_marking_ids` (frozen). Exporting a PNG runs the set as a PDF export does and answers `awaiting_image` with the job and its stamp: the markings the image must print, when the run was computed, each source by id, name and state age, and the flags. The browser draws the image itself (the canvas it shows, deck.gl keeping its drawing buffer), prints the stamp above it (markings first, the view and when it was drawn, each source's live state age by name, the flags, a scenario overlay's label or the past time where shown, the count not placed) and the state glyphs' legend below, and hands it back (`completeImageExport`, gateway `POST /canvas/render-jobs/:jobId/image`, file.export, the exporter's own job only): a PNG no wider than the job's canvas at its scale, filed as the exporter's export under the Files rules, and only if the canvas's inputs then carry no marking the image does not print (refused `canvas.markings_changed` otherwise). A job is completed once, before its hour runs out. No headless browser opens a canvas as anyone; the renderer's claim, complete and fail endpoints are gone. Tests: canvasExport (begun with its stamp, completed once, a non-PNG refused, another member's job not found), web canvas (exported as a PNG in a real browser, filed and completed).
- D226 (implementation 2026-11-23, SFTP through the Silo Agent; spec 14.4, 10.4, 10.7; golang.org/x/crypto/ssh and github.com/pkg/sftp approved 2026-11-23): no table change. An SFTP manifest may now set transport.viaAgent. The cell resolves the server from the manifest's sftp:// base and the connection's parameters (`utils/sftpTarget.util.ts`, shared with the credential service) and sends it with the pinned host_key_sha256 as `sftp.list` or `sftp.read` work; the connection's login, kept in the cell, is sealed to the agent for that work, now for an ssh_key login too (the private key and its passphrase join the sealed document; the agent holds them as locked secrets until parsed). The agent reaches only a host its owner's targets allow, at the addresses allowed; refuses any server key but the pinned one before offering the login (source_refused untrusted), and a refused login as source_refused login; lists a directory's regular files and reads a file in 2 MiB chunks within its bound. The read context's file access sends a file share's and an agent SFTP connection's reads to the agent (`filesFor`), and the parsing stays SFTP's. golang.org/x/crypto takes the password as a Go string and parses the key into its own structures, so for the session they live in Go's heap. Tests: agentSftp (through the built agent: rows parsed, a wrong password said as the server's refusal), Go TestSFTP (an in-process SSH server: list and read with a password and with a key, a key not pinned refused, a refused login, a host outside the targets, a file over its bound, a missing directory).
- D227 (implementation 2026-11-23, the base map under a map layout; spec 29.3, 29.12, 32.8; maplibre-gl and pmtiles approved 2026-11-23; replaces D87's signed URL): no table change. files reads the cell's Protomaps PMTiles archive (`tiles` bucket, `MAP_TILES_KEY`) by byte ranges with `pmtiles` through the store adapter's `getRange`, so every store serves it (GCS, S3-compatible, a self-managed one) and no URL to the store reaches the browser; the archive's header and directories are cached per process (a new archive goes under a new key). `mapTilesSource` (gateway `GET /map-tiles`, clone.view) now states the archive's format, zooms, bounds and attribution; `readMapTile` (gateway `GET /map-tiles/:z/:x/:y`, clone.view) answers one tile decompressed, none outside the archive's zooms, and `map_tiles.out_of_range` off the tile grid; an archive that is missing or not one is `map_tiles.unconfigured`, one of raster tiles `map_tiles.not_vector`. In the web client a map layout draws MapLibre under the deck.gl canvas, loaded only then, taking no input of its own: the canvas's camera moves it (layout units are Web Mercator, so a map zoom is the canvas zoom plus log2(WORLD/512)), hidden beyond MapLibre's 24 zooms. Its tiles come by a `silo://` protocol that calls the gateway, so the session and the gateway's checks apply to each; its worker is copied into the export at build (`public/maplibre/`, under the gateway's worker policy). The style is the Protomaps layers without labels, sprites or glyphs (no font service; labels would compete with the clones'), each colour a step off the theme's surface, so state stays what is seen first (29.7); the attribution is shown in the corner. A cell without tiles, a tile refused, a first tile that fails or three in a row give "Base map unavailable", with why, and the coordinate grid. A PNG export draws the base map under the canvas and prints its attribution; a PDF of a map still prints none, and says so. Fixed: on a layout change the canvas fitted its camera to the previous layout's positions (the new placement arrived later for the same members, so it never refitted); a placement now carries the layout it was made for, and the canvas is laying out until its own arrives. The grid's latitude labels were centred on the left edge and clipped; they start from it. Tests: mapTiles (an archive written byte by byte: metadata, a tile read by ranges, none beyond its zooms, off the grid refused, no archive), web baseMap (the camera, the style against MapLibre's validator, tile addresses), web canvas (a map over the cell's own tiles, the water drawn in the theme's colour at the centre, every tile through the gateway, exported with them; tiles that cannot be read give the note and the grid).
- D228 (implementation 2026-11-23, the 3D asset view; spec 29.2, 29.5, 29.6, 29.7, 29.10, 29.12, 58.6; three approved 2026-11-23): `clone.render_jobs` gains `drawn_plan_id` and `drawn_asset_model_id` (at most one, frozen, each with its index): what the exporter's browser drew besides the set. canvas-layout `readAssetModel` (gateway `GET /canvas/asset-models/:assetModelId/model?offset=`, clone.view) serves the checked .glb in parts of at most 4 MiB, the model's markings checked at every part, a purged model nothing; `placeOnAssetModel` (gateway `POST /canvas/asset-models/:assetModelId/placements`) names the node each object stands on, by its own anchor first and then the first predicate it matches (the plan's matching, now one function for both); an object no anchor places is named with why. A canvas view keeps `assetModelId` under the 3D layout only (`clone.model_needs_3d`), and on open a purged model falls back to the next layout with "The 3D model was purged, so the next layout is shown instead."; a model the opener may not read is counted as withheld. In the web client the 3D layout is offered first where the type's objects are anchored to a model (29.2's precedence), drawn with three.js: the model read in parts with its progress shown, parsed by GLTFLoader (Draco, meshopt and KTX2 decoded by three's own decoders, copied into the export under `/three/`, which is why pages now allow `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`: WebAssembly compiled, never JavaScript evaluated), drawn in quiet neutrals (a part an anchor names a step stronger, the selection's parts tinted with the accent; the model's own colours are a layer, off at first), so state is told only by the 28.4 glyphs, drawn over it on a second canvas with labels that do not collide, several clones on one part as the worst state with a count. Orbit, pan and zoom (OrbitControls, no damping), frame all and frame the selection (one step, never animated); click, Shift-click, box, lasso and the arrow keys over where each clone is on screen. A PNG export takes both canvases. Fixed: an export that drew a site plan carried the set's markings but not the plan's own; files `previewExportMarkings` and `createExport` now take `carriedMarkingIds` (each must exist, `files.marking_unknown`), which the file carries and freezes with its inherited markings, and canvasExport passes the plan's (PDF of a site plan) or what the browser drew (PNG). Not built: mesh compression where absent and up to three levels of detail at upload (29.5 targets; they need a mesh library, to be approved), and a saved camera (29.6, for every layout).
