Tests: spatialAssets (a model read whole and from an offset, placement by anchor then predicate, a view keeping its model and falling back when it is purged), files (a carried marking printed, stored and frozen; refused unprinted; an unknown one refused), gatewayWebClient (the page policy), web modelScene (groups by node, framing distance, labels), web canvas (a real .glb imported into a Silo, contacts on its parts by predicate, neutral until the model's own colours are asked for, the keyboard over what is on screen, the selection framed, exported with the model recorded on the job).
- D229 (implementation 2026-11-23, app branches; beyond the spec: the first of the Foundry-comparison features Tommy asked for on 2026-11-23, no chapter covers it): `workspace.app_branches` (an app's line of work beside main: its name, unique among the app's open branches; the published version it was opened from, the base of its merge; an ontology branch it may be built on; open, merged with the main version its merge became, or abandoned; frozen identity) and `workspace.app_versions.branch_id` (a branch's draft, one per branch, only ever a draft: a check and a unique index). A branch is opened by an editor (owner or edit share) of an app with a published version, from that version; built on an ontology branch, its draft validates against that branch's head (studio's check now takes a branch; reading a branch needs `ontology.branch`, so an editor without it is refused). Its draft is saved like main's, with findings, and never submitted (`studio.branch_draft_merges`): it merges into main's next draft by a three-way merge of the definitions' structure (`studio/appMerge.service.ts`, pure): variables by name, pages and their widgets by id, event bindings by their source, Functions and Action types as sets (a removal on one side honoured), a page's title and the mobile settings as values; the same change on both sides taken once, a change on one side taken, different changes to one element a conflict named by its path (`pages.home.widgets.peak`) and returned with base, main and branch until a person decides each (main's or the branch's); order is main's unless only the branch reordered. The merged draft takes main's head ontology version, is validated against main, and goes to review like any draft (author never reviewer). A merge waits while main has a draft or a version in review (`studio.main_in_progress`), and a branch on an ontology branch merges only once that branch has (`studio.ontology_branch_open`, `studio.ontology_branch_abandoned`). Comparing two versions lists each element added, removed or changed by the same paths. Abandoning keeps the record. Events `app_branch_opened`, `app_branch_merged` (decisions counted), `app_branch_abandoned`. In the web client the editor works on main or on a branch; the branches panel opens, compares, merges (each conflict shown both ways with a choice) and abandons. Fixed: the editor's reloads could land for the line worked on before a switch. Tests: appMerge (both sides kept, conflicts decided, compare), studioBranches (opened from the published version, a branch draft refused review, both sides' changes merged, main busy refused, a conflict decided, an ontology branch's merge waiting and its read needing ontology.branch, abandoned kept), web studio (a branch opened, a widget added, compared, merged into main's next draft).
- D230 (implementation 2026-11-23, staged releases of an app; beyond the spec, the second part of app branching and release): `workspace.app_releases` (a published version rolled out: the version it brings, the version everyone not yet reached keeps, rolling out, complete or rolled back; one rolling out per app, a unique index) and `workspace.app_release_stages` (up to five, each one to twenty scopes, each with its subtree; released by whom and when). A reviewer approves a version in stages (`approveVersion` with `stages`, app.publish in every scope named); it is published as any version and its first stage released at once. Which version a viewer opens without naming one is now decided by the app's latest release: a member of a released stage's scope or of a scope below one opens the new version, everyone else the version before; editors (owner, edit shares) always open the newest; once the last stage is released the release completes and everyone opens it; rolled back (`rollBackAppRelease`), everyone opens the version before again and the new one stays published for its editors to fix or replace. The next release keeps everyone else on what they open then, never on a rolled-back version. A first version reaches everyone (`studio.release_needs_previous`), and no version is approved while a release rolls out (`studio.release_in_progress`). `promoteAppRelease` releases the next stage (app.publish in its scopes) and the last completes it. Events `app_release_started`, `app_release_stage_released`, `app_release_completed`, `app_release_rolled_back`. In the web client a version in review can be approved in stages (scopes per stage) and the rollout panel shows each stage, releases the next and rolls back. Tests: studioReleases (stages by scope subtree, the owner on the newest, one release at a time, completion, rollback, the next release after a rollback), web studio (approved in stages from the editor, shown rolling out, rolled back).
- D231 (implementation 2026-11-23, app packages between organisations; beyond the spec, the release-to-environments part of app branching and release): `files.file_provenance.source_app_version_id` (source kind `app_package`, with its index; only studio may file one, `files.app_package_source_refused`). An editor (owner or edit share) exports a published version (`studio.package_needs_published` for a draft) as a package into Files (`exportAppPackage`, keyed, file.export decided by Files): JSON naming its format and version, the app's name and description, the source version, the markings it carries by name (printed, as every export prints them), the definition, and every ontology element the definition names anywhere (a widget's columns, a filter's properties, a text's `{{label:…}}`) by kind and API name, a property with its type's (`studio/appPackage.service.ts`, pure). Its lineage input is the app version and it carries the version's markings (D228's carried markings), so the file is governed as any export. Imported (`importAppPackage`, keyed, app.create), each element is found in this organisation's main ontology and Action types by API name and its id put in place in one pass (an id replaced is never replaced again); what is not found is named in the answer and the draft's validation says what it breaks; the draft is validated against main's head. It becomes a new app's first draft, or main's next draft of an app the person may edit (refused while that app has a draft or a version in review). A keyed retry answers the file, or the app and draft, the first request made. Events `app_package_exported`, `app_package_imported`. In the web client an editor exports from the app's release section, and Studio's directory imports a package file, listing what was not found. Fixed: the lineage architecture rule counts app version inserts by file; branch drafts now go through `apps.service.ts`'s `insertDraft`, where versions' lineage is written at publication. Tests: studioPackages (the mapping, export through Files, an import from another organisation's ids mapped back to the same app, a missing element named with findings, into an existing app, a file that is not a package refused), web studio (exported, then imported from the file as a new app).
- D232 (implementation 2026-11-23, workbooks: spreadsheets over live data; beyond the spec, the first half of spreadsheets and reports): permission `workbook.save` (members hold it; 135 permissions, Super admin 127); `workspace.workbooks` (owner, name, the document as typed, derived visibility, archive); `workspace.view_shares.workbook_id` (a share to open, view, or to copy, copy; one per workbook and grantee); `files.file_provenance.source_workbook_id` (kind `workbook`); lineage node kind `workbook`. A workbook's document holds up to twenty sheets of cells as typed (values, or formulas beginning with "=", at most 50,000 cells) and up to ten live ranges, each an object set, its properties (up to thirty), an anchor cell and a limit (up to a thousand). Formulas are a closed language (`workspace/formula.service.ts`, pure, the same module in the browser through the web client's Turbopack root): numbers, text, booleans, blanks and errors; references, sheet-qualified references and ranges; arithmetic, comparison and concatenation with spreadsheet precedence; SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTBLANK, IF, IFERROR, AND, OR, NOT, ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, ABS, INT, SQRT, POWER, MOD, LEN, UPPER, LOWER, TRIM, CONCAT, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, SUMIF, COUNTIF, AVERAGEIF, VLOOKUP, INDEX, MATCH and TODAY (the evaluation date the caller gives); no function reaches outside the workbook; a cycle evaluates to #CYCLE! and a formula that does not parse to #PARSE!, never a loop or a refusal. Saving (the owner, workbook.save) checks each live range is on a sheet, inside the grid, over no typed cell and no other range, and over a set and properties of its type the owner may see; anyone else is told it does not exist before anything of the edit is read. A live range is read for whoever opens the workbook, as them (`readWorkbookRanges`: the executor's object set run, its pages up to the limit; a property the opener may not see left blank and counted; a set they may not read refused with why); nothing read is stored. Shared like a saved view (37.4, the owner's policy as ceiling), to open or to copy; copying needs a copy share and workbook.save. An export (`exportWorkbook`, keyed, file.export through Files) reads the ranges as the exporter, evaluates every formula over them, and files a spreadsheet of values only (`render/xlsx.service.ts renderWorkbookXlsx`: a sheet per sheet, text as inline strings, no formula), with a first sheet printing its markings and any range not read for the exporter; its lineage is the workbook and the type versions and connections its ranges read, so it carries their markings. Events `workbook_created`, `workbook_saved`, `workbook_archived`, `workbook_shared`, `workbook_share_revoked`, `workbook_exported`. In the web client workbooks are a tab of Studio (the rail stays spec 33.3's eleven items): a directory and an editor whose grid is a window moved by keys, the wheel and Go to (no style attribute), a formula bar, sheets, live ranges inserted at the selected cell and shown apart, sharing, copying and export. Tests: formula (precedence, functions, lookups, cycles and parse errors, live values), workbooks (refusals of a range over typed cells, an overlap and a foreign property; read for the owner; shared to open and to copy; exported with its formula computed over the live range and the type's marking printed), web studio (typed, a live range inserted, its SUM computed as the server computes it, exported). Test cells start workspace after Files, which it now calls.
- D233 (implementation 2026-11-23, reports; beyond the spec, the second half of spreadsheets and reports): permission `report.save` (members hold it; 136 permissions, Super admin 128); `workspace.reports` (as workbooks: owner, name, the document as written, derived visibility, archive); `workspace.view_shares.report_id` (view or copy); `files.file_provenance.source_report_id` (kind `report`); lineage node kind `report`. A report's document is up to a hundred blocks in order: a heading (title or section), text, an object set's objects with up to twelve properties and a limit (up to 500), or a rectangle of a workbook's computed cells (up to 12 columns by 500 rows, the first row as the header where asked). Saving (the owner, report.save) checks each objects block's set and properties as workbook ranges are checked, and that each workbook block's workbook is one the owner may open, with that sheet. Reading (`readReportBlocks`) reads every live block for whoever opens the report, as them: objects through the same read as a workbook's live range, figures by opening the workbook as them, reading its ranges and evaluating its formulas (`workbookFigures`), a workbook that does not reach them refused with why; nothing read is stored. Shared and copied as workbooks are; the sharing of both is now one module (`workspace/documentShares.service.ts`) over the share rows' document arms (`viewShareRepo.*Document`, a fixed column per arm). An export (`exportReport`, keyed) reads the blocks as the exporter and files a PDF (`render/pdf.service.ts renderReportPdf`: portrait A4, headings, wrapped paragraphs, tables repeating their header across pages, notes for a block not shown or cut, the markings at the head and foot of every page); its lineage is the report and what its blocks read, so it carries their markings. Events `report_created`, `report_saved`, `report_archived`, `report_shared`, `report_share_revoked`, `report_exported`. In the web client reports are Studio's third tab: a directory and an editor of blocks (add, edit, move, remove), each live block shown as the person sees it, sharing, copying and export. Tests: reports (refusals of a workbook the owner may not open and a foreign property; the figures computed and the first objects read for the owner; a recipient refused the workbook not shared with them; the PDF's text and markings), web studio (text, workbook figures and a table of suppliers saved, shown and exported).
- D234 (implementation 2026-11-23, process mining; beyond the spec): permission `process.save` (members hold it); `workspace.process_analyses` (owner, name, document: the source and an optional reference model; derived visibility; archive), shared as workbooks and reports are (`view_shares.process_analysis_id`, the generic document sharing), `files.file_provenance.source_process_analysis_id` (kind `process_analysis`), lineage kind `process_analysis`. The model generator learnt the plural `process_analyses`. A source is either events (an object set whose objects are events: its case, activity and time properties, up to 50,000 read) or a state property's captured changes (Capture's `readHistory`, which now lets workspace call it: a case is an object, an activity a value it moved into, with the value it left at its first observed change so where it started is not lost). Mining is pure (`workspace/processMining.service.ts`): each case's events in time order are its trace; activities with their events, cases, starts and ends; the directly-follows steps with how often, in how many cases, and their median and 90th-percentile times (nearest rank); the twenty commonest variants with share and median duration; case durations; rework (an activity done more than once in a case); and, against the owner's reference model (allowed steps, starts and ends), the cases that fit and the deviating steps, starts and ends. An analysis is mined for whoever opens it, as them (`readProcessAnalysis`): a set they may not read, a history withheld, no Capture Silo, or Capture unreachable is said, never an error; events without a case, an activity or a readable time are skipped and counted; nothing read is stored. Exported into Files as a PDF of the same tables (its lineage the analysis, the type versions and connections it read, or the Capture Silo for history, as recognition records its reads). Report tables now size their columns by content. Events `process_analysis_created`, `process_analysis_saved`, `process_analysis_archived`, `process_shared`, `process_share_revoked`, `process_analysis_exported`. In the web client process analyses are Studio's Processes tab: the source and reference model (a step per line), the process map (activities placed by the canvas's layered-graph layout, steps drawn thicker as they are taken more often, labelled with count and median time; SVG with classes), variants, steps, rework and conformance. Tests: processMining (quantiles, the graph with timings, variants, durations, rework, conformance, events from captured changes), processes (an event set mined with conformance; a foreign property refused; a recipient without access refused; Capture unreachable said; the PDF's tables), web studio (an analysis drawn as a map).
- D235 (implementation 2026-11-23, data pipelines; beyond the spec): permission `pipeline.save` (members hold it; 138 permissions, Super admin 130); `workspace.pipelines` (owner, name, document; archive) and `workspace.pipeline_runs` (running, completed with its rows and the Import Silo file it wrote, or failed with why; no values). A pipeline's inputs are up to five object sets, each with up to fifty properties (its columns named by the properties' API names) and a limit (up to 50,000); its steps are a closed set (`workspace/pipelineEngine.service.ts`, pure): filter by a CEL condition, compute a column from a CEL expression (CEL compiled by the expression evaluator, server-side, every column dyn, within bounds; a row an expression fails on is left out of a filter and blank in a computed column), select (rename, reorder, drop), join another input on equal keys (inner or left; its columns prefixed with its name; at most 200,000 rows), aggregate (count, count distinct, sum, average, minimum, maximum), dedupe, sort, limit; a step's error names the step. A preview runs the steps over the inputs as the person reads them and keeps nothing (the first hundred rows, the total, each input's rows, cut or withheld columns, and the step that failed). A run (the owner, keyed) reads the inputs as them, runs the steps and writes the table as CSV (RFC 4180, a cell that would start a formula given a leading quote) into an Import Silo source through siloes-import's upload (which now lets workspace call it, deciding silo.import as the person), so the output is the customer's, in a Silo they chose, with its retention, and is read through the Silo's connection like any other data. A run never declassifies: it is refused unless the output Silo carries every marking of what the inputs read (worked out as an export's would be), and the refusal names the missing markings. Every run is recorded (`pipeline_run_started`, `pipeline_run_completed`, `pipeline_run_failed`; also `pipeline_created`, `pipeline_saved`, `pipeline_archived`). Scheduling runs is not built: a pipeline runs when its owner runs it. In the web client pipelines are Studio's Pipelines tab: inputs with their properties' API names, steps in order (a form per kind), the output Silo (a source of the pipeline's own made in it), preview, runs. The Files test cell can start Import Siloes. Tests: pipelineEngine (the steps, a join's two kinds, errors naming their step, CSV), pipelines (preview and a failing step; a run into a Silo source; refused until the Silo carries the inputs' marking; a member without silo.import refused and the run recorded failed), web studio (a pipeline's preview grouping suppliers by region).
- D236 (implementation 2026-11-23, AI agents; beyond the spec): what a customer builds of Ask for a purpose. Called "AI agents" throughout (`ai_agent.*`) because `agent.*` already names the Silo Agent. Permission `ai_agent.save` (members hold it; 139 permissions, Super admin 131). `workspace.ai_agents` (owner, name, description, a brief of up to 8,000 characters, up to fifty object type ids, tools: a non-empty subset of answer, find_objects, propose_action, propose_cron; visibility; archive; lock version); `workspace.ask_threads.ai_agent_id` (set when the thread is made, frozen, never on a saved view's thread; indexed); a `view_shares.ai_agent_id` arm, shared to ask (view) or to copy (copy) through the one document-sharing module, whose arms now carry their column, audited resource type and noun in one table. Saving screens the name and brief with the shared value-pattern detector (both reach a model with every question; `workspace.ai_agent_value_pattern`) and checks each type is in the ontology; holders see the brief, since what shapes an answer is never hidden from the asker. Asking: `createThread` takes `aiAgentId` (the person's own, or one shared with them live under its owner's policy, not archived; titled by the agent unless named); every question re-checks that and refuses a tool the agent does not allow (`ask.ai_agent_unavailable`, `ask.ai_agent_archived`, `ask.ai_agent_tool`) before compile; Ask's query engine sends the agent to `compileQuestion` (`aiAgent`: id, name, brief, types, tools). Compile offers the model only the agent's types of those the reader may see (`withinAiAgent`, before a clarification's narrowing and the large-vocabulary narrowing; links only between types kept), refuses when none is visible (`compile.ai_agent_nothing_visible`), sends the brief as the first documentation entry (title "AI agent brief: <name>"; a value pattern the gateway finds there is refused as the brief's, `compile.ai_agent_brief_refused`), adds one constant instruction line saying how such documentation is used, does not offer changes or Crons to the model when the agent proposes neither, and refuses a change or Cron the agent's tools do not allow before anything is charged (`compile.ai_agent_tool`). Instructions stay constant and no record value reaches a model (62.1). The plan runs as the asker; a proposed change or Cron stays a draft a person submits. `compile_requested` carries `ai_agent_id`; `ask_question_compiled` carries `ai_agent_id` and `ai_agent_version` (the agent's lock version), so a reviewer sees which agent, as saved when, shaped a plan. Events `ai_agent_created` (with `copied_from`), `ai_agent_saved`, `ai_agent_archived`, `ai_agent_shared`, `ai_agent_share_revoked` (counts and lengths, never the brief). In the web client AI agents are Studio's "AI agents" tab (directory; editor with name, description, brief with its length, types from the reader's vocabulary, what it may do, shares; a read-only view with the brief for holders, and a copy for a copy share; "Talk to it" starts an Ask thread), and Ask's thread shows the agent, what it may do and its brief, offers "Ask an AI agent" beside "New thread", and asks with the agent's first tool where it does not answer questions. Tests: aiAgents (types, value patterns, stale saves, owner-only edits; shares to ask and to copy; archive), ask (a thread with an agent: the brief and tools sent to compile, the agent version audited, a tool refused before compile, a share revoked and an agent archived stopping the next question), query (the brief as documentation, only the agent's types offered, nothing visible refused, a brief with an email refused as the brief's, a change it may not propose refused uncharged), askEngine (the agent forwarded; intents off when it proposes nothing), delegation (139/131), web studio (made, a brief with an email refused, saved with a type, talked to in Ask with its brief shown and sent).
- D237 (implementation 2026-11-23, media sets; beyond the spec): the first half of unstructured media. `files.media_sets` (owner, name, description, the Import Silo its items are kept in; archive; lock), `files.media_items` (its Files upload, kind image/video/audio/document, type, size, frame size, duration, pages, `captured_at` as checked text `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS`, the camera's local time, since it names no instant and timestamps are timestamptz; removal leaves the upload in Files) and `files.media_set_shares` (membership, scope or organisation; view or contribute; as file shares: never a marking). `siloes.silo_files.content_class` gains `media`: such a file is kept as its own type and never read by the import worker. A pure parser (`siloes-import/mediaFacts.service.ts`, no library) reads, from a file's first and last 512 KiB, its kind and type and what its bytes say: PNG, JPEG (size turned by EXIF orientation; DateTimeOriginal), GIF, WebP (VP8, VP8L, VP8X), AVIF (ispe); MP4 and QuickTime (mvhd duration, a video track's tkhd frame, its index at either end; an audio-only file is audio), WebM and Matroska (EBML Info and Tracks, an unknown-size segment included); WAV, FLAC (STREAMINFO), Ogg (Vorbis, Opus with pre-skip; length from the last page), MP3 (Xing/Info or VBRI frames, else constant bitrate behind an ID3 tag); PDF page count from a readable page tree. A fact it cannot read is left out; SVG is never media. Storing a Files upload with `media: true` refuses, before anything is stored, what is not media (`import.not_media`) and answers with the facts; a retried store reads them again from the stored file's ends. Access, decided here (see the coverage's note for the spec owner): making a set and adding to it need `file.upload` and the Silo's own checks (silo.import on it, its markings, open: `checkFilesSilo`); seeing a set needs ownership or a live share (Files' sharing rules: `file.share`, organisation-wide only where permitted); opening an item needs that, every marking on the Silo (checked by the Silo at every open), and the Silo open, but not silo.import, through `openMediaUpload`, which opens only media-class files and is callable only by files. An item opens in the reply up to the reply bound, else, or when asked (video and audio, so they seek), through a signed short-lived link where storage signs one; the page policy now allows the object store's origins (and blob:) for images and media. Opening and its refusal are recorded as for any file (`file_opened`, `file_download_refused`, with the set). Events `media_set_created`, `media_set_saved`, `media_set_archived`, `media_set_shared`, `media_set_share_revoked`, `media_item_added`, `media_item_removed`. In the web client media sets are Files' second tab: a directory (yours, shared, archived), a new set over an Import Silo (provisioning ones included: a Silo with no definition yet keeps files, and Files' own upload now offers them too), a set's gallery filtered by kind and paged, thumbnails that are the images themselves read as they scroll into view, several files added at once (each refused file said why), an item opened beside the gallery (image, video and audio players, a PDF to download, its facts and markings), shares and archive. The Files test cell starts Import Siloes before Files. Tests: mediaFacts (every format, the index at either end, cut-short bytes, not media), mediaSets (made by an uploader only; facts recorded and the Silo file kept as media; CSV and SVG refused with nothing stored; paging and kinds; a viewer without silo.import opens an item, refused once the Silo is marked and opened once cleared, the refusal recorded; contribute still needs file.upload; removal by the owner only, the upload kept; archive), gatewayWebClient (media-src and img-src), web storage (a set made, filled with a CSV refused, its image drawn, its video's length and frame shown).
- D238 (implementation 2026-11-23, media linked to objects; beyond the spec): the second half of unstructured media. `files.media_links` (an item, an object type and the object's Silo id (24.7: derived from the type and its keys, never a record value), made by a person or by the set's rule, who linked it, removed with who removed it; one live link per item and object) and a set's link rule on `files.media_sets` (`link_object_type_id`, `link_property_id`, `link_pattern`, all or none). The rule is a filename template, not a regular expression: one `{key}` (the longest run with no slash that lets the rest match) and at most two `*` (the shortest run of anything), case-insensitive, so the worst filename is matched in milliseconds; its property must be text, a number or a choice. The keys an item's name gives are matched by equality against that property, through the executor's `runPlan` as the person adding the item or applying the rule (a thousand keys to a plan, an `in` filter; a masked or redacted value matches nothing), at most five objects per key; files is now one of the executor's and the ontology's callers. An item added to a set with a rule is linked then; the rule applied later (its owner) links what is already there, never twice (`items`, `keyed`, `linked`, and why nothing could be read where the executor refused). A person links and unlinks an item on an object's page (the set's owner or a contributor; a viewer may not). An object lists the items linked to it to those who may see their set, as a set's reader sees them (`listObjectMedia`). Item views carry their links. Events `media_link_rule_set`, `media_links_applied`, `media_item_linked` (by person or rule), `media_item_unlinked`. In the web client the set's owner writes the rule (objects, whose property, the pattern) and applies it; the item viewer names the objects it is linked to, each a link to the object's page, with unlink; the object view has a Media section (its linked items as a gallery, opened in place, and a form to link one from a set the viewer may add to). Tests: mediaLinks (the template: greedy key, escaped text, case, a 255-character worst case under a second; a rule's type and property checked; an item linked on add, a key naming nothing or no key linking nothing; link and unlink on the object, once; the rule applied later, never twice; an object's media shown only to those who see the set, and a viewer may not link), web storage (a rule saved, a photo named by a supplier's registration linked to it, the supplier's page showing it drawn).
- D239 (implementation 2026-11-23, notebooks; beyond the spec): an analysis as cells, declarative because no sandbox for running code is approved (and none is needed for what a cell does). Permission `notebook.save` (members hold it; 140 permissions, Super admin 132). `workspace.notebooks` (owner, name, document; visibility; archive; lock), shared to open or to copy through a `view_shares.notebook_id` arm and the one document-sharing module; exports into Files with a `notebook` source (`file_provenance.source_notebook_id`) and a `notebook` lineage node kind. Cells, in order, each table named so later cells read it (checked by the contract: a cell reads only a table made before it, and no two cells make the same one): text; objects (a saved object set's chosen properties, read as a workbook's live range is); question (the owner asks; the workspace's query engine compiles it as finding objects, so never a change, charged by compile, its values bound under a fresh binding id each time; the cell keeps the plan, its binding and the owner's label, never the question, a record value; a plan is set only by asking, so a save that changes one is refused, and a copy copies each binding under its own; a clarification is answered by asking again with the candidate chosen); transform (a pipeline's closed steps, D235, over an earlier table, joining others by name); statistics (`notebookEngine.service.ts`, pure: rows, empty, distinct, the most frequent values; for a column whose every value is a number, minimum, maximum, mean, interpolated median and 90th percentile, sample standard deviation); chart (bars counted or summed per category, at most fifty; a histogram's bins; points for a scatter, sorted for a line; at most 5,000 rows read, what cannot be drawn counted as omitted). Running computes every cell for the caller, as them, and stores nothing: objects through the executor under their access, a question's plan through `runCompiledPlan` with its binding (unmetered); a cell whose table cannot be made says why, and so does each cell reading it, while the rest stand; a step's error names the step. The owner may run a draft they have not saved; anyone else runs what was saved. Export: a sheet per table and one per statistics cell, as computed for the exporter, with the markings of what the cells read (the type versions and connections of object reads and of a plan's answer). Events `notebook_created` (with `copied_from`), `notebook_saved` (cell counts by kind), `notebook_archived`, `notebook_shared`, `notebook_share_revoked`, `notebook_exported`, `notebook_question_compiled` (the plan and the tokens charged). In the web client notebooks are Studio's Notebooks tab: cells added, moved and removed, each with its editor (a transform reuses the pipeline step editor) and its result beneath it (a table of up to 200 rows, the statistics, a chart drawn as SVG with no library); saved, run, exported, shared, copied. Tests: notebookEngine (quantiles, numeric columns, bars, bins, points), notebooks (cells in order with nothing stored; a broken step named and the cells reading it refused; a plan set only by asking; a compiled plan answering; shared to open and refused for a reader without the connection; only the owner runs a draft; the export's sheets), notebookQuestions (asked as finding objects with a fresh binding each time, the question never kept, audited; a clarification answered; a refusal; another member may not ask), delegation (140/132), web studio (a notebook reading suppliers, grouping them by region, summarising and drawing them). Also: the photo-taken time of a media item (D237) is checked text, not a zoneless timestamp, as the build rule requires.
- D240 (implementation 2026-11-23, machine learning models; beyond the spec): the last of the eight Foundry-comparison features. Permission `model.save` (members hold it; 141 permissions, Super admin 133). `workspace.ml_models` (owner, name, description, task regression or classification, the saved object set it learns from, up to fifty feature properties, a label property never among them, the published version; visibility; archive; lock) and `workspace.ml_model_versions` (append-only: version number, status trained or failed, what it learnt from as it was then, rows learnt from and held out, headline figures in the clear (RMSE, MAE and R²; or accuracy, macro F1, log loss and the number of classes: never a value), the fitted model sealed in `artifact` under the organisation's data key bound to the row (its encoder holds the categories it learnt, record values; workspace is now a record-value caller and the column is on the build rules' encrypted list), the markings of what training read (worked out as an export's are), and why it failed); shared to see and predict with through a `view_shares.ml_model_id` arm, view only. The arithmetic is pure, with no library (`mlEngine.service.ts`): an encoder (a number standardised, its gaps the mean, with its training deciles kept; a category one-hot over its ten most frequent values and other, with its shares; at most 400 columns); ridge regression in closed form (Cholesky, the intercept unpenalised); multinomial logistic regression with L2 by Adam over seeded mini-batches (the same data fit the same model); both visit only a row's non-zero columns, so twenty thousand rows of 368 columns fit in well under a second. Training reads the set as the owner (as a live range: their access, a property they may not see blank; at most 20,000 objects), holds out the fifth of objects a stable hash of their ids picks, needs twenty labelled objects (a regression's label numeric; a classifier's ten most frequent classes, two at least), and records importance (each feature's standardised weight, one-hot columns summed) and, for a classifier, the confusion matrix and each class's precision and recall, sealed. A version opens, and predicts, only for someone holding every marking it carries. Predicting reads a set of the type it learnt from (its own by default) as the caller, up to 5,000 objects, and answers with each object's prediction (a classifier's confidence too), how many features were withheld from them (predicted as missing), and drift: the population stability index of each feature against training (under 0.1 stable, under 0.25 moderate, else shifted); nothing is stored. Events `ml_model_created`, `ml_model_saved`, `ml_model_archived`, `ml_model_shared`, `ml_model_share_revoked`, `ml_model_trained`, `ml_model_training_failed`, `ml_model_published`, `ml_model_predicted` (counts only). `readRange` now also answers each row's object id, which never leaves the service. In the web client models are Studio's Models tab: the definition (what it predicts, from which set, from which properties), training, versions with their figures, what a version learnt (importance as bars, the confusion matrix with precision and recall), publishing, predictions with the drift said plainly and each object linked, and shares. Tests: mlEngine (the encoder; ridge recovering a line and a category's effect; three classes separated; the same fit twice; a stable one-in-five hold-out; drift for the training population and a shifted one), mlModels (a label of the task's kind; trained over 83 invoices with accuracy and the total leading importance, the artifact sealed; a failed version saying why; unpublished refused, then predictions with stable drift and the prediction audited; shared, refused where the reader cannot read the objects; a version trained over a marked type refused to a reader without the marking), delegation (141/133), web studio (a model made over suppliers and its failed version saying twelve objects are too few).
- D241 (implementation 2026-11-23, pipeline schedules; follows D235): a pipeline run unattended. `workspace.pipeline_schedules` (one per pipeline: its own service principal, kind automation, owned by the pipeline's owner; five fields in the organisation's time zone, no oftener than every fifteen minutes (the scheduler's own `checkSchedule`); active or paused for failures or because the pipeline was archived; the connections its inputs read; failures in a row and how many pause it; next and last run; a lease), claimed across organisations by `workspace.claim_due_pipeline_schedules` (security definer, identifiers only, five-minute lease); `pipeline_runs` now record who started them, a person or the principal (`started_by_principal`), and the run view says person or schedule. Setting one needs pipeline.save, and the owner able now to write the output (siloes-import `checkFilesSilo`, now callable by workspace: silo.import on it, its markings, open) and to read every connection its inputs read; changing the pipeline re-grants what its inputs read. Policy (spec 60.4): a pipeline's principal is granted read on those connections and `silo.import` (`PIPELINE_PRINCIPAL_PERMISSIONS`), each bounded by its owner at every run, with its owner's markings, as a Cron's is; not the Cron grants. An Import Silo upload now accepts a principal holding silo.import (siloes-import `uploadSource`), which only such a principal is granted by default. The workspace service runs the due sweep (`workers/workspace/pipelineDue.worker.ts`; options `sweep`, `sweepTickMs`, `now`): a due schedule moves to its next time, counts the times it missed (never backfilled, `pipeline_run_skipped`), runs as its principal through the same run path as a person's (a failure recorded, not thrown), and on a failure tells the owner (a new notification kind `pipeline_run_failed`, sourced to the run: `workspace.notifications.pipeline_run_id`, notify's templates and the web's list) and pauses after the failures it allows in a row; an archived pipeline's schedule pauses; resuming counts failures afresh; removing a schedule revokes its principal and keeps its runs. Events `pipeline_schedule_set`, `pipeline_schedule_removed`, `pipeline_schedule_paused`, `pipeline_schedule_resumed`, `pipeline_run_skipped`. In the web client the pipeline editor has a Schedule panel (presets or five fields, how many failures pause it, its state, next and last run, resume, remove) and runs say when the schedule started them. Tests: pipelineSchedules (too frequent refused; set with its principal; a member who may not import refused; run by the sweep as the principal; missed times counted with one run; failures telling the owner and pausing; resumed; archived pauses; removal revokes the principal), web studio (the schedule waits for an output).
- D242 (implementation 2026-11-23, predictions in notebooks; follows D239 and D240): a notebook predict cell scores a set's objects (the model's own, or another of its type) with a model's published version, as a model's predictions are made (the reader holding every marking it learnt under, reading the objects as themselves), into a table of each object's id, prediction and (for a classifier) confidence, with a note when the objects have drifted from what the model learnt from; an objects cell may add each object's id (`withIds`) so a transform joins predictions to properties. Saving checks each predict cell's model is one the owner may see; a model refused to a reader says why in that cell, and the rest stand. A notebook's export carries the markings of the objects scored. `mlModels.service predictFor` answers with what it read for that. In the web client the notebook editor has a Predictions cell (a published model, the objects, how many) and an objects cell's option to add ids; a table shows its note. Tests: mlModels (a notebook scoring the invoices and joining each prediction to its invoice, large ones predicted open).
- D243 (decisions 2026-11-23, applied): (1) opening a Files upload, and a media set's item, needs the file's own access (its creator, a share to download, or the set's share) and every marking on its Silo now; not silo.import, which is for putting data into a Silo (siloes-import `checkedUpload` no longer demands it; Files decides who may open the entry). This departs from spec 41.4. (2) Only a person or a scheduled pipeline's principal puts a file into an Import Silo: any other principal is refused before its permissions are asked (`siloes.person_required`), whatever role it holds (`uploadSource` asks `pipelineScheduleRepo.grantedToPrincipal`). Tests: fileUploads (a member who may not import opens a file shared to them, until the Silo is marked beyond their clearance, refused and recorded), pipelineSchedules (another principal refused).
- D244 (implementation 2026-11-23, the migration window read-only; spec 6.4): from a tenant migration's window until the directory routes the organisation to its new cell (`tenantMigrationRepo.writesPaused`: read_only to source_purged on the source, importing to reauthorising on the destination), every write in the organisation is refused, so nothing is written that the export would leave behind. Before, only Actions and Crons paused, and an edit between the export and the directory's move was lost. Public routes now say whether they write: a GET reads; any other method in an organisation's context writes unless it declares `reads: true` (it keeps nothing the organisation would miss: at most the audit record of the reading, a cached plan, its charge or when it last ran; 32 routes, among them search, plan runs and compiled questions, object views, previews, notebook runs, predictions, clone states and download links). For a write the gateway sends `writes` with the session (resolveSession and resolveClientSession), and auth reads the pause in Postgres each time, never from a copy, refusing with 409 `tenant_migrations.writes_paused` (retryable) before the body is read; people and API clients alike. SCIM changes are refused as 503 (unavailable, which provisioning clients retry); a scheduled pipeline (D241) writes nothing and lets its lease lapse. The export waits `WRITES_SETTLE_MS` (11 minutes: the longest request bound a cell may configure and a minute more) after the window opens, so a write admitted just before it has finished. Not changed: change streams and webhooks from source systems, which carry the systems' own data.
- D245 (implementation 2026-11-23, OPC UA method input arguments; spec 20.3, 47.1, 47.4, 47.7): a method is called with input arguments, which D194 refused. The manifest's custom action declares them in the method's order (`opcua.arguments`: each its name, OPC UA built-in type Boolean, SByte, Byte, Int16, UInt16, Int32, UInt32, Int64, Float, Double or String, and the custom action's input it is taken from, default its name); a body's JSONata may compute them by name instead; an inverse method takes none (it is called with none, 47.6). `action.actuation_allowlists.arguments` (jsonb, a method's only, one to ten) bounds each one: a number by its least and greatest value, text by the values it may take, a Boolean either way; the request is refused without them. They are signed with the entry (in its canonical text only where present, so entries without them read as before). At intent, connect-runtime resolves the arguments as the method would be called (type-checked) and actions checks them against the entry, names in order (policy_gate) and each value within its bounds (intent); the preview shows them as the proposed values. The Action type's custom inputs name exactly the arguments' inputs where there is no body (`action_type.inputs_mismatch`). The agent checks the entry's arguments against the method's own InputArguments property (name, type, scalar), each value's type and bounds (refusals arguments, data_type, range), and sends each as its declared type; a dry run reads the simulator method's declaration. An agent on an earlier release refuses a list holding such an entry whole, so nothing it cannot check is written.
- D246 (fix 2026-11-23, machine learning importance; D240): importance summed a category's one-hot weights against a standardised number's weight, so a category with many values could outrank the feature that decides the label (the models test failed on some runs, the hold-out following object ids). Importance is now the spread of each feature's contribution to the score over the training population: a number's weight on the standardised scale, a category's weights' standard deviation under its training shares (unchanged by a constant added to every value's weight), averaged over the classes.
- D247 (implementation 2026-11-23, the saved camera; spec 29.6): a canvas view's camera was stored as it was opened, never as it stood. The canvas now keeps where the camera is (2D: its centre in layout units and zoom; 3D: its position and target) and Save stores that; opening a view takes its saved camera for the layout it was saved with, the first time that layout is drawn, instead of fitting or framing. No schema change: `clone.canvas_views.camera` already held both.
- D248 (implementation 2026-11-23, links between systems; spec 66.9, 21.8, 43.7): a link route may read its referenced end in another system than its key, `ontology.link_type_routes.referenced_connection_id` and `referenced_object` (both or neither; never a junction; never declared_fk, since no manifest declares a key into another system), naming the other linked type's contributing object there and reading `referenced_field` there. So Siloes link to elements within one another (a component in one Import Silo, its specification in another) and retrieval returns both in one answer: the planner's hop reads each end in its own system (the executor's keyed lookup already did), the object view's links follow it, policy checks the referenced field in its own system, a link rule writing the key checks the other end's identifier there, and the blast radius reports the records in the key's system that name a deleted record (hop 1). A route's identity includes its referenced end.
- D249 (implementation 2026-11-23, mesh compression and levels of detail; spec 29.5; libraries approved by Tommy 2026-11-23): a model is compressed and simplified at registration (`canvas-layout/meshLevels.service.ts`, glTF Transform core and extensions with meshoptimizer; not glTF Transform's functions package, which brings the native sharp library). Level 0 is the checked model compressed with EXT_meshopt_compression and its filters (KHR_mesh_quantization declared for the normalised attributes they write) where it has no mesh compression and that makes it smaller; levels 1 and 2 keep about a half and a seventh of each triangle list's triangles (welded by position, simplified, compacted, compressed), every node, name, transform, material and texture kept; a level is kept only where it is at least a quarter smaller than the one before. A primitive that is not a triangle list or has morph targets is kept whole; a Draco-compressed model is served as it came; a model glTF Transform cannot read is served whole and logged. `clone.asset_models.lod_refs` holds each level's key, `bytes` the full level's size, and `validation_report` adds `compression` and `levelsOfDetail` (each level's bytes, triangles and share); the view model carries `levels` and `compression`. `readAssetModel` takes `level`. Registration may take up to four minutes for a large model. The browser draws the coarsest level first, swaps in the full model once read, and draws a coarser level when the model's radius is under about a third, then an eighth, of the view's half-height, reading a level only when it is wanted; the camera never moves for a swap.
- D250 (implementation 2026-11-23, load shedding and quotas; spec 12.4): each process measures its event loop's delay (p99 a second, `infra/load.infra.ts`); from `SHED_START_MS` (200) each `SHED_STEP_MS` (50) more sheds the next class in the spec's order (`SHED_ORDER` in endpoint.contract.ts: recognition runs, index rebuilds, simulations, export rendering, new subscriptions, new compiles, saved view runs, Crons, Action execution, session authentication). A contract names its class (`shed`); one naming none, approvals, revert and audit among them, is never shed. A shed request is refused at the door, before its body is read, as `capacity.shed` with a retry time. A shed Cron records `automation_run_skipped` reason `capacity` and is not backfilled; index refreshes, organisation exports and pipeline schedules wait a tick. Quotas per organisation: a request window at the gateway beside the session and address windows (`GATEWAY_REQUESTS_PER_ORGANISATION`, 30,000 a minute), and change events in one-second windows per organisation (5,000) and per connection (1,000), a delivery over either refused whole as rate limited, so providers retry and the agent spools; concurrent plans, model calls and live objects already had theirs.
- D251 (implementation 2026-11-23, the purge ledger and restore checks; spec 8.2, 12.5): every requested purge writes a ledger entry (`contracts/platform/purgeLedger.contract.ts`: a Silo wipe's target, receipt ids whose values went, Files entries, a plan or model) in the transaction that completes it, as an outbox row on the new topic `platform.purge_ledger`, which the outbox relay delivers to object-backup (`cell/purge-ledger/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<time>.<id>.json`) rather than the bus, so a restore of pg-control does not rewind it; a moved organisation's purge is its existing purge receipt. Each owning service replays its kind (`replayPurgeLedger`, called by maintenance): wipes only delete, so a replay removes what a restore brought back and nothing else, with no new ledger entry. `src/scripts/restore.script.ts`: `manifest` keeps every pg-control table's row count from one snapshot (as `silo_migrate`) in object-backup with each backup; `check` compares a restored database with it; `replay` sends every entry since the restore point to its owner before the cell opens. Retention sweeps need no ledger (they run again by themselves); BigQuery and object stores are not rewound by a database restore.
- D252 (implementation 2026-11-23, the paging signals; spec 13.2): the Redis key audit (SCAN, never KEYS) reported as gauges, at most every ten minutes (`redis_session_keys_without_ttl` and `redis_data_keys_without_ttl` from auth, `redis_state_keys_without_ttl` from the state plane); secret unwraps in the last five minutes per credential process (`credential_unwraps_5m`). With the existing request, gate, outbox and redaction signals, every page 13.2 names has one; runbooks in `docs/siloOperations.doc.md`.
- D253 (implementation 2026-11-23, the backup sentence; spec 8.2, 70.6): every Silo disclosure, and the switch's, ends with "Deleted data leaves Silo's backups as they expire, within 12 months, and is never brought back into service." (`BACKUP_DISCLOSURE`). The disclosure texts are with counsel (`docs/siloDisclosureReview.doc.md`).
- D254 (implementation 2026-11-24, support tickets; web client U4): `platform.support_tickets` (reference `SUP-` and eight Crockford base-32 characters, unique in the cell; raiser; subject; category question, problem, access, billing, feature or security; severity low to urgent; status waiting on Silo, waiting on the customer, resolved or closed, with checked resolved and closed times; the client page it was raised from; up to ten correlation ids; up to twenty references `refs` as {kind, id} from a closed set; the member of staff looking after it; version) and `platform.support_ticket_messages` (member or staff author, the staff member's name, the words; never edited or deleted). Both under tenant RLS; `platform.support_tickets_waiting` and `platform.support_ticket_by_reference` (security definer, identifiers only) let admin-portal's staff side work across organisations. A subject or message matching a value pattern is refused (`support.value_pattern`, kinds named, never the text); the web client warns of the same patterns as the person types. The raiser sees their tickets; a holder of `org.operator_access.view` sees all (listing asks `listHeldPermissions`, so ordinary members record no refusals; opening another's ticket is an `authorise` decision). Staff capability `support.tickets`; staff act in the customer's audit log as admin-portal, naming the operator (`support_ticket_raised`, `support_ticket_replied`, `support_ticket_updated`). A staff reply raises `support_replied` for the raiser: `workspace.notifications.support_ticket_message_id` is the source (one per reply) and `support_ticket_id` rides beside it for the link.
- D255 (implementation 2026-11-24, notification links): emailed items link to `/notifications/?organisation=<slug>&id=<id>` and pushes to `/notifications/` (they named `/<slug>/notifications/<id>` and `/notifications`, which a static export cannot serve); new public route `readNotification` (the member's own item) lets that page open the item and go to where it is dealt with. Password reset and invitation emails link to `/reset-password/?organisation=<slug>#token=` and `/accept-invitation/?organisation=<slug>#token=`, sign-up's to `/sign-up/complete/#token=` (they named per-organisation paths the export cannot serve).
- D256 (implementation 2026-11-24, the directory): policy `listDirectory` and public `readDirectory`: every member's display name and state and every live scope, for any member (decided by the service). Sharing names a colleague or a team, and pages name who did something; `listMembers` and `listScopes` are administration and gave an ordinary member neither. Names and states only: no address, role or grant.
- D257 (implementation 2026-11-24, findings' version): `findingView.version`. An organisation disposition (`dispositionRecognitionFinding`) names the finding's version, which no read returned, so no client could make one.
- D258 (implementation 2026-11-24, running a saved object set): public `runOntologyObjectSet` (reads, `ontology.view`) runs a saved object set through the executor's `runObjectSet` as the reader, so Explorer can show what a set holds; `gateway` joins that contract's callers.
- D259 (implementation 2026-11-24, held permissions for the client): policy `listMyPermissions` and public `readMyPermissions`: every catalogue permission with its description and whether the member holds it anywhere (organisation-wide, on a scope they belong to, or on any live scope), by the rule `authorise` uses. The web client disables what a person may not use and names what it needs (spec 33.3) before they try; the server still decides every request.
- D260 (implementation 2026-11-24, OAuth clients listed; the catalogue's permission): oauth `listOAuthClients` and public `listOAuthClients` (`oauth_client.manage`): the organisation's own and dynamically registered clients, newest first, live ones unless `includeRevoked`, each with whether it holds a sealed secret, never the secret or where it is sealed. A client could be registered and revoked but not seen; the OAuth apps page lists them. Public `browseConnectorCatalogue` now asks `connection.create` (was `connector.build`): the catalogue is what a connection is made from (spec 14.9), so whoever may create one may browse it.
- D261 (implementation 2026-11-24, scan runs listed): discovery `listScanRuns` and public `listScanRuns` (`discovery.authorise`; the service also takes `discovery.review`, and nothing while discovery is off): an authorisation's runs, newest first, each with its counts. A run started could be read only by the id its start returned, so a person who left the page lost it.
- D262 (implementation 2026-11-24, the builder opens its drafts; spec 16.4): public `listConnectorVersions` (forwards connect-registry's `listManifestVersions`) and `getConnectorDocument` (new connect-registry `getOwnManifestDocument`), both `connector.build`. The document is returned only for the organisation's own private connector (`connector.not_own` otherwise): a certified connector's manifest stays with the services. "A half-built connector stays a draft the visual builder can open" needed a way to read it.
- D263 (implementation 2026-11-24, confirmation sessions listed): fde-orchestrator `listSessions` and public `listFdeSessions` (`fde.view`): an engagement's confirmation sessions, newest first, with agenda and counts. A session could be started and ended but not found again after a reload. The sessions path, untested until now, is covered (start, list, decide within it, end, ending twice refused).
- Web client U8 (2026-11-24, Connect rebuilt): `setConnectionWrites` moves from Ontology's Action types to the connection's Tests and writes tab, beside the write test that earns it; `listWebhookDeliveries` moves from Webhooks to Governance's Changes, where each change's receipt shows where its webhooks went. The Cmd-K panel matches object types against the vocabulary already in the browser before the search index, so a type is found by its first letters even where the index is not built.
- D264 (implementation 2026-11-24, an approval names its subject): `chainView.subject` = {kind, id, siloId}: the one of `mutation_id`, `purge_request_id`, `discovery_authorisation_id`, `declassification_id`, `receipt_purge_id` the chain holds, and for a Silo purge its Silo (which reading the purge needs). An approver quotes the hash of what they read (`decideApproval.diffHash`); only a change's subject was reachable from the chain before, so a scan, purge, receipt purge or declassification could not be opened, read and quoted from the approval itself.
- D265 (implementation 2026-11-24, a revert's change names its revert): `mutationView.revertId` (a revert's own change: the revert it carries out; null otherwise). A revert's conflicts are decided by its id, which only `requestRevert` returned, so a person who left the page could not decide them.
- Web client U9 to U11 (2026-11-24): Ontology rebuilt (types and links with element editors on a branch, branches with rebase choices, proposals with derivation decisions, versions and rollback, derive, field aliases, Action types, resolution, detectors); Governance rebuilt (approvals reading each subject, changes with canary confirmation, execution, deliveries, receipts, reverts and purges; Crons; lineage; purpose sessions; declassifications; audit log with integrity; staff access). `confirmMutationCanary` moves from Action types to Changes, where a canary is confirmed. The canvas engine moved to `src/canvas` and the Clone Canvas page was ported onto the new components, the object panel shared with the object page.
- D266 (implementation 2026-11-24, an app's publications are listed): `listAppPublications` (GET /studio/apps/:appId/publications; studio `listPublications`): the app's live publications, every one for whoever may edit it, otherwise only those the caller may withdraw (their own, or on a scope where they hold app.manage); a caller who holds nothing on the app and may withdraw none is told there is no such app. Withdrawing needed a publication's id, which only the publish call returned, so a publication made by someone else, or in an earlier visit, could not be withdrawn. Repository `appPublicationRepo.liveForApp` (existing).
- D267 (implementation 2026-11-24, custom object view layouts are listed): `listObjectViewLayouts` (GET /studio/object-view-layouts, ontology.view; studio `listLayouts`): the custom layouts in force, and those an ontology change marked invalid while no later one is active for their type, each with its type, the app and version it comes from, its author and when it changed; metadata only. The invalidation notification names the layout row, which nothing else exposed; Studio's Object view layouts page resolves it from this list and opens the layout's editor. Repository `objectViewLayoutRepo.customInForce`.
- D268 (implementation 2026-11-24, a pipeline run is read by its id): `getPipelineRun` (GET /pipeline-runs/:runId; workspace `readRun`): one run, for the pipeline's owner only (anyone else: `workspace.pipeline_run_not_found`). A failed scheduled run's notification carries only the run's id; the Pipelines page reads the run and opens its pipeline's runs.
- Web client U12 (2026-11-24, Studio rebuilt): apps (directory with inherited apps, a new app from a template checked by `previewApp` before it is made, package import, copy), the app runtime (widgets, canvas and map embeds, scenario control, Ask scoped to the app), the editor (definition, versions with staged approval and rollback, branches with conflict decisions, rollout, publications with withdrawal, package export, sharing, archive), object view layouts, workbooks, reports, notebooks, process analyses, pipelines with schedules and runs, AI agents and ML models, each with its own address. A blocked button's reason is now its description only, beside it, never part of its name.
- D269 (implementation 2026-11-24, a scenario's runs are listed): `listSimulationRuns` (GET /simulation/scenarios/:scenarioId/runs; simulation `listRuns`): the scenario's own runs (not its branches'), newest first, without their results, for whoever holds the scenario. `compareSimulationRuns` needs two run ids, and only the latest was readable, so runs could be compared only within one visit. Repository `simulationRunRepo.listForScenario`.
- Web client U13 (2026-11-24, Scenarios rebuilt): scenarios (own and shared, new failure scenario, latest run, runs listed and any two compared, sharing, copy, branches), branches (every branch of the scenarios a person holds; one branch checked against the record on opening, Actions staged on an object through the object view's own Action form, staged again, conflicts decided per property, compared with its scenario or a sibling, promoted, closed), the dependency graph (derive, state, confirm with a resource's capacity, revise, retire) and lead times observed from history.
- D270 (implementation 2026-11-24, a Silo's purges are listed): `listPurges` (GET /siloes/:siloId/purges, silo.purge; siloes-capture `listPurges`): the Silo's purges, newest first, each with what it was of, its state, who asked and whether its receipt is written; the impact is still read per purge by `getPurge`. A purge's receipt could be read only by an id the request had returned. Repository `purgeRequestRepo.listForSilo`.
- D271 (implementation 2026-11-24, an Import Silo's sources are listed): `listSiloSources` (GET /import-siloes/:siloId/sources, silo.import; siloes-import `listSources`): upload points and watched locations, in the order made, each with its definition, where files are dropped and when it was last read. A watched location's drop point was shown only once, when it was made. Repository `siloSourceRepo.listForSilo` (existing).
- D272 (implementation 2026-11-24, a scope's members are listed): `listScopeMembers` (GET /admin/scopes/:scopeId/members, scope.manage at the scope; policy `listScopeMembers`): who is in the scope directly, each with whether it is their primary scope and since when. Members could be added to and removed from a scope by id, but not read back. Repository `scopeMembershipRepo.activeForScope`.
- D273 (implementation 2026-11-24, who may declare a purpose is listed): `listPurposeEligibility` (GET /governance/purpose-definitions/:purposeDefinitionId/eligibility, clearance.grant; policy `listPurposeEligibility`): a purpose's live eligibilities (a member, a role's holders, everyone in a scope or a service principal), each with who granted it and until when; revoked ones are left out. Eligibility could be granted and revoked by id, but not read. Repository `purposeEligibilityRepo.list` (existing).
- D274 (implementation 2026-11-24, the web context policy is read): `readAskWebPolicy` (GET /ask/web-policy, any member; ask `readAskWebPolicy`): the organisation's switch and whether the cell has a web search provider, which anyone in the organisation may read since it shapes their answers; and the policies of the scopes the reader may manage (policy `listPermittedScopes` for ask.web.manage, which now lists ask among its callers), each with its domain lists, whether its scope holds marked data now, how many markings an admin covered, and who set it when. The policy could be set but not read back. Repository `askWebPolicyRepo.forScopes`.
- D275 (implementation 2026-11-24, a member's automatic top-up is read back): `readMemberAllowance`'s balance now carries `autoTopup`. It could be switched on and off but not seen.
- D276 (implementation 2026-11-24, a result read again whole): `readResult` (GET /results/:queryId, its own actor's, which the executor checks; executor `readResult`): the result's header (columns with their data types, measures, coverage, lineage, periods, flags, branch) and its first page, from the data plane while it lives, without running anything (31.2: every representation from one result object). Clients could read only pages, which carry neither the columns' types nor the lineage a figure needs.
- D277 (implementation 2026-11-24, a person's chosen representation is read back): `readViewPreference` (GET /render/preferences?savedViewId= or ?canvasViewId=, any member, for a view they may open, otherwise `render.view_not_found`; canvas-layout `readPreference`): the representation they last chose for that view, or null. It could be set but not read, so the choice did not persist (31.2). Repository `viewPreferenceRepo.readFor` (no lock). The canvas now opens as the list or the canvas the person last chose.
- D278 (implementation 2026-11-25, time buckets and required links in plans; spec 37.8, 26.11, 27.7): a plan's `aggregate.groupBy` key may carry `bucket`, a calendar unit (day, week, month, quarter, year, financial quarter, financial year), on a date or timestamp property: the key is the first day of the period containing the value in the organisation's calendar (the planner's own period arithmetic, `bucketStart`, financial years and week starts included), and its column is a date. Anything else is refused (`plan.bucket_type`), a financial unit without the calendar's financial year too (`plan.financial_year_unset`); a bucketed aggregate is never pushed down, never the Warehouse's, never an index facet. A linked plan node may be `required`: the parent keeps only the objects linked to one there, as a filtered node narrows it, though it has no filter of its own (not the root; it never leads the read).
- D279 (implementation 2026-11-25, analysis over object sets; spec 37.8, 37.10): compile `compileAnalysis` turns a chain of typed steps (filter, traverse, derive, select, group, time series, pivot, compare; inputs at earlier positions only, at most four traversals, every literal a placeholder) into one plan per step (two for a comparison), each an object set as the objects of its type reaching the earlier steps' required, filtered nodes, checks every plan against the reader's vocabulary and bounds (a refusal names the step), and keeps an analysis manifest (`ontology.compiled_manifests` kind analysis, standard, with lineage over every type and link its plans use) with its values sealed in a binding under the analysis's own id. `runAnalysis` runs the steps in order, each under its bound (members for a set, default 10,000; groups for a result, default 1,000), and stops at the first refusal, by the engine or by the bound (`analysis.step_bound`, naming the step, the bound and the count), the rest not run and the earlier results kept; `getAnalysis` gives the steps, and the values only to the person who bound them. The workspace records the steps once in `workspace.analysis_steps` (write-once by manifest and position) and serves `createWorkspaceAnalysis`, `readWorkspaceAnalysis` and `runWorkspaceAnalysis` (ontology.view). A view of kind analysis runs step by step: its result is the last step's (both sides of a comparison, `comparedRef`), its refusal carries the step and the bound. A saver may make a view of an identical manifest someone else first kept when they bound their own values to it (`planBindingRepo.boundBy`). The client's `analysis_step_refused` now names the spec's operations (`ANALYSIS_STEPS` is the chain's operations). Never metered when built by hand.
- D280 (implementation 2026-11-25, an object named exactly; spec 37.8): the reader's vocabulary gives each type's `primaryKey`, the identifying property, where the reader may see it unshaped (otherwise null), so a client can name one object in a filter. An object view's link group offers Analyse these where the object's key is decided and visible: the object, then the objects it links to, as the first two steps.
- D281 (implementation 2026-11-25, an Ask answer continued as an analysis; spec 37.8): filter and traverse steps may carry a period as the asker wrote it, resolved again on every run. compile `analysisFromPlan` makes a stored plan into steps (the deepest filtered type first, each link followed back to the answer's objects with each linked node's conditions, then its aggregate), keeps the plan's own placeholders with the values its binding holds, and keeps the chain; a plan that is not a chain (branches, as of a moment, a history, an interface, a linked node only shown, a measure over linked objects) is said not to be one, with why, and a limit is said not kept. workspace `createAnalysisFromTurn` (public `createWorkspaceAnalysisFromTurn`, ontology.view) continues only the caller's own turn. Saving a view with `fromBindingId` now also needs the values to be bound by the saver (`planBindingRepo.boundBy`): someone else's turn on an identical plan was accepted before, so their values could be copied into another member's view.
- D282 (implementation 2026-11-25, a Studio chart continued as an analysis; spec 37.8): no table change. studio `appChartSteps` (callers: workspace) makes a chart of an app the viewer may run into steps for their parameter values and filter controls: the set's type, filtered as its CEL filter keeps it, each link the set follows, a filter step for each facet chosen, then the chart's measure by its grouping. The filter is read, not run (`services/studio/chartSteps.service.ts`, over `celTree`, the checked syntax tree from the expression service): every part that does not read the object is evaluated with the viewer's values (`region == null || object.region == region` is everything or one region), and what remains must be a conjunction of a declared property compared with a value (eq, ne, ordering, in, contains, starts_with, null checks; either of two values of one property becomes in), whose values become the steps' parameters; analysis_steps keep placeholders only. A part with no typed form (two properties compared, arithmetic over a property, a disjunction over different properties, a negated list), one that reads now (a period is the step's, resolved on every run), a value of another kind than the property's, a failing part under a negation or an either, or a link from a type to itself followed backwards is said not to be steps, naming the part, never approximated. Where the steps keep different objects from the chart they say so as notes: a step's "is not" leaves out objects with no value, which CEL's != keeps; a filter control's search has no typed form and its words never leave the browser (only that one narrows is sent). workspace `createAnalysisFromAppChart` (public `createWorkspaceAnalysisFromAppChart`, ontology.view; Studio decides whether the viewer may run the app) compiles and records the steps under the analysis's own id. The web client starts it from the chart widget's Analyse button, and starting from an Ask answer or a chart now shows what the steps do not keep before opening Analysis (both dropped those notes before).
- D283 (implementation 2026-11-25, Ask compiling a question into a chain; spec 37.8, 26.10, 36.10): no table change. compileQuestion takes `chains` (Ask sends it for a harder question on the Answer tool: the composer's "A harder question", which already demanded query.advanced but changed nothing in the compile); the model may then answer with outcome analysis, an ordered chain of steps in the vocabulary's names reading earlier steps by position. Compile checks every name on the type of the set each step reads (a link from that type, select on a group, time series or pivot step, compare over two sets of one type), makes the question's literals the chain's parameters, plans and bounds every step (`compileChain`, against the version the question was compiled on), keeps the analysis manifest with its values under the turn's binding, and charges once as an advanced compile (3 tokens) now that the chain exists; a seat without query.advanced is refused, free, saying so. It then runs the chain step by step; Ask keeps the turn as an answer whose manifest is the chain and whose result is the last step's (a comparison's first side), records the steps in analysis_steps, and the turn view states the chain's operations (`chain`, from the manifest). Re-running a turn (or a Cron over it) runs a kept chain whole through runCompiledPlan, free; Analyse further on a chain continues the same chain with the turn's values copied; the composer's check shows a chain as its steps. An unknown name in a chain widens a narrowed vocabulary as a plan's does.
- D284 (2026-11-25, commissioning the HSM; spec 61, D206): no table change. The real-hardware PKCS#11 test ran only under the generic profile on slot 0, so it could not prove a Luna (a Luna in FIPS mode refuses the host's IV): it now runs under the profile and partition it is given (`TEST_PKCS11_PROFILE`, `TEST_PKCS11_TOKEN_LABEL`, the key labels, the import key pair when named) and checks fresh IVs per wrap, the MAC key and the import key's public half. docs/siloOperations.doc.md section 9 is the commissioning procedure: the three keys a partition holds, the settings, the start-up check, registering the wrapping key, the real-hardware test, rotation, failover, and what is not yet proven on a real Luna.
- D285 (2026-11-25, behind a customer's ingress on 443; spec 10.2, 7.3): no table and no code change; the arrangement is proved. One front port routes by TLS server name: the agent's hostname passed through untouched (the agent sends it as SNI by default, `serverName`), the web hostname ended there and re-encrypted to the gateway with the client's address appended (`TRUST_PROXY_HOPS`). `tests/services/ingress.test.ts` runs the Go agent binary through it (enrolment and the tunnel; an ingress decrypting the agent's hostname refused, its issuer named), counts two clients apart at the gateway while ignoring a client's own X-Forwarded-For, and upgrades the live WebSocket through it. docs/siloOperations.doc.md section 10 is the installation guidance.
- Web client U14 (2026-11-24, Files and Siloes rebuilt): files (all, by folder, shared; a file's drawer with download, rename, move, share stating whether each recipient can open it, delete with receipt or purge; upload in one request or a signed transfer; a saved view exported as CSV, Excel or PDF), folders within folders, media sets (gallery, items added in bulk, viewer, link rule, sharing, rename, archive) and an object's media; Siloes (every Silo and how they connect, turned on, a Silo's page with retention and purge), Capture (types, properties, the Action ledger and its rows), Import (files, sources, definitions drafted, written or from the catalogue and probed, the carve-out, values to confirm), the Object Index, the Warehouse (made, resumed, synced, reconciled, exported, SQL access, Action ledger, handed over), purges with receipts and charges.
- Web client U15 (2026-11-24, Settings rebuilt): every Settings page in the spec's groups: the organisation (name and logo, also shown in the organisation switcher; calendar; domains proved by DNS; terminology), people (members by status, invitations, suspension, removal, each member's roles and scopes; seats and pools), access (roles and their permissions, assignments and orphaned grants; scopes as a tree with each scope's members (D272); service principals; SCIM tokens and group mappings), single sign-on, security (markings, clearances, resource markings; declassifiers; field policies; purposes with who may declare them (D273); Silo staff access), approvals and change (routing policies superseded never edited, the floor; change windows, freezes and exceptions), sharing (the ceiling and scopes that narrow it; Ask's web context for the organisation and in scopes, read back (D274)), data (Siloes, inference, discovery, the organisation export read in parts and checked against its SHA-256 before it is saved, cell migration), billing (plan and entitlement, invoices, checkout, the payment portal, buying tokens and simulations; the token ledger and each member's allowance with automatic top-up (D275); contracts and their use). Signing out of a single sign-on session ends the provider's session too where it offers single logout; Cmd-K reports which command ran from which page (palette_command_run). Every public route is now called from the client; the old client's settings pages are deleted.
- Web client U16 (2026-11-24, closure): the old client removed; every page opened in a browser and audited for landmarks, headings, names, alternative text, unique ids and ARIA references (`tests/accessibility.test.ts`); fixes to the sidebar, dialogs and tabs (every tab-filtered list in its tab panel).
- Web client U17a (2026-11-24, results as chapter 31 says): `src/results` reads the 31.4 signals from the result object, chooses among the archetypes that fit by the fixed precedence and offers the rest, draws each in SVG (Figure, Ranking, Series, Distribution with outliers marked by sign and word, Composition, Comparison of what two systems disagree on, Chain, Hierarchy and Network through the canvas's layouts, Table), assembles prose from the result alone, and switches Prose, View and Data without fetching. The choice and any override are recorded (`recordRenderSelection`, surface view); each person's representation is kept per saved view (D277). Flags appear in every representation; a selection shows where it came from, opens the object or the objects behind a group, and lands on its row in Data. Ask answers, saved views, dashboard tiles and object sets use it. A tile draws its archetype at or above that archetype's minimum legible size, otherwise Figure or Table, says so on the tile and records `dashboard_tile_fallback`.
