- Web client U17b/U17c (2026-11-25, analysis over object sets): the builder at /explorer/analyses/ (Explorer's Analysis section; also from a type's Analyse button with its filters, and Open in Analysis on a saved analysis view): a fresh set of a type, then filters, links followed in either direction, computed values, groups (time buckets on dates), a series over time, a pivot, two sets compared, and the objects behind any group selected in a step's output; every step's output drawn by the result view; a refused step shown with its bound and count, the steps after it not run, and recorded; saved as a view of kind analysis that keeps its own copy of the values. Since: an analysis begun from an object view's link group (D280) and from an Ask answer, Analyse further (D281).
- D149 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B5: SAML with the cell's service provider key pair; spec 55.5, decision 2026-11-14): the cell's SP key pair comes from the deployment (SAML_SP_PRIVATE_KEY and SAML_SP_CERTIFICATE, PEM, from GCP Secret Manager; SAML_SP_NEXT_PRIVATE_KEY and SAML_SP_NEXT_CERTIFICATE during a rotation), held by the credential service; Silo never generates it. AuthnRequests and LogoutRequests are signed with it (RSA-SHA256, HTTP-Redirect); encrypted assertions are decrypted with it, the current key first and then the next during a rotation; and a provider may require encryption (requireEncryptedAssertions: an answer whose assertion is not encrypted is refused, read without verifying, the library verifying). The SP metadata is generated by @node-saml (no SAML XML written by hand) at GET /api/v1/sso/saml/metadata, the entity id: the assertion consumer, the signing certificates (both during a rotation), the encryption certificate and, with ?organisationId=&providerId=, that provider's single logout address, /api/v1/sso/saml/slo/<organisation>/<provider> (an IdP-initiated message carries no session, so the address names the provider). A provider's single logout address (HTTP-Redirect) is read from its metadata. Single logout from either side: signing out with POST /api/v1/session/single-logout ends the session at once, clears the cookie, and returns the provider's address with a signed LogoutRequest naming the person (the linked identity's subject) and the session (its SAML session index, now kept on iam.sessions with its provider: an identifier at the provider that signs no one in); the provider's LogoutResponse lands on the sign-in page. A provider's LogoutRequest to the single logout address, verified by the library against its certificates, ends that person's sessions from it (that session's alone where it names a session index) and is answered with a signed LogoutResponse; one not signed by a configured certificate is refused. Each is recorded as single_logout (an auth event this build adds: who started it, how many sessions it ended).
- D148 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B4: backfill on recovery; spec 18.5, 18.7): a live group whose source comes back healthy after being stale or down, or that lost changes in a gap noted since it was read, is read again under a subscriber's own permissions, within the live bounds, by the state plane's watch. The read refreshes live state: a value changed since the read began is kept, anything older is replaced, the changes observed meanwhile are applied over it, objects no longer in the set leave the group and new ones join. Each subscriber is sent the group's state anew; where the stream had looked live (a gap) it is first told the clone is rebuilding. stream_backfill_completed records it (the connection, how many objects and subscriptions, recovered or gap). A backfill that cannot be read (a set grown past its bounds, a refusal) leaves the clone saying it is not live and is tried again in a minute. A fix with it: the value-pattern check (spec 7.8) set aside UUIDs before looking for long digit strings, since a UUID's last group holds ten digits in a row about once in forty and refused a question naming one.
- D147 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B3d: compiling against an ontology branch; spec 25.3): a plan compiles against a branch for a person holding ontology.branch: a structured plan naming a branch version, or a question or the vocabulary given branchId (compile against that branch's head; the ontology decides ontology.branch). A branch version read by its id is now decided too: the ontology's getVersionManifest demands ontology.branch of a person reading a version on a branch, and the planner's manifest cache serves a branch's manifest to services only, so a person's read always reaches that decision (a plan pinned to a branch version runs for no one else). A plan on a branch reads live only: the Object Index and the Warehouse hold main's objects, so neither answers it, and an as-of or history question on a branch is refused. A result computed on a branch says so (branch: its id and kind) in the answer, the plan's explanation and an export's head ('Computed on an ontology branch (working), not main'); lineage already recorded the branch on every column. A branch never changes main. Crons and shared views always run against main: a Cron over a view compiled on a branch is refused (cron.plan_on_branch), as is sharing such a view (workspace.view_on_branch, read from the plan's version and its branch in the store); Studio apps are bound to main's sequence already.
- D146 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B3c: partial aggregate pushdown for a resolvable type; spec 27.7): a resolvable type may be declared to hold each object in exactly one of its contributing objects (the systems split the objects between them): disjointSources on the type definition, kept in the type version's match strategy beside its keys, versioned and reviewed like any change (source_partition_changed, compatible), refused on a single-source type or one with a single contributing object. The engine relies on it only where the entity graph does not contradict it: resolution's checkSourcePartition answers whether any object is bound to live records in two contributing objects, and one such object sends the aggregate back to merged objects. Where it holds, each system computes its share per group (the plan's filters pushed to each, as each object's one record holds its only values) and the shares are added by group key: counts and sums add, a minimum or maximum is the least or greatest of the shares, an average is the summed sums over the summed counts; a distinct count is never split. Every key and measure is read plainly and as stored in every system, and every system must compute it natively, or the aggregate is computed over merged objects. The answer states the form (partial_pushdown or merged). The planner's pushdown is now parts, one a system; a single-source type's is its one.
- D145 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B3b: computed properties over linked objects; spec 21.11): a computed property whose function declares link types is now evaluated in the query path. It is the reader's only where its own inputs are shown to them plainly and every link it reads is theirs, joining its type, with every linked input shown plainly; otherwise it is absent for them. The planner reads its linked objects through a hidden hop from its node for each link (the link's default route, or its only one; several and no default is refused), selecting only the linked properties the function declares; hidden hops are followed and never shown (no link in the result, no column), at most four a plan. The executor evaluates such a property once the hops are read, giving CEL links.<link api name> as a list of the linked objects' declared values by API name beside the object's own; an input disputed, unchecked or empty, on the object or a linked one, leaves no value (unchecked). Filters on it apply after the hops, sorts and aggregates as for any property; the Index, a split plan and the Warehouse never answer a node holding one, and an as-of or history question with one is refused (it is computed from the systems now). The object view follows its object's hidden hops and shows the value.
- D144 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B3a: plans over an interface; spec 21.9, 26): a plan's root may name an interface instead of an object type (a plan with no hops, no as-of or history): its filters, period, selections, groups, measures and sorts name the interface's required shared properties. The planner and executor expand it to one sub-plan per implementing type the reader may see (each property the type binds to the shared one), each the engine's own run; a type the reader may not see contributes nothing and is not named, any other refusal refuses the whole; a marking on the interface the reader does not hold withholds the plan without saying why. Objects keep their own type, their values named by the shared properties, ordered across types by the plan's sort and cut to its limit; groups are keyed by the shared properties' values and combined exactly (counts and sums add, minimum and maximum of the types', averages weighted by how many values each measured), and a distinct count over more than one type is refused (plan.measure_across_types). The answer states the contributing types and how many objects each. The bounds stage explains it as one node per type (interface). The model is offered interfaces (their shared properties and implementing types) and may stand a question's plan on one, without links or a period.
- D143 (implementation 2026-11-17, a fix: how long callers wait; spec 7.1, 27.4, 39): a service call waited at most ten seconds and every service route answered 504 after HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS (30 seconds), whatever the operation's own bound, so a question legitimately running past ten seconds failed with a timeout while the executor's wall-time bound was sixty, and a keyed operation retried into 'the first request with this idempotency key is still running' (a probabilistic scenario run under load did exactly that). A contract may now declare timeoutMs, its own bound and a margin to answer with the refusal that bound gives (one second to 270 seconds, inside the gateway's five-minute request bound); the service client waits the call's own timeout, else the contract's, else the client's default, so every caller and the gateway's forwarding wait as long as the operation may take, and a service's deadline on the route is the listener's timeout or the contract's, whichever is longer. The executor's runPlan, runObjectSet and readObjectView declare RUN_TIMEOUT_MS (130 seconds: EXECUTOR_WALL_TIME_MS, now at most 120 seconds, and a margin), so a long question is refused at its bound, never cut off by its caller first; compile's compileQuestion, compilePlan and runCompiledPlan that much and a minute for the model; simulation's runScenario and openBranch, which walk through several plan runs, the longest a contract may declare. The object view keeps to the executor's wall-time bound as a plan run does, refusing with query.bound_wall_time.
- D142 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B2b: the object view's sections; spec 34.2, 34.4, 34.5, 39.7, 67): the object view's remaining sections each have a server read, so the client loads them side by side and one failing never blanks the others. Actions (34.5) are part of readObjectView: each confirmed Action type whose current version targets the type (actions' listActionTypes now takes objectTypeId and is open to the executor), other than system types and those that create objects (they act on the type, not this object), that the reader may see (policy's resolveAccess on its markings), with the record it writes (the object's record in the first system the type may write through), its risk class, physical flag, revert behaviour and parameter declarations for the form, and its submission criteria checked against that record as just read, the way the mutation path checks them at resolve (CEL over the properties the reader reads plainly, by API name, within the same bounds): available; criteria_failed, disabled with the criterion; checked_on_submit, where the criteria read the parameters; no_record, where the object has no record in a system the type writes through. No system is read again for it, and the view never writes: submitting enters the mutation path, which checks again. Actions or policy not answering leaves the section null and the rest of the view standing. The timeline (34.4) is two reads: Action commits from the ledger (actions' listObjectCommits, already public) and observed changes from Capture (siloes-capture's readObjectChanges, public POST /api/v1/siloes/object-changes): one object's transitions, newest first and paged by time, across the captured properties the reader may see, each value under the reader's field policy (the property's own and its source fields', the strictest, as the planner decides: a masked value shows at most its last four characters, a redacted one nothing, saying which); only Capture Siloes count (a Warehouse's history is its own); no Capture Silo holding the type, or Siloes off, is 'unavailable', for the client's "Changes before this session are not held. History requires Capture." Findings naming the object were already served (recognition's listObjectFindings, 38.10). Scenarios (34.2, 39): simulation's listObjectScenarios (public POST /api/v1/simulation/object-scenarios) lists the scenarios the reader holds (their own, or shared and live under the owner's sharing policy, 39.7) whose branch stages an Action targeting the object (its manifest names targets by Silo id) or whose latest completed run, of the scenario or of a branch, reaches it, with the branch, staged Action and staleness, and the run's effect (fails, delayed, constrained), delay, period unavailable and probability.
- D141 (implementation 2026-11-17, backend stage B2a: the object view's read; spec 34.2, 34.3, 23.4, 68.4, 58): the executor's readObjectView (public POST /api/v1/objects/view, ontology.view) reads one object live now under the reader's access, on the engine's own machinery and never from the Object Index. An object is opened by a record's reference (its connection and the identifier the record has there, as Actions name targets) or by its Silo id. By reference, a single-source type's system is read for that record by identifier (pushed down where the system can, else within the step bound); a type merged across systems has each system read within bounds and the record's object found through the entity graph. A Silo id alone cannot be turned back into a record (the entity graph keeps identifiers only as keyed hashes), so the type's population is read within bounds and the object found among it; a type over the bounds is refused with the bound, never shown from part of it. No such object, an object in a system the type is not read from, and a type the reader may not see are one answer, not_found, so existence is never disclosed. A system that does not answer leaves the view partial instead of refusing it: the answering systems are shown, each property one of its systems could not vouch for says partial, the system is listed under incomplete with why, and its values are unchecked (23.5), never settled by the one that answered; the record asked for being in that system, or nothing answering, refuses. A bound reached always refuses. The view carries: the banner's markings (policy's readMarkingBanner: the markings on the type and on the properties shown, their own and their source fields', which the reader holds all of or would not see the object); the binding (a single system's identifier, or the match key with each key's declared normalisation); each property in the generated layout's order (the primary first, 34.6) with the decided value as shown and its state, the system it came from, the field authority deciding a declared value with who declared it, when and why (resolution's listFieldAuthorities, now open to the executor; resolution's merged value now keeps from and authorityId), and each system's own reading (connection, source object, field, connector version, read time, the value under the reader's field policy) so a disagreement shows both values with their systems; the extraction flag on a reading from an Import Silo (method, document, location, the model's score, confirmed), from siloes-import's readRecordExtractions by the record's row reference, asked only for records a read says came from a Silo's store (connect-runtime's read now returns the Silo holding its records), so an ordinary object view never depends on siloes-import; properties withheld by a field policy, by name only, while a property whose existence a marking restricts is omitted without statement (the planner's reader access now keeps withheld properties per type: denied by policy with the property's and its fields' markings held); the records it was read from; and each link type joining the type that the reader may see, by direction (a link from the type to itself listed once, forward), with its count and its first 20 objects by title, or the refusal that stopped it (a bound, a system not answering), each link followed on its own so one refusal never spoils the rest. A plan takes at most four links, so further links are planned in rounds, the root read again by its Silo id. object_view_opened (now a query event) records the object, the reader and how many properties were withheld, never a value; every open is recorded (the spec's default). The timeline, Actions, findings and scenarios sections are B2b.
- D140 (implementation 2026-11-17, web client stage W3: Explorer and Cmd-K's search; spec 34.1, 33.5): Explorer is app/web's /explorer/, its state in the address (the search, the type, the filters as JSON, the order, a saved view), so a result can be linked to. Types: the reader's vocabulary, which now also gives each type's plural name, description, resolution class, title property (only where the reader may see it), the interfaces it implements that the reader may see, each property's description, each link type's forward and reverse names, and the interfaces themselves; types are grouped by interface, the rest under "Other types". Search across types: search's typed, unmetered searchObjects (surface explorer, audited), grouped by type with the count exact or "at least", an index answer with its refresh time, and every system not searched listed with why. A type: a structured plan (unmetered, ontology.view) of its objects under the filters, the title first then up to seven shown properties, sorted by a header the reader may sort on (never a masked or redacted one); the result is the federated engine's within bounds, and one over the bounds is refused with the bound (and the count, where the source can count) stated, never shown by its first members; a disputed value reads "Systems disagree" and is never resolved by picking a side, one no system could be asked about says so; pages are the executor's own (its page count, read with readResultPage while the result lives). Facets are generated, never configured, and only for properties read plainly: listed values with counts for text, enumerations and booleans (an aggregate grouped by the property, most frequent first, under the other filters), a range with its extent for numbers and dates; counts that cannot be read within bounds leave the facet usable without them, saying why. Filter values travel as plan parameters, never in the plan. A result is saved as an object set: an ontology filter set whose CEL predicate is the filters (strings quoted with JSON's escapes, moments compared as ISO text, the property identities it reads), private, then a saved view of kind object_set; a saved view opens in Explorer run again as the opener, its members by title a page at a time, with Follow for another's. Cmd-K (spec 33.5): after a short pause, objects by title (searchObjects, surface cmdk), object types (searchVocabulary), the person's saved views and those shared with them, product commands, and "Ask: text" last; it says how objects were found and names the systems not searched. Objects open the object view, which arrives in W4 (a page stands in, saying so). Tests: app/web tests/plan.test.ts (columns, facets only for plain properties, parameters not values, facet aggregates, predicates and their quoting, filters in the address), tests/explorer.test.ts (Chrome over the recognition cell: types, a merged type with its disagreements unresolved, a facet with counts filtering the set and kept in the address, a sort, saving and reopening a set found through Cmd-K, a type over the bounds refused with the bound, search naming every system not searched), tests/browser.test.ts on a shared helper (tests/browser.helper.ts); tests/services/query.test.ts (the vocabulary's new fields).
- D139 (implementation 2026-11-17, web client stage W2: Home's briefing, following, Cron sharing and notifications; spec 33.7, 40.8; Tommy's decision 2026-11-17 on following): the spec's Home briefs on Crons and object sets a person "follows" without defining following; Tommy chose an explicit follow. workspace.follows holds a person's follow of another's Cron or another's saved object-set view (resource_type cron or view, a reference without a key, unique per person and resource, grants nothing); what a person owns they follow without a row. Following (PUT/DELETE/GET /api/v1/workspace/follows, the person's own records) needs read access to the target, checked as the person by its own service: the scheduler for a Cron, the workspace for a view; a view must be an object set whose set the person can read (a set private to its owner is refused, saying the owner can share the set: the briefing reads its definition as the person); following one's own is refused (workspace.follow_own); deleting a Cron or archiving a view ends the follows of it. Cron sharing (spec 40.8, "shareable as saved views and Lenses are"; until now not built, so nobody but owners and managers could see a Cron): a Cron is shared through workspace.view_shares (a new automation_id arm, access always view: visibility and run history, never authorisation), under the owner's effective sharing policy, evaluated when the share is written and again whenever access is resolved, as for scenarios and canvas views; a sharee reads the Cron and its runs (getCron, listCronRuns, listCrons which=shared) and never changes it; only the owner shares, revokes and lists shares (PUT /api/v1/crons/:id/shares, POST .../shares/:shareId/revoke, GET .../shares); automation_shared is audited (shared, revoked); deleting a Cron revokes its shares. The briefing (GET /api/v1/workspace/briefing, workspace readBriefing) reads five sections in parallel, each on its own: a section whose source failed is unavailable with the source's public reason, never an empty list. Approvals waiting: approvals' inbox with forMe (chains with an open step the member may decide now: decide()'s qualification checks are now one function, slotFor, run by decide and by the inbox), oldest first. Crons that fired: scheduler listFiredRuns (workspace only), runs since the marker on owned Crons and followed ones still readable. Findings: recognition listFindingsRaisedSince (workspace only; raised after the marker, current, not dismissed for the organisation, withheld when the reader may not see what they examined) on the object types of the object sets the person owns or follows (the set's base type), each listed with those sets; it is the set's type, not membership of the set, that is matched, since a set is a query over the sources and the briefing does not run it. Favourited clones: by type and reference (live state joins with the Clone Canvas). Favourited apps the person can still open (studio getApp as them) and the dashboard's tiles. "Since last visit" is last_home_seen_at, and before a first visit the last seven days; reading the briefing changes nothing, the page marks Home seen after showing it, and a tab keeps the marker it opened with (sessionStorage, ?since=) so a reload does not empty it. The notifications panel in the top bar: the person's notifications newest first, unread marked, a sentence per kind (a notification carries references, never text), linking to where each is dealt with; opening one marks it read, an escalation asking for acknowledgement is acknowledged there, and the unread count follows. The Follow control (app/web src/ui/FollowButton.tsx) is placed on Crons and saved views as their pages arrive (Governance, Explorer). Tests: tests/services/briefing.test.ts (sharing, policy and revocation; following and its refusals; the briefing's sections, the marker, a revoked share hiding runs, an unavailable source; follows ending with the Cron), tests/services/approvalMarkings.test.ts (the inbox's forMe), app/web tests/browser.test.ts (the briefing's six blocks in order and the notifications panel in Chrome).
- D138 (implementation 2026-11-17, web client stage W1: foundation, sign-in and the shell; spec 33, 29.9, 55, 60, 7.3): the web client is app/web, the Next.js client spec 29.8 names (Next 16.4.6, React 19.3.1), built as a static export: no server of its own, the same files for hosted and self-managed cells. The gateway serves it at its public origin beside the API under /api/v1 (GATEWAY_WEB_ROOT), from files loaded and indexed at start (never resolved against the file system), so the session cookie (__Host-, SameSite=Strict) and the cross-site rules stay as they are; a page carries no data. Each page's Content-Security-Policy allows exactly its own inline scripts by SHA-256 (computed at load), scripts and styles from the origin, no unsafe-inline or eval, nothing framed or framing it; content-hashed assets are cached for a year and pages revalidate by ETag; text is precompressed with Brotli; a page's path without its slash redirects within the origin (built from the normalised path, so //host never leaves it); anything else is the export's 404 page, while unknown API paths stay JSON. Pages open from links on other sites; the API still refuses cross-site requests. A static export has no page for an id it did not know at build, so ids travel in the query string. Typed calls: definePublicRoute now keeps each route's input and output as a type (TypedRoute, RouteInput, RouteOutput; a symbol-keyed property nothing sets at runtime), every route is exported by name (the route arrays list them; the policy admin routes' forward helpers are generic over the forwarded contract), and src/scripts/webRoutes.script.ts writes app/web/src/api/routes.generated.ts: each browser route's method, path and whether it is keyed, with a type-only import of its definition, so no server code reaches the bundle; tests in both projects fail when it is not current. The client sends x-silo-csrf on every state-changing call and an Idempotency-Key on keyed ones, and states refusals in the gateway's own words with the correlation id to quote. New server routes for the shell: GET /api/v1/session/person (auth readOwnProfile: the person's own name and email, also before their second factor) and GET /api/v1/workspace/rail (workspace readRail: the eleven items in their fixed order, each open or disabled with the permission class it needs, Siloes absent until a Silo is enabled; one policy listHeldPermissions call, workspace only, unaudited, for permissions held organisation-wide or on a scope the member belongs to; Home, Explorer, Studio and Governance are every member's, since what they show is filtered by what the person may see). Sign-in: the organisation first (whether it signs in by password, by its identity provider or both), then credentials, then a TOTP code or a security key (WebAuthn's JSON forms, no library), or setting up an authenticator where the organisation requires a second factor; SSO starts bind the flow to the tab (sessionStorage), and the OIDC callback and SAML completion pages finish it; the return path is only ever this origin's own page. The shell's five regions: the rail (collapsible, kept as a preference; disabled items are aria-disabled buttons naming what they need), the top bar (organisation and cell, the Cmd-K field, notifications, the identity menu with organisation switching, theme and sign-out), the page, the Ask panel (open state kept), the status line; residency and the unread count are decoration, so the shell opens without them. Cmd-K runs product commands for now; object search arrives with Explorer. Areas of later stages say so plainly. Design tokens meet WCAG 2.2 AA in light and dark (a test checks every pair), system fonts only, reduced motion honoured. Next's telemetry is off in every build. Tests: app/web/tests (api: calls, CSRF, keys, refusals and types that must fail to compile; contrast; browser: the built export served by the gateway in a cell of real services, driven in the installed Chrome through playwright-core 1.64.1: sign-in back to the page asked for, rail, Cmd-K, the kept collapse, the identity menu, sign-out, a member's disabled item, and no script or style blocked anywhere), tests/services/gatewayWebClient.test.ts (serving, policy, caching, Brotli, redirects, the 404 page, traversal probes, cross-site), tests/services/workspaceGateway.test.ts (rail, Siloes, identity), tests/architecture/webRoutes.test.ts.
- D137 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A18: SQL Server change data capture; spec 10.3, 10.4, 18.1, 18.2): the agent reads SQL Server's change tracking (agent/internal/cdc/sqlserver.go), with the login only it holds (SELECT and VIEW CHANGE TRACKING on the captured tables). It polls once a second, each read in a snapshot transaction, as SQL Server documents for consistent results: the version the database is at, each captured table's minimum valid version, and CHANGETABLE(CHANGES ...) joined to the table on its key, up to that version. Only the tables the manifest streams by capture are read, sent in cdc.start as for binlog, each naming its schema (stream.cdc_schema_required covers both methods). The database must track changes and allow snapshot isolation, and each captured table must track changes; otherwise the reader refuses and logs which. Change tracking keeps each row's net change since a version, not every change on the way: an insert or update carries the row as it stands in the snapshot (a row gone from it since is skipped, its delete following), a delete its key's columns. It records no commit time, so a change's source time is when the agent read it, within the poll of its commit. Positions are change tracking versions written as LSNs are, so every method's positions now compare as numbers in the cell (laterPosition no longer lets change tracking's replace); a change's place is its row's version and its index there, the same on a re-read, so the cell's de-duplication holds. SQL Server keeps tracking for its own retention: a capture whose last version is older than a table's minimum valid version (cleaned up, or tracking turned off and on again) is lost, as a purged binary log is; acknowledging and dropping touch nothing on the server. A source that does not log what capture needs now fails with its own category, source_not_configured ("the source does not log what change capture needs: the reading agent's log names the setting"), not not_configured, which still means the agent holds no replication login; this corrects D136's binlog refusal too. SQL Server values come from one function for reads and capture (agent/internal/values/sqlserver.go). Tests share tests/services/agentCaptureSource.helper.ts (cell, pool, connections, bus, the built agent started and stopped) with the MySQL capture test; tests/services/agentSqlServerCapture.test.ts runs the built agent against real SQL Server: a publication and an unqualified table refused; committed rows as deltas as reads give them; another tracked table's rows never reaching the cell; resuming from the acknowledged version losing and repeating nothing; tracking restarted past it lost; tracking turned off stopping the reader with the reason, and capture not lost; dropping with nothing on the server.
- D136 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A17: MySQL change data capture; spec 10.3, 10.4, 18.1, 18.2): the agent reads a MySQL (8.0 or later) server's binary log as a replica does (go-mysql's binlog syncer), with the replication login only it holds (REPLICATION SLAVE and REPLICATION CLIENT). The binary log carries every database and table of the server, so the agent reads only the tables the connection's manifest streams by capture, which the cell sends in cdc.start (schema and table, from the manifest as it stands when the reader starts; an object added since is read from the next start): every other row stays on the customer's host, and a binlog capture is refused at set-up unless each captured object's source names its schema, the database (stream.cdc_schema_required). The server must log what capture needs: log_bin on, binlog_format ROW, binlog_row_image FULL, binlog_row_metadata FULL (so rows name their columns, their table's key and their enumerations' labels) and no partial JSON updates; otherwise the reader refuses as not configured and logs which setting (agent.cdc_not_configured), and the stream says why. The reader registers as a replica under the slot name the owner confirmed (seen in SHOW REPLICAS), with a server id derived from the capture, clear of the small ids real replicas use. A server keeps no slot for its readers: it keeps its binary logs by its own retention, so the agent resumes from the cell's acknowledged position (or its spool's last whole transaction) while the server still holds that file, and a file purged before it was read loses the capture (cdc_slot_lost), as an invalidated Postgres slot does; acknowledging tells the server nothing, nothing in the spool is at risk from the server, and dropping a capture drops nothing on the server (the agent removes its spool and reports it dropped at once). Positions are the binary log's own: the file's number and the offset after the event, written as Postgres LSNs are (hex, "file/offset"), so they compare as numbers in the cell (laterPosition) and order the spool; a change's place is its transaction's start and its index there. A transaction ends at its XID, or at COMMIT for tables without transactions; one with no captured rows goes up as a position at most every ten seconds. Values as reads give them: integers as numbers (unsigned ones whole, as text beyond 2^53), decimals as their digits, DATETIME as its wall clock in UTC, TIMESTAMP as its moment, zero dates as null, binary (collation 63) as hex, ENUM as its label and SET as its members' labels, JSON as its text. An update carries its new image; a delete its key's columns only. setChangeCapture's publication is logical replication's only (stream.publication_required, stream.publication_not_used); change tracking is still refused (stream.cdc_method_unsupported). The dev MySQL in the `sources` profile logs full row metadata. Tests: agent/internal/cdc/mysql_test.go (positions, server ids, logins, values, labels, rows), tests/services/agentMysqlCapture.test.ts (the built agent against real MySQL: the owner confirms a slot name and the reader shows by it in SHOW REPLICAS; a publication and an unqualified table refused; committed rows as deltas in log order with labels, unsigned integers and moments as reads give them; another table's rows never reach the cell; resuming from the acknowledged position losing and repeating nothing; a purged binary log lost; dropping with nothing on the server).
- D135 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stages A15 and A16: SQL Server and Oracle through the agent; spec 10.4, 10.7, 14.4): two more dialects on one database/sql session (agent/internal/work databasesql.go), each with its read guard, its values and its error numbers. SQL Server with go-mssqldb v1.11.2 (@p1 placeholders; a cell-held password a field of its configuration, never in a connection string; the target's addresses pinned by its dialer): SQL Server has no read-only transaction, so a read must be one SELECT (or WITH), nothing after it, refused as 42000 before it runs otherwise, and runs in a transaction always rolled back; the login's own permissions (db_datareader, and db_datawriter only where writes are granted) are the real guard, and the docs say so. Oracle with go-ora v2.9.0 (pure Go, no Oracle client; :1 placeholders; the agent's own connector builds each connection from a configuration whose password is a field): a read is one SELECT too (go-ora also refuses bound DML on that path), in a transaction begun SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY, which the server enforces as a second guard (ORA-01456, kept as 25006); the login's database is the service name; the login is an ordinary unquoted Oracle user, since Oracle's clients log on without regard to case. TLS by the login's sslmode as for Postgres (Oracle's prefer tries TCPS, then the plain listener). Values: decimals and money keep their digits; a uniqueidentifier its text (SQL Server sends its first three groups little-endian); Oracle NUMBER whole numbers within 2^53 as numbers, anything else as its digits; DATE and TIMESTAMP without a zone as their wall clock in UTC; binary and RAW as hex. Error numbers are kept as the SQLSTATEs they stand for (SQL Server 208 and ORA-00942 as 42S02, 18456 and ORA-01017 as 28000, unique and constraint violations as 23000, deadlocks as 40001; anything unmapped HY000). The cell's engine takes a moment at exactly midnight UTC in a date field as its date (how Oracle's DATE gives a date); a moment in the day there is still a counted mismatch. Test containers join the `sources` profile: SQL Server 2022 (no arm64 image; under Docker's x86 emulation on Apple silicon) and Oracle Database 23ai Free. The binary is about 30 MB with all four drivers. Tests: agent/internal/work (both dialects' values, the one-SELECT rule), tests/services/engineCoerce.test.ts, tests/services/agentSqlServer.test.ts and agentOracle.test.ts (the built agent against real databases: reads with both logins, reads that are not one SELECT refused, a granted write and a mismatch rolled back whole, a wrong cell-held password as 28000), on a shared helper (tests/services/agentSource.helper.ts) with the MySQL test.
- D134 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A14: MySQL through the agent; spec 10.4, 10.7, 14.4): the agent's SQL work is one session per call behind a dialect (Postgres, MySQL), on a login it holds (a DSN, pooled: up to four idle connections each) or the cell's (D132, one connection, closed and wiped). MySQL and MariaDB with go-mysql's client (module approved 2026-11-17): prepared statements on the binary protocol (the cell's ? placeholders); a read in `START TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, which the server enforces (a write in it fails 25006, as in Postgres), rolled back; a granted write in one transaction, with `CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS`, so a row a statement matched counts even where its value was already there (expectRows), rolled back whole on a mismatch; every session in UTC (`time_zone '+00:00'`) and utf8mb4. TLS by the login's `sslmode` as for Postgres (`prefer` falls back to plain only where the server offers no TLS; `verify-full` checks the certificate and name). Values as the cell reads them: integers as numbers (text beyond 2^53), decimals as their digits, DATETIME and TIMESTAMP as UTC moments to the millisecond, DATE as a date, a zero date as none, BIT as a number, binary as Postgres's hex. MySQL's own SQLSTATE is kept (42S02 a missing table, 28000 a refused login). An agent-held MySQL login is a `mysql://` URL in the agent's configuration; discovery's catalogue introspection stays Postgres's. The cell's engine now takes 1 and 0 in a boolean field (MySQL's TINYINT(1), Oracle's NUMBER(1)); anything else there is still a counted mismatch. The cell already generates MySQL statements (its SQL builder); nothing changed there. A MySQL 8.4 container joins docker-compose under the `sources` profile (`npm run sources:up`; never started with the rest), binary log on in row format for change capture. Tests: agent/internal/work (MySQL values), tests/services/engineCoerce.test.ts, tests/services/agentMysql.test.ts (the built agent against real MySQL: reads with both logins, read-only enforced, a granted write counting matched rows and rolling back whole, a wrong cell-held password refused as 28000; skipped where MySQL is not running).
- D133 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A13: logins locked in memory; spec 10.7, 10.8): the password of a cell-held login (D132) is unescaped from the opened document straight into its own mapped pages outside Go's heap (the garbage collector never moves or copies them), locked into memory with mlock (VirtualLock on Windows) and marked not to dump, handed to the driver as a view of those pages, and wiped and unmapped when the call ends (agent/internal/login Secret). Transient copies while decrypting and parsing are wiped at once; the driver's working copies during authentication are its own. Through memcall, memguard's memory layer (module approved 2026-11-17 with memguard), not memguard's LockedBuffer: memguard panics the process and wipes every buffer when a lock fails, which a container's 64 KB memory-lock limit makes likely under load; here a lock that cannot be taken leaves the password off the heap and wiped but unlocked, and the agent warns at start (`agent.logins_unlocked`). The agent also sets its core-dump limit to zero at start (spec 10.8). Modules: github.com/awnumar/memcall v0.4.0 (and golang.org/x/sys). Tests: agent/internal/login (the password in a Secret, given back on Zero); tests/services/agentBinary.test.ts (cell-held reads through the built agent).
- D132 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A12: logins for connections through the agent; spec 10.7, 6, 61.3): "Cell-held by default: credential unwraps for one call and passes the secret through the tunnel; the agent zeroes it after the call. Agent-held at the customer's choice: ... the cell never sees it, and unwraps record held_by_agent." A connection through the agent chooses its custody at creation (`connect.connections.credential_custody`, `cell` by default, frozen; `agent` refused without an agent pool). Cell custody: the login is stored like any connection secret (every auth field sealed in `connect.connection_credentials`); the database's address is the connection's parameters (`host`, `port`, `database`, `sslmode`, read by the agent's SQL work). For each piece of work, the connect-runtime replica giving it to an agent (in `give()`, so relayed work is sealed where it lands) asks the credential service (`sealAgentCredentials`, callers connect-runtime), which stays the only opener of secrets: it checks the connection is usable for the reason, that the agent is of the connection's pool, not revoked and has a sealing key; opens the login (each row in `iam.credential_unwraps` with the reason and the asker); and seals `{expiresAt, params, username, password}` to that agent's X25519 key (`connect.agents.sealing_key`) with HPKE (RFC 9180 base mode, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM; `src/utils/hpke.util.ts` on Node's KEM, checked both ways against Go's `crypto/hpke`), the info binding `silo.agent_credential.v1`, the organisation, the agent, the connection and the work id; valid for two minutes. The password is assembled into the sealed document from the opened bytes and never becomes a JavaScript string; the plaintext is zeroed. connect-runtime puts the sealed login in the work's payload and never holds it in clear. The agent (agent/internal/login) opens it with its private key only for that work, before its expiry, refuses a system its configuration's `targets` do not allow (host names, `*.` wildcards, addresses, networks; a name outside them must resolve wholly inside the networks and is reached at those addresses only: without this a cell could aim the agent anywhere on the customer's network, which discovery allows only on a signed, approved authorisation), connects once for the call, then closes and zeroes the password, held in bytes it owns and given to the driver as a view of them. Refusals come back as `login_refused` (`no_key`, `sealing`, `expired`, `target`), logged by connect-runtime. The agent makes a new sealing key at enrolment and at each certificate renewal (sent with the signing request; the cell stores it with the new certificate) and keeps the one before for work sealed before the cell heard. Agent custody: the cell refuses to store the login's secrets (`credential.agent_custody`); each use is recorded `held_by_agent` (`iam.credential_unwraps.outcome`, no key version) against a row standing for each secret field (custody `agent`, no value). Change capture reads continuously, through tunnel drops and beyond any one call, so its replication login is always the agent's own. Not done: locking the agent's copy in memory (mlock; memguard is not approved). No module added (HPKE is in Go's standard library and on Node's KEM). Tests: tests/utils/hpke.test.ts (sealing and opening, binding and tampering; interop with Go's crypto/hpke both ways), agent/internal/login (opening and binding to agent, connection and work; expiry outside and inside; another key; renewal keeping the key before; the password's unescaping; targets by name, wildcard, address, network and resolution), tests/services/agentLogins.test.ts (sealed for one agent and piece of work, opened only with its key, recorded; agents of another pool, revoked or keyless refused; agent custody stores nothing and records held_by_agent; the tunnel seals for the work it gives), tests/services/agentBinary.test.ts (the built agent reads through a cell-held login after renewing its key, refuses a target its host does not allow, and every use is in the ledger).
- D131 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A11: updates through Fleet; spec 10.7, 11.1, 11.2, 11.4, 10.9): Fleet is the only path by which an agent binary reaches an agent, and the agent trusts no cell for what it runs. Global tier: fleet-control's artefact store holds each agent binary by the SHA-256 of its bytes (`agent-binaries/<hex>`), put there by the build (`src/scripts/putAgentBinary.script.ts`, `npm run fleet:agent-binary`); an agent channel takes a release only once every binary it names is there and hashes right (`fleet.agent_binary_missing`); a cell's Fleet agent reads a binary in 4 MB parts (`readAgentBinary`). The cell's Fleet agent: fleet-control runs inside the cell with `FLEET_ROLE=cell_agent` (a service's needs may now depend on its configuration; this role opens no database). So far it pulls the cell's agent channel (agent-stable for a commercial cell) every `FLEET_AGENT_POLL_MINUTES` (15), checks the head and the release (both signed by the Silo release key, `FLEET_RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEY_FILE`; the head on this channel naming this manifest by id and digest; the target; the texts canonical), copies each binary into object-files at `agent-binaries/<hex>` hashing every byte, and installs the release in connect-runtime (`installAgentRelease`, callers fleet-control), which checks it all again, the stored binaries' bytes included, and keeps it (`connect.agent_releases`: the manifest and the head as the exact canonical text signed, so the agent verifies the same bytes without canonicalising anything). The rest of the Fleet agent (cell releases, migrations, gates, change policy) is phase 9. Waves (11.4): connect-runtime's rollout worker (every minute, every replica, one at a time by the running row's lock) starts a rollout for the newest release received (`connect.agent_rollouts`; a newer one supersedes it), over the agents of automatic pools: wave 0 Silo's own organisations (`CONNECT_AGENT_FIRST_ORGANISATIONS`), 1 a stable 5% of agents and 2 a further 20% (by a hash of the agent's id, `connect.agent_update_wave`), 3 all; each soaks `CONNECT_AGENT_WAVE_SOAK_HOURS` (24), and one with no agent to update or watch passes at once (`connect.agent_wave_size`). Gates, read every minute over the agents the rollout reached (`connect.agent_rollout_health`, counts only): heartbeat, an agent that took the release and has not come back on it within 30 minutes, or came back and stopped heartbeating within its first hour on it; error rate, an agent with at least 20 pieces of work since updating that failed more than 5% of them itself and more than twice its rate before (`work_done`, `work_failed`, counted by the tunnels and flushed with heartbeats; failures are internal errors and answers broken off, never a source's own refusal); and an agent refusing the release, or undoing it because it would not start. A failure halts the rollout, and every agent it updated is told to go back to the version before (`rollback`), which it does from the binary it kept. Offers (10.7): the agent asks `GET /v1/update` hourly over mutual TLS; a pinned pool takes its pin, an approval pool the version approved (`setAgentPoolUpdatePolicy`, `approveAgentPoolUpdate`, `agent.manage`, audited as `agent_update_policy_set` and `agent_update_approved`, not in chapter 77), an automatic pool the rolling release once the agent's wave started (else the last fully rolled out); a pin or an approval overrides the waves; a version named must be one the cell received and no older than any of the pool's agents runs (agents never download an older version). Only a later version is offered, and a pool's agents take it one at a time (the pool row locked; the next once the one before came back, or after 30 minutes). The agent downloads `GET /v1/update/binary/:sha256` (only a binary of a release the cell holds, for its own platform) and reports a refusal or an undone update (`POST /v1/update/report`). The agent (agent/internal/update): built with the Silo release keys (`-X main.ReleaseKeys`), it takes an update only when the head and the manifest carry valid signatures by those keys over the exact texts (a known key's signature that fails refuses outright), the head is on agent-stable and names the manifest (a release registered but never promoted is refused), the target and its platform's binary, version and digest match the offer, the version is later than its own and has not failed on its host, and the downloaded bytes hash to the digest. The installed binary is a launcher: `run` starts the agent as a child process (the update kept in `stateDir/bin`, 0700, if later than the installed binary and intact), restarts it onto an update it took (exit 75, after finishing work in hand for up to a minute), and undoes an update whose binary exits with a failure within two minutes, going back to the binary before and remembering the version as failed; the child stops when the launcher goes (its stdin closes). Versions (10.7): an agent heartbeating another version is recorded at once with `agent_updated` (from, to, direction); `agent_update_refused` records refusals and undone updates (both catalogued). An agent below the last three minor releases the cell has received is outdated (`version_outdated_at`), and refused 90 days later (`connect.flag_outdated_agents`, every tick): a refused agent gets no work and reads no captures, but may update; a version change judges it afresh. `listAgentReleases` (agent.view) shows the releases, the rollout and the floor. Sovereign: the sovereign agent takes no update through the tunnel; its releases come as bundles cleared staff countersign, which the on-premises Fleet agent will carry (phase 9). No Go module added. Tests: agent/internal/update (the release check against tampering, other keys, an unpromoted release, other targets, platforms and versions; version order; downloads kept only whole; the kept binaries and going back; the launcher's child); tests/services/agentUpdates.test.ts (a real fleet-control, the cell's Fleet agent and connect-runtime: binaries required before agent-stable; forged, unpromoted, altered and non-canonical releases refused; one at a time; pins and approvals; waves; the refusal, heartbeat and error-rate gates; going back; outdated and refused agents); tests/services/agentUpdate.test.ts (the built agent takes a promoted release over the tunnel and restarts onto it, undoes one that will not start, and refuses one a compromised cell forged).
- D130 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A10: discovery through the agent; spec 10.5, 19.1 to 19.4): a scan runs on the Silo Agent only on a scan discovery signs, and every step is checked where it happens. Signing: discovery signs one scan per run with its own Ed25519 key (`DISCOVERY_SCAN_KEY`; never the execution grant key, so neither signer can sign the other's), over `silo.discovery_scan.v1\0` and the scan's JSON text, as D129 does. The scan names the run, the organisation, the agent and the authorisation, carries the approved authorisation document as the exact canonical text whose SHA-256 the approvers quoted (discovery refuses to sign if the stored document no longer hashes to it), and must begin within five minutes; it runs once. Checking: connect-runtime checks it before giving it to the agent (`DISCOVERY_SCAN_PUBLIC_KEY`; `discovery.scan_refused` with the reason); the agent checks it again with the key the cell gave it at enrolment and renewal (`discoveryKey`), refuses a replay, and takes targets, methods, the host bound and the expiry from the document alone; the host's `discoveryDisabled` refuses everything. Refusals end the scan as `refused:<reason>`. Running: connect-runtime gives the agent `discovery.scan` work (the replica holding its tunnel; another replica passes the request on once, `relayed`); the agent runs host configuration (ODBC data sources, mounts, cron and named files, reporting only systems within the targets and never a credential, user, database name or command), catalogue introspection of the connections it holds credentials for (Postgres: a fixed compiled list of catalogue statements in a read-only transaction; planner row estimates; never a row), and a port scan with read-only identification (banners, Postgres's SSL request, SQL Server's pre-login, HTTP HEAD), at 50 new hosts a second, 2 connections per host, within the host bound and the expiry. OPC UA and MQTT are reported as unavailable until the industrial transports (chapter 20). Reporting: connect-runtime passes the agent's events to discovery in numbered reports (`reportScanEvents`): when 200 accumulate, at each finding, and at least every 5 seconds even when empty. discovery takes each with the run locked, in order and once (`report_sequence`), on whichever replica receives it: nothing about a run lives in one process, which replaces the in-process consumer. Each report is held to the authorisation as before (targets, methods, distinct-host bound in `connect.discovery_run_hosts`, value-like names refused), and its answer says whether to go on. Revoking or switching off stops runs in the same transaction, and the next answer tells connect-runtime, which abandons the work: the endpoint closes the agent's stream, and the agent's work context ends, so it stops within seconds. Probes the agent made before it heard are still logged. A run whose reports stop for two minutes (its agent, tunnel or replica gone) is ended by discovery's sweep as `agent_silent` (`connect.discovery_runs_silent`, cross-tenant through the function alone). Sovereign: the agent's discovery package is compiled out under the `sovereign` build tag (the binary carries none of its code, which a test checks), its heartbeat says discovery is off, and connect-runtime gives a sovereign agent no scan key. Tests: agent/internal/discovery (signature, binding and replay refusals; targets; identification; the bound, the rate and expiry; host configuration without credentials; catalogue introspection of a real database, structure only); agent/cmd/silo-agent (the sovereign binary has no discovery); tests/services/discovery.test.ts (reports taken once and in order, the bounds, a scan that cannot start, a silent run, revocation and the switch); tests/services/agentDiscovery.test.ts (the built agent scans through connect-runtime and discovery, refuses forged and replayed scans, and stops when its authorisation is revoked).
- D129 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A9: signed execution grants; spec 5.6, 10.4, 10.9, 17.1): a write through the Silo Agent runs only on a grant actions signs. No table: a grant is single use and lives five minutes. The grant (contracts/actions/grant.contract.ts) names the Action (a mutation, or a conformance run's write class), the organisation, the connection, the target (source object and statement count) and the payload's hash: SHA-256 of the statements' JSON exactly as the agent receives it. actions signs it with Ed25519 over `silo.execution_grant.v1\0` and the grant's JSON text, which travels as that text (with the key id and signature), so every checker checks exactly the bytes signed and no canonical form has to agree across languages. The hash is known before signing: connect-runtime's `prepareWrites` runs every check of `writeRecords` and renders the statements without sending them; actions' execute signs per connection plan and phase (the canary too); conformance's write class asks actions (`signSandboxWriteGrant`, conformance only, a connection not revoked or halted). connect-runtime checks the grant before the write leaves the cell (signature, key id, expiry, organisation, connection, object, statement count, hash: `write.grant_refused` with the reason). The agent pins the public key the cell gives it at enrolment and each renewal (`grantKey` in the enrolment answer; agent/internal/grant), and checks it again over the statements' raw bytes, refusing a replay; refused, it runs nothing and answers `grant_refused` with the reason, which the cell audits as `agent_write_grant_refused` (catalogued, read first). A granted write runs in one read-write transaction; a statement changing other than its expected rows, or any failure, rolls it all back. Keys: `EXECUTION_GRANT_KEY` (actions, PKCS#8 PEM) and `EXECUTION_GRANT_PUBLIC_KEY` (connect-runtime, SPKI PEM), from the deployment, required in production. Tests: agent/internal/grant; tests/services/writeback.test.ts (unsigned and mismatched refused before leaving the cell); tests/services/agentBinary.test.ts (the built agent refuses unsigned, mismatched and replayed writes, each audited, applies a granted one, and rolls back a row-count miss); actions and conformance write paths sign throughout.
- D128 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A8: store-and-forward; spec 10.6, 9.4, 10.8, 9.1): the agent's reader no longer writes to the capture stream; every change goes into a spool on the agent's host, and an uploader sends the spool up the stream in log order, so a dropped tunnel or a slow cell pauses only the upload ("CDC readers slow and spool"). The spool (agent/internal/spool): one queue per slot under the state directory, append-only segments, each opening with a random salt; a record's frame is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key derived (HKDF-SHA-256) from a host key (state dir, 0600) and the segment's salt, its index the nonce, so no key and nonce repeat even when every segment has gone; its header (log order, position, commit time, change count, spooled time) is authenticated and readable, never a value. A record that does not open (tampered, torn by a crash) ends its segment and is a gap record. Bounds: 10 GB and 7 days by default (30 for `airGapped`; `spoolMaxMb`, `spoolMaxDays`). At the size bound the reader waits, keeping its replication connection alive with status updates, because the source still holds what is unread; only when the slot is about to be invalidated (wal_status unreserved, or safe_wal_size under a quarter of max_slot_wal_keep_size, checked every minute on a connection of its own) may the oldest segments go, and Postgres then also hears what is spooled durably (synced each second), so the slot survives and that part of the spool is kept as the only copy (meta, reported as `cdcSpooled`). Past the age bound the oldest goes. What a dropped segment held unacknowledged is a gap record (counts and a commit-time range, no values). The cell receipts every record by its spool id (`cdc.ack` `received`), a part of a large transaction included, so a transaction larger than the spool passes through; Postgres hears only acknowledged positions (and, at risk, the spooled ones). Positions with no changes (empty transactions, keepalives) go up at most every 10 seconds, so the cell's acknowledged position keeps up; the recorded position never moves back. Readers outlive the tunnel; the heartbeat names the slots it reads (`cdcSlots`) and the spools holding what only they have (`cdcSpooled`), and the cell gives those slots back to that agent whoever held the lease meanwhile (`cdc_slots` taken over; the replication slot serves one reader). A reader resumes past what its spool holds; one that finds the slot already past the acknowledged position (another agent's spool held the rest) records a gap. cdc.stop drops a spool holding nothing only it has (the source re-sends the rest). Gap frames are audited (`agent_spool_gap`, connect event, catalogued), kept with the stream's health (redis-state `cs:` gains `gap_reason`, `gap_changes`, `gap_from`, `gap_to`, `gap_at`), shown in the stream status (`capture.lastGap`), and acknowledged (`cdc.gap_ack`). The capture lease is 30 seconds (9.1's pool failover). Logs carry the spool's size and gaps once a minute (10.8). Tests: agent/internal/spool (order, sealing at rest, receipts, reopening, both bounds, tampering, fresh salts) and tests/services/agentCapture.test.ts (with the cell down the agent reads on into its sealed spool, waits at a 1 MB bound through a 3,000-row transaction, and every change arrives once; a damaged spool is a gap record, audited and shown, with nothing the source holds lost).
- D127 (implementation 2026-11-17, Silo Agent stage A6: work across replicas; spec 10.3, 7.3): every cell runs at least three connect-runtime replicas, and the agent endpoint's load balancer sends each agent's tunnel to one of them. Each replica writes, with every heartbeat of an agent it holds, the agent's entry in redis-data `tun:` (the keyspace the design already named, now with `pool_id`, `relay_url`, `healthy` and `active_calls`: the calls the agent reported plus those its replica has given it), and removes it when the tunnel closes unless the agent has opened another meanwhile; a replica that dies stops refreshing, and its agents fall out within 30 seconds. connect-runtime now uses redis-data. Work goes to the pool's least-loaded healthy agent wherever its tunnel is: the agents held here, and the pool's agents with a tunnel (`connect.agents.tunnel_connected_at`) that other replicas list healthy, least loaded first, an agent held here first on a tie. One held elsewhere has the work relayed to its replica (`relayAgentWork`, connect-runtime to connect-runtime, at the replica's own address `AGENT_RELAY_URL`, normally `https://$(POD_IP):<HTTP_PORT>`; the service client's `replicaUrl` keeps the service's scheme and verifies TLS against the service's own name), which gives it to that agent only if it still holds it healthy (else `agent.not_here`) and answers with the result frames, a source's SQLSTATE intact, within the usual 8 MB response bound. Never queued (spec 10.6). A relay refused as `agent.not_here`, or a replica that cannot be reached, passes the work to the next agent (at most three tries), but a write (`sql.transaction`) only when it cannot have reached the agent (not here, or the connection refused), so a write never runs twice. A replica without `AGENT_RELAY_URL` publishes nothing and only relays. A registry that cannot be read leaves each replica giving work to the agents it holds. Tests: tests/services/agentRelay.test.ts (two replicas: relayed reads and refusals, least loaded across replicas, an entry its replica no longer holds and a replica gone, a write passed on only when refused, unhealthy and closed agents out of the choice).
- D126 (implementation 2026-11-16, Silo Agent stage A7: Postgres change data capture; spec 10.3, 10.4, 18.1, 18.2, 18.7): `connect.cdc_slots` gains `publication`, `acknowledged_at`, `lost_at`, `dropped_by` and the `dropping` status (the table section above). Setting it up (change-stream `setChangeCapture`, stream.enable, gateway `POST /connect/connections/:id/stream/capture`): the caller shows the slot name and the publication and sends them back with `confirmed: true`; one live capture per connection; the manifest's objects that stream from `cdc` must share one method, and only `logical_replication` is read today; the connection must be bound to an agent pool; `cdc_slot_created` names who confirmed. The lease (connect-runtime `agentCaptures.service`): on each heartbeat an agent renews its leases (a third of the way through a 60-second lease) and takes at most one more slot of its pool that no agent holds, up to 16, told `cdc.start` with the acknowledged position; a slot whose capture stream never opens, or ends, is given up and offered again, to another agent at once and to the same one after a wait that doubles to 5 minutes; a closed tunnel gives up all its agent's leases. The capture stream (`POST /v1/cdc/:slotId`, NDJSON): `started`, then `changes` frames, a committed transaction at a time (a large one in parts of at most 500 changes or about 1 MB, only the last carrying the position to acknowledge), and `lost`, `dropped` or `error` (the kind and SQLSTATE only). Each frame goes to change-stream (`reportCapture`, from connect-runtime) before the position is recorded on the slot, fenced by the lease, and sent down as `cdc.ack`; the agent tells Postgres only acknowledged positions, so the source keeps its log until Silo has the changes. A quiet publication holds no log back: transactions with nothing published and idle keepalives move the position on once everything sent is acknowledged. Decoding (the built-in decoder, spec 18.2): a row belongs to the streamed object whose SQL source is its schema (default `public`) and table and whose stream declares `cdc`; columns become fields (a field's column, else its name) read as reads read them; the identifier fields give the entity; each change's place in the log (16 hex digits of the commit LSN, `/`, its index in the transaction) is its source sequence, sorting as text in log order and never read as a number. Resuming never makes the slot again: a slot gone or invalidated (42704, 55000) is lost (`cdc_slot_lost`), the stream stale until a new capture is set up. Dropping (`dropChangeCapture`, stream.manage) marks the capture `dropping`; the agent reading it, or any agent of the pool, stops the reader and drops the slot (`DROP_REPLICATION_SLOT ... WAIT`, a slot already gone counting as dropped) and reports it (`cdc_slot_dropped`, naming who asked). Sources are used in the order webhook, change data capture, polling: capture while an agent reads it; a capture set up that no agent reads, or lost, shows the stream stale with the reason (no reader, no replication login on the reading agent, the source's refusal by SQLSTATE), and polling stands in where declared. A slot left without a reader still holds the customer's log; Postgres' `max_slot_wal_keep_size` bounds that, and a slot it invalidates is reported lost. End to end (tests/services/agentCapture.test.ts, skipped without a Go toolchain): the built binary reads a real publication with a replication login only it holds; deltas arrive in log order with declared fields only; the source lets its log go only up to the acknowledged position; stopping the agent leaves the stream stale and the restarted reader resumes with nothing lost or published twice; a slot dropped behind Silo's back is lost; an agent without the replication login refuses and the stream says why; dropping has the agent drop the slot.
- D125 (implementation 2026-11-16, Silo Agent stages A3 to A5: the Go binary, reads end to end, certificate renewal; spec 10.1, 10.2, 10.4, 10.7, 10.8): `agent/` is a Go module (go 1.27; pgx, pglogrepl), one static binary of about 11 MB for Linux x86-64 and ARM64 and Windows x86-64. `silo-agent enrol` makes a P-256 key that never leaves the host and enrols with the token; `silo-agent run` holds the tunnel (heartbeats every 10 s, one answer stream per piece of work, jittered reconnect, an HTTP CONNECT proxy, a TLS-inspecting proxy reported by the issuer it showed, stopping when revoked) and a loopback health endpoint. Its one configuration file may hold agent-held logins, so a file group or world can read is refused, and the health endpoint must be loopback. Reads: Postgres, in a read-only transaction (a write in a read fails with 25006), rows in frames to the bound, values as the cell's own Postgres reads give them (numerics as text, moments in UTC to the millisecond, a date as a date), a failure as its SQLSTATE only; writes are refused until signed execution grants exist. Logs carry counts, durations and outcomes, never a statement or value; crash dumps are off; memory is capped (512 MB by default). End to end (tests/services/agentBinary.test.ts, skipped without a Go toolchain): the binary is built, enrols, and answers connect-runtime's reads of a customer database through the executor. Renewal: the agent renews when less than 10 days are left (at 20 of 30) with a new key, over mutual TLS with the current certificate (`POST /v1/renew`); the cell gives the agent and its service principal the new fingerprint in one transaction, only while the old one is still theirs (`agent_certificate_renewed`), the live tunnel follows it, the agent reconnects with the new certificate, and the old one then opens nothing. A tunnel whose fingerprint another replica renewed is closed as replaced (the agent reconnects), not as revoked.
- D114 (implementation 2026-11-15, history over a time range; spec 69.16: "history questions, trends and time scrubbing read the history tables"): a plan may carry `history` (a period expression and the asker's words): one object type, no aggregate, no as-of, no node period, and the properties whose changes it lists selected on the root. The planner resolves the period on the organisation's calendar and answers from the Warehouse or refuses: the objects as they stood at the period's end (or at the Warehouse's last sync, for a period still running, stated as the period's end), each with every change in the period to a shown property from `<type>__history` (`readWarehouseHistory`; `changesBetween`), oldest first, with the value before and after. A period before the Warehouse's history began is refused (`query.history_unavailable`), one not yet begun too (`plan.history_future`); more changes than one answer may hold are refused, never truncated. The changes travel on each object in the result pages (record values), the period and its source in the result header (no values). A value the reader's field policy masks is masked in its changes, a redacted one withheld. Compile does not yet write as-of or history plans (both reach the engine as stored or structured plans).
- D113 (implementation 2026-11-15, SOAP writes and WS-Security; spec 14.4, 15.1, 42.5): a SOAP connector's write names its operation (`writes.<op>.soap`: action, operation, namespace, qualified, declared parameters); the engine builds the envelope from the parameters the manifest's JSONata gives (escaped element text, in the declared order; only declared parameters), sends it, reads a create's identifier from the response Body by the result expression, and fails a write on a Fault by its code. - D112 (implementation 2026-11-15, GraphQL mutations; spec 14.4, 42.5): a GraphQL connector's write names its mutation (`writes.<op>.mutation`: the root Mutation field, its typed variables, what it selects back); the document is printed from the manifest by graphql-js and holds no value, the values travelling as declared variables built by the manifest's JSONata (only declared variables are sent). Custom actions stay REST's. The registry checks each mutation's variable types parse.

No schema change.

A run reads no question: the findings are read as the Cron with no Lens, and its notification counts the findings raised since the last check, never values.
- D109 (implementation 2026-11-15, discovery's ontology proposals; spec 19.4): a promoted finding's structure reaches derivation whole. A connector manifest object may declare `uniqueKeys` (field sets the source declares unique); discovery writes a table's unique constraints there. Before, references were dropped.

A member's token charge that would be refused (`allowance_exhausted`, `no_allowance`, or `daily_limit_reached` with nothing purchased) asks billing's `autoTopUp` to buy the smallest number of hundreds that covers it (£20 per 100) on the subscription's payment method; metering records the purchase as automatic and the charge is tried once more, from the purchased balance. When billing cannot (no payment method, a declined card, the day's limit) the refusal stands, with its message extended and `autoTopup: failed` and the reason's code in its details. Also fixed: the onboarding grant (200 tokens, once ever) was given only when the balance row was first opened, so a member who bought tokens (or switched auto top-up on) before a seat never received it. `token_balances.onboarding_granted_at` (new) records when it was given; the grant is applied to an existing balance that has not had it.
- D107 (implementation 2026-11-15, seat counts synced with the payment provider; spec 72.2, 74.5): billing's `buySeats` (billing.manage) raises the self-serve subscription's quantity, prorated to the rest of the period and invoiced now; a released purchased seat lowers it to the seats still billable with no proration (no refund; the next invoice bills fewer), asked by auth after the release (`syncSeatCount`). - D106 (implementation 2026-11-15, provider cost per model route; spec 73.5, 74.4, 74.7): a model route may carry its provider's prices (`pricing`: pounds per million input tokens, and per million output tokens, thinking charged as output). - D105 (implementation 2026-11-15, Siloes at provider cost plus 10%, invoiced in arrears; spec 74.1, 74.2, 74.5): `billing.silo_charges` (new) holds one line per organisation, month, Silo and store, summed by billing's sweep from `storage_measurements` when the month closes (`billing.silo_charges_due` lists the organisations with a closed month to charge, or charges still pending). Per line: mean bytes held, bytes scanned and egressed, the provider cost of storage, compute and egress, the storage cost the entitlement's `storage_included_bytes` covers (`included_cost`: all of it while the organisation's mean held bytes, summed over its Silo stores, are within what is included; above that, each line's storage cost times included over held), the billed provider cost, the 10% (`uplift`, checked as `round(provider_cost * 0.1, 6)`) and the amount to the penny. A self-serve subscription's card is charged automatically; an Enterprise contract's invoice is sent with its payment terms and purchase order (the payment provider's `createUsageInvoice`, keyed by organisation and month, so a sweep that stopped part way finds its invoice); each line's description states the provider cost and the 10%. A shortened retention window lowers the next measurement, never a past one (measurements are insert-only).

The class runs per streamed object on an active connection (`startChangeStreamClass`, connector.verify or the owner; 202, read back as a conformance run with `classes_run = {change_stream}`): change-stream opens a probe on the object (redis-state, 15 minutes; the source in use, the watermark standing now), and conformance creates a test record, edits it twice and deletes it through connect-runtime's sandboxed writes. The state plane asks each source's mode again every minute and ends a subscription whose mode moved, so its viewer is told: Silo never moves a clone from live to polled unannounced. Also fixed: connect-runtime's request bucket holds at least one token, so a declared rate under one request a second still sends.

Each object type, property and link type on main has its names and description embedded (a link type, which has no description, by its two directions between its two types), with the hash of the text, through the model gateway's `embedTexts` on the cell's embedding route (Vertex AI text embeddings in the commercial cells, the self-hosted model's embeddings endpoint in the sovereign one; vectors of the route's dimensions, 1536, checked on every reply), screened as any prompt and recorded in `platform.model_calls` (`request_type = 'embedding'`, caller `ontology`).
